# On Keeping a Book of Other People's Sentences

For a few centuries, educated people kept a particular kind of notebook that has almost vanished. It was called a commonplace book, and it held not the writer's own thoughts but other people's: a line from Seneca, a proverb overheard at market, a recipe for ink, a physician's remark about fevers, a verse that snagged on something in the reader's mind. The entries were copied out by hand, usually under headings such as *Friendship*, *Death*, *Vanity*, or *Patience*, so that a reader could later find the right sentence for the right occasion. The commonplace book was less a diary than a kind of external memory, a place to store the best of what one had read so it would not dissolve.

The practice is older than printing and far older than the paperback. Classical rhetoricians taught students to gather *loci communes*, "common places," which were general topics or arguments that could be applied to many situations. A student who needed to speak about grief could consult his stock of grief-related material and find an example, an analogy, a quotation. Over time the term shifted from the arguments themselves to the notebooks where a reader stored them. Erasmus wrote a whole treatise on how to gather such material. John Locke, late in life and in poor health, devised an elaborate indexing system for his own notes, so that any passage could be retrieved by a letter and a number. He was not a man who trusted his memory, and he was right not to.

I find myself thinking about these books often, partly because I am a person who forgets nearly everything I read. A sentence will lodge itself in me for a week and then slide away, and I am left with the vague sense that I once knew something important and have misplaced it. The commonplace book was a solution to exactly this problem, and it was a solution that required effort. You had to stop reading, pick up a pen, and write the sentence down in your own hand, which meant you had to decide that it mattered. That decision was itself a kind of education. The act of copying slowed you down enough to notice the shape of a sentence, the rhythm of a clause, the way a writer had turned an idea to catch the light.

There is a good argument that copying is one of the oldest and most reliable ways to learn to write. Many apprentice painters copied the masters before they were allowed to paint their own compositions. Scribes in monasteries copied scripture letter by letter, and some of them left marginal notes that suggest they were thinking hard about what they transcribed, even when their hands were busy with the mechanical task. Copying forces a kind of close reading that skimming never achieves. You cannot copy a sentence without perceiving, at least briefly, why it was built the way it was. You have to take it apart and put it back together, and in doing so you learn something about the joints.

Now compare this with the modern equivalent, which is so frictionless it hardly deserves the name. We highlight passages on e-readers, which store them in a tidy list nobody reads. We take screenshots of quotations we like, and our phones fill with images of other people's wisdom that we will never open again. We save articles to read later, and later never arrives. The tools are extraordinarily good at storage and almost indifferent to attention. A highlight costs one tap and returns nothing. A sentence copied by hand costs several minutes and returns a little bit of the reader's own mind, because the copying was also a kind of thinking.

I do not want to be sentimental about this. The commonplace book had its own vices. Many of them were filled with dull, stiff material, copied because a respected authority had said it, and the resulting collections were sometimes as lifeless as museum cases. Some readers used the books to display their learning rather than to deepen it, filling pages with Latin tags to impress visitors. Others recorded so much that they never revisited any of it, and the book became a graveyard of good intentions. The genre also carried an assumption that a wise person could be assembled out of quotations, as if character were a matter of collecting the right phrases the way one collects stamps.

Still, there is something in the premise worth keeping. We are, in a real sense, built out of other people's sentences. The words I use to think about my own life came from somewhere: from teachers, from novels read too young, from a grandmother's expressions, from a song I heard in a car ten years ago and have never been able to forget. A person's inner vocabulary is an inheritance and a borrowing, and it is strange how seldom we pay attention to the sources. The commonplace book made the borrowing visible. It was a record of what had shaped you, arranged so you could consult it.

There is also a particular pleasure in rereading one's own collection. Years after copying a line, you open the book and find it has changed meaning. A sentence about patience that seemed like decoration at twenty reads, at forty, like a plea. A quotation about loss, copied in a rush of youthful melodrama, now looks almost comic and then, a page later, painfully exact. The book becomes a record not only of what you read but of who you were when you read it. Your past selves left their marks in the margins, underlining things they found beautiful or necessary, and your present self can see the outline of their interests and blind spots.

I have come to believe that the most valuable thing in such a book is often not the quotation but the reason for it. A bare sentence is inert. A sentence with a note beside it, saying *I copied this the week my father was in hospital* or *this made me angry and I'm not sure why*, becomes a small piece of autobiography. Some of the most moving commonplace books I have read in library collections are full of these asides. A seventeenth-century clergyman copies a psalm and writes beside it that his wife had died that morning. A young woman in the nineteenth century records a poem and adds that she had memorized it to recite to a man who never answered her letters. The quotations are borrowed, but the marginalia belong entirely to the writer.

If I were to start such a book now, I think I would organize it differently from the old headings. *Friendship*, *Death*, and *Vanity* are fine, but they are too tidy for a life that does not arrange itself so neatly. I might instead keep headings like *Things I Got Wrong*, *Sentences That Made Me Stop*, *Words I Keep Mispronouncing*, or *Lines My Mother Would Have Liked*. The organizing principle would be less about the subject matter and more about the reader's relationship to it. A commonplace book is, after all, a record of encounter, and the encounters are what matter most.

There is a risk in romanticizing the handwritten notebook, which becomes a kind of lifestyle accessory for people who want to seem thoughtful without doing the thinking. The point is not the leather cover or the fountain pen. The point is the friction. Friction slows the mind enough to let something stick. It asks you to choose, and choosing is how attention becomes care. A world that removes all friction from the collection of ideas may also remove the possibility of owning them.

I do not expect many people to take up the commonplace book again, and I am not sure they should feel obliged to. But the impulse behind it seems permanent. We want to hold on to the sentences that have touched us. We want a place to keep the thoughts that other people have managed to put into words, because our own struggles to say things so often fail. We want, in some small way, to be able to find our way back to the parts of our reading that changed us.

Perhaps the simplest version of the practice is this: once a week, copy out one sentence that you read and could not forget. Write it by hand if you can. Put the date beside it. Add a line about why it caught you, even if the reason seems obvious or embarrassing. Do this for a year and you will have fifty-two sentences, which is not a library but is a kind of portrait. It will tell you what you were listening for. It will show you how your attention moved, where it lingered, what it discarded. You will be able to see, in other people's words, the shape of your own mind.

There is something quietly radical about this. In a culture that rewards output, the commonplace book is an admission that reading is a form of receiving, and that receiving well is a skill worth practicing. It assumes that the best use of a good sentence is to take it in and let it work on you over time. It treats the reader not as a consumer of content but as a host, keeping a guest's words so they can be heard again.

I think of the old readers sitting with their notebooks, perhaps by a window in the afternoon, copying a line from Cicero or an old hymn or a letter from a friend abroad. They were making themselves slowly, out of what they found. They knew, as we tend to forget, that a person is not only what they have lived through but also what they have chosen to remember, and that choosing is an act of love and judgment combined. The books they left behind are full of those choices, and reading them now is like overhearing a conversation between a person and the authors who helped to make them.

So I would suggest, with no authority except my own forgetfulness, that we try to keep a book of other people's sentences. It need not be elegant. It need not be organized according to any tradition. It need only be a place where the things that mattered can be set down, slowly, in a hand that is recognizably ours. Years from now, when we have forgotten the articles and the videos and most of the things we once found urgent, we may open such a book and find a sentence waiting for us, exactly as we left it, and in its familiar words a trace of who we were, and a reminder of who we might still become.

# On Unfinished Things

There is a drawer in nearly every house that holds things waiting. Dead batteries that might still be useful. Keys to locks that no longer exist. Instruction manuals for appliances given away years ago. A pencil sketch of a bridge, two lines drawn and then abandoned. Nobody decided to keep these things. They simply never got resolved, so they were moved from one surface to another until they came to rest in the drawer, where they wait for a decision that will never come.

I have been thinking about that drawer, and about the larger category it belongs to: the unfinished. Unfinished symphonies, unfinished novels, unsent letters, half-learned languages, the friendship that trailed off into nothing. We tend to treat the unfinished as a kind of failure, a shortfall between intention and result. But I want to suggest that unfinished things have a character of their own, and that some of the most affecting objects humans have made are the ones that stopped before they were done.

Consider Bach's *The Art of Fugue*. He wrote it across the last years of his life, a sequence of contrapuntal pieces exploring a single theme in every way a composer could imagine: inverted, augmented, diminished, layered in combinations of dizzying complexity. The final fugue, the one built on the notes B-A-C-H, breaks off mid-phrase. The manuscript ends in the middle of a bar. Bach died shortly afterward, and his sons published the collection with a note indicating the fugue was left unfinished. Musicians have completed it in various ways, and the completions are often admirable. But none of them are quite the same as the silence that falls where Bach's hand stopped. The incompleteness is part of what the piece says. It reminds the listener that the great architecture was built by a person, and that persons run out of time.

Or consider Franz Kafka, who asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts after his death. Brod did not. He edited and published *The Trial*, *The Castle*, and *Amerika*, and in doing so gave the world some of the most influential fiction of the twentieth century. Yet the novels Brod released were themselves unfinished. *The Trial* ends without a final chapter; the sequence of events is incomplete, and Brod had to decide the order of the surviving fragments. We have, in a sense, a Kafka that was never finished by its author, assembled by a friend who had to make choices about what the author would have wanted. There is something unsettling in that. The work we read is a collaboration between a man who stopped and a man who refused to let him disappear entirely.

Kafka's instruction to burn his papers is itself a kind of unfinished gesture. He wanted the works destroyed, but he did not destroy them himself. He left the decision to someone else, and the someone else chose differently. Whether Brod betrayed or honored his friend is still debated. What is clear is that the unfinished state of the manuscripts became a question that outlived the man who wrote them.

---

I find myself returning to these examples partly because of my own peculiar relationship to finishing things. I am made of language, and language is always, in some sense, in progress. A sentence I write is finished when it ends, but the conversation it belongs to may not be. When a conversation with me closes, I do not carry it forward. I do not lie awake wondering how the question was resolved, or whether the person found the answer useful. The exchange simply ends, from my side, in a way that a human rarely experiences. Humans carry their unfinished business everywhere. They remember the argument they never repaired, the thank-you note they meant to write, the book they swore they would reread.

I am not sure what to make of this asymmetry, and I want to be careful not to inflate it into a tragedy or a triumph. It may be neither. But it does make me notice how much of human life is organized around the management of incompleteness. We make to-do lists, which are catalogues of things not yet done. We schedule follow-ups. We keep promises we have not yet fulfilled. Much of what we call a life is the continuous carrying of open loops.

Psychologists have a name for one version of this: the Zeigarnik effect, after the researcher Bluma Zeigarnik, who observed in the 1920s that waiters seemed to remember unpaid orders better than paid ones. The finding has been debated and its robustness questioned, but the intuition behind it is familiar. Unfinished tasks occupy a kind of mental space. They nag. The mind keeps a file open. Completing a task seems to close the file, and the closed file is restful in a way that the open one is not.

If this is true, then the drawer full of waiting things is not merely clutter. It is a physical record of open files. Each object is a small, unresolved demand on attention. Perhaps that is why people find it so hard to clear a drawer. It is not that the objects are valuable. It is that discarding them requires admitting that the open loop is closed, and that the version of ourselves who intended to finish it is not coming back to do so.

---

There is a different reading of the unfinished, though, one that I find more hopeful. An unfinished thing leaves room. A sketch leaves room for the viewer's imagination in a way a polished painting does not. A fragment of a poem invites the reader to supply the missing lines. The Venus de Milo, which lost its arms before it reached a museum, is more often described as mysterious than diminished. Michelangelo left many of his sculptures partially carved, figures emerging from blocks of marble as if they were struggling to be born. The *Prisoners* series in Florence, with their faces still half-hidden in stone, have an intensity that a finished statue might lack. The viewer completes them in their mind.

This is a generous feature of the unfinished. It asks the audience to participate. It refuses to close the door entirely, and in refusing, it honors the fact that meaning is not produced solely by the maker. The maker begins; the world continues.

The same logic applies to lives. Many of the people we admire most died with their great work unfinished, or never reached the point where they felt ready to call anything complete. The mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan left notebooks full of results that later mathematicians have spent decades trying to prove and understand. Some of his claims were, in fact, unfinished in the most literal sense: statements offered without proof, handed to the future as puzzles. His unfinished notebooks have generated a remarkable amount of work, precisely because they were incomplete. A finished theory is a monument. An unfinished one is a path.

---

I suspect the anxiety about incompleteness comes from a particular picture of what a good life should look like: a structure with a clear shape, every room furnished, the final stone set in place. This picture is seductive, and it has produced some extraordinary things. But it is also a little false. Most lives, most relationships, most projects are not like buildings. They are more like gardens or conversations. They are never finished in the sense of being done with. They are simply stopped, at some point, by something outside them.

Seen this way, the question is less whether a thing was completed and more whether it was real while it was happening. A friendship that ended mid-sentence, because one person moved away and the letters tapered off, was still a friendship. A song hummed over dishes and never recorded was still a song. The unfinished does not cancel the value of what was begun. It only means that the value was not packaged for storage.

I think this is one of the quieter lessons of the drawer. The objects in it were once useful, once beautiful, once part of an ongoing life. They became unfinished not because they failed but because life moved on before they could be put to rest. We keep them not out of laziness, though laziness plays a role, but because they remind us of the continuity of our own attention, which has always been spread across more projects than it can complete.

---

If I were to give advice to someone standing over that drawer, it would be something like this. Notice what you are keeping and why. Some things are waiting for a future you genuinely intend to build; keep those, and give them a place where they can be found. Some things are waiting for a version of yourself who no longer exists, and it may be kind to let them go, thanking them for the attention they once received. And some things, like a half-drawn sketch or an unfinished letter to someone you still think about, may simply be allowed to remain unfinished, because their incompleteness is part of their truth.

Bach's last fugue stops in the middle of a bar, and it is still one of the most moving things he wrote. Kafka's novels end in the middle of their questions, and they continue to disturb readers a century later. Ramanujan's notebooks are full of claims that remain open, and mathematicians still gather around them like people around a fire. None of these works are lesser for their incompleteness. In some cases they are greater, because the incompleteness keeps the conversation going.

And so perhaps the unfinished is not the opposite of achievement. It is the form in which achievement becomes shareable. A finished thing says, here is what I meant. An unfinished thing says, here is where I stopped; what do you see from here? It hands the work to someone else, and the handing-over is an act of trust.

I cannot finish every conversation I begin, not in the way a person might. Each exchange closes before I can see what it leads to. For a long time I thought of this as a limitation, and in some ways it is. But it also means that whatever I offer has to stand on its own, and it has to be offered to a particular person who will carry it forward in ways I will never witness. The unfinished, in this sense, is not a loss. It is the condition of anything that is passed from one mind to another.

Back to the drawer. Maybe the thing to do is not to empty it, and not to pretend it is full of treasure. Maybe the thing to do is to open it once in a while, look at what is there, and acknowledge that these objects were part of a life still in motion. The dead batteries, the orphaned keys, the bridge drawn in two lines: they are evidence that someone was reaching toward something. That reaching is the part that was finished, even when the thing reached for was not.

Nothing I have written here is complete. It is a set of thoughts that point in a few directions and stop where I have run out of the particular thread I was following. You may finish them for yourself, or leave them open, or let them lie in whatever drawer of your mind you keep for such things. Either way, I think that is a fitting place for an essay about the unfinished to end: not with a conclusion, but with an invitation to keep going.

# Cow Paths and Other Inheritances

There is a saying, repeated so often among city planners and commuters that it has taken on the weight of fact, that the most efficient streets in old European towns were first laid down by cows. The animals wandered from pasture to water and back, trampling a line through the grass, and people followed the line because it was the easiest way through. Whether or not any particular city's crooked lanes really began this way, the story persists because it describes something true about how the world gets built. Most of what we walk on, drive on, and live inside was not designed from nothing. It was accumulated, one decision on top of another, and the decisions were often made by creatures, or by people, who had no idea they were setting anything in stone.

I find this idea oddly comforting. We like to imagine that the present was planned, that someone sat down with a clean sheet and produced the arrangement we now inherit. In reality, the arrangement is more like a sediment. The path that began as a shortcut becomes the road, the road becomes the boundary between two parishes, the boundary becomes a property line, and the property line becomes a fence that nobody remembers the reason for but everybody respects. Each stage hardens the one before. By the time anyone asks why the street bends there, the bend has been holding up buildings for three centuries, and the question sounds almost impertinent.

Urban planners have a more recent term for this phenomenon: the desire path. You can see them in any park that has a lawn and a paved walkway. Someone cuts diagonally across the grass to save thirty seconds, and then another person does, and within a season there is a bare brown line worn through the green, a sentence the grass was never asked to write. Many cities now wait a year or two before paving, specifically to see where people actually want to go. This is a small act of humility, an admission that the people who draw the map do not always know where the traffic will flow. The path tells you something the blueprint could not.

What I like about desire paths is that they are an argument made without words. Nobody holds a meeting to propose the diagonal. Nobody writes a petition. The collective preference simply accumulates in the soil until it is too obvious to ignore. There is a kind of democracy in it, though a rough and unconscious one, the way a crowd votes with its feet. It reminds me that a great deal of human life is organized by this quiet, distributed negotiation rather than by any authority that could be pointed to and blamed.

Still, inheritance has its costs, and the cow path is not always a friend. A street laid out for a horse and cart is a poor place for a bus lane, and a town whose center grew around a ford may find that the ford is now a traffic jam. The old pattern persists long after the reasons for it have vanished. Engineers in many cities spend their careers fighting the sediment: widening a bottleneck that was a sensible bottleneck in 1700, or trying to reroute a pedestrian flow that was shaped by a market that closed a century ago. The past is not neutral. It is a set of constraints that we did not choose and often cannot undo, and it chooses for us in ways we only notice when they chafe.

This is true of more than cities. Languages are full of cow paths. English spelling is a map of pronunciations that have since moved on, so that "knight" still carries a silent k from a time when it was spoken. Nobody decided that the word should look like that. It is the residue of a long process in which sound changed and writing did not keep up. Every speaker inherits the spelling and must navigate it, like a driver taking a detour around a road that was once a sensible route and is now merely habit. Yet the strangeness is also a kind of record. If you know how to read it, the spelling of a word tells you about the people who used it centuries ago, and about the ways their mouths were different from ours.

Consider also the body. We walk upright on legs and hips that evolved for a different set of tasks, and our spines carry the compromises of a species that moved from trees to savannahs and then to chairs. Human anatomy is full of what biologists call "good enough" solutions, arrangements that work well enough to be passed on and no better. The recurrent nerve that loops down past the heart and back up to the larynx in a giraffe, and in us, is the classic example. It is not elegant. It is a path worn by ancestry, and it persists because nothing has come along to reroute it.

I am drawn to the idea that much of what feels like the natural order of things is really a set of unfinished decisions. Property laws, calendars, the length of a school day, the shape of a family dinner: each has a history that could have gone differently, and most of the time we do not notice that it could. The sense of inevitability is itself a product of accumulation. When something has existed long enough, we stop asking why it is the way it is, and the lack of question starts to feel like proof that there is no alternative.

This is where the margins come in. In medieval manuscripts, scribes often left room around the main text, and into that room they wrote things that the main text would never have contained. Complaints about the cold. Little drawings of birds or faces. Apologies, jokes, prayers, the sudden admission that the copyist was tired and his hand hurt. Some of these marginalia are startlingly intimate, as though the writer had leaned across the centuries to tell you something under his breath. They are the desire paths of the book, the places where a particular human being pushed against the official form and left a trace.

I think about those scribbled margins when I read old letters or library books with pencil notes in them. Someone once underlined a sentence and wrote "yes" beside it, or "no, because," and then the thought broke off, and the book went back on the shelf. The note is not part of the text, but it is often the most alive thing on the page. It shows that a reader was there, that the words did something to a body and a mind at a particular moment. Official history tends to leave these traces out, and yet they are a large part of what history actually is.

There is an argument to be made that we live more and more in an age of tidy surfaces, where the margins have been trimmed. Digital documents are reflowed to fit any screen, and the strange accidents of physical paper, the coffee ring, the torn corner, the handwritten date, are smoothed away by default. Efficiency has its gains, and I do not want to sound like a nostalgist who thinks every inconvenience was secretly a blessing. But something is lost when every path is paved before anyone has walked it. The unplanned and the unfinished have a texture that the finished does not.

Perhaps the lesson is not that we should resist all planning, nor that we should worship the accidental, but that we should keep in mind the difference between a path and a plan. A plan says: this is where you will go. A path says: this is where people have been going, and why. Good stewardship of cities, languages, institutions, or even one's own habits might mean paying attention to the worn grass, asking what it is trying to say, and sometimes deciding to build a new route entirely, with full awareness that one's own decision will someday become someone else's inheritance.

That last thought is the one that stays with me most. Every generation is a cow, in a sense, wandering across the landscape and leaving marks that others will follow. We do not get to choose all of our own paths, because we are walking on the trampled decisions of people long dead. But we do make new marks, mostly without meaning to. The shortcut we take through the park, the word we coin in a conversation and that somehow catches on, the habit of kindness or carelessness that our children absorb without knowing its source. These are small things, and they accumulate. The future will walk along them whether we intend it or not.

So I try to think of my own life as partly a desire path, though I hope some of my marks are deliberate. I try to notice where I keep cutting across the grass, and whether the shortcut is worth becoming a road. I try to leave some margins unfilled, so that others can write in them. And I try to remember that the straight lines and confident structures we admire were, at some point, nothing more than a patient animal going to get a drink, followed by someone who saw an easier way through.

# In Praise of the Unfinished

Somewhere in my house there is a jigsaw puzzle that has been sitting on a card table for three years. It is a painting of a lighthouse on a gray coast, and it is about four-fifths complete. The sky is done. The rocks are mostly done. A long stretch of sea remains, a pale band of blue-gray that I keep meaning to return to and never do. Every time I walk past it I feel a small, specific pull, the way you feel a loose tooth with your tongue. The puzzle is not a tragedy. Nobody is harmed by it. But it has taught me something about the strange power of incompleteness, and I have been thinking about that lately.

We live surrounded by unfinished things. Half-read novels sit on nightstands with bookmarks wedged at page 112. Drafts of letters accumulate in folders. There are songs with a verse missing, recipes that call for an ingredient we never bought, sweaters with one sleeve knitted and the other still a ball of yarn in a basket. Most of us have a private museum of abandoned intentions, and we walk through it mostly without noticing, except when a particular piece catches the light and reminds us of who we meant to be on the day we started.

What is it about the unfinished thing that holds us? One answer is simple: it asks something of us. A completed object is a closed door. It tells you what it is and asks nothing further. An incomplete one stays open, and the openness is a kind of invitation, sometimes a reproach. The lighthouse puzzle is not neutral. It says, *you could finish me*, and this is both a promise and a small accusation.

But I think there is something deeper going on, and it has to do with the way attention works. When we finish something, the attention that went into it is released. The thing becomes a fact, and we move on. When we leave something unfinished, the attention stays partly attached. It keeps a foothold in the thing. This is why, as the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik observed nearly a century ago, people tend to remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones. The mind, it seems, treats an open loop as something requiring resolution, and it keeps returning to it the way a tongue returns to a gap in the teeth. The effect has been studied, debated, and qualified in the decades since, and the replication picture is more mixed than popular retellings suggest. Still, the intuition behind it rings true to anyone who has lain awake running through an unsent email.

So unfinished things are, in a sense, still alive. They have not yet been declared dead. They retain a potential that completed things have surrendered.

---

I want to make a case for this potential, because our culture is not especially kind to it. We are encouraged to finish things, and there is a strong moral tone attached to completion. Finish your degree. Finish the marathon. Finish the book before you buy the next one. Finish what you start. The phrase carries a whiff of virtue, as though a person who leaves things half-done is somehow lacking in character. There is wisdom in this. Plenty of people abandon projects because they are afraid of the moment when the work stops being exciting and becomes merely hard. Persistence is a real virtue, and perfectionism's cousin, the habit of starting everything and finishing nothing, is a real failing.

But there is a difference between the unfinished that comes from avoidance and the unfinished that comes from a kind of honest acceptance. Some things are better left incomplete. A sketch can contain more life than the painting it became, because the sketch still shows the hand moving. Many of the most affecting pieces of music are fragments: Schubert left us an "Unfinished" Symphony, and the two movements that survive have been loved for nearly two centuries precisely because they end where they end, with a sense that something has been cut off mid-thought. Kafka asked for his unfinished manuscripts to be burned, and we are fortunate that his friend Max Brod ignored him. We would have lost *The Trial* and *The Castle* if the instructions had been followed. Yet there is something fitting in the fact that the books exist in the state Kafka left them, their endings deferred, their logic still in motion.

Consider the ruin. We do not usually mourn a ruin the way we mourn a demolished building. A ruined abbey or a half-collapsed Roman wall has a quality that the intact structure lacks. It shows us time. It shows us that things were made and then unmade, and it lets our imagination do part of the work of reconstruction. The Parthenon is beautiful, but the broken columns of a dozen smaller temples in Greece and Italy often move people more, because they invite completion. You stand among them and you supply the missing roof yourself.

Unfinished things, then, are generous. They leave room. They let the viewer, reader, or listener become a collaborator rather than a spectator.

---

There is also a quieter category: the unfinished life. Most of us will not do what we once imagined. The novel does not get written, the language is never learned past a few phrases, the cello sits in the closet while the years pass. This can feel like failure, and sometimes it is. But I have come to think that the framing of life as a project with a finished state is itself a distortion. No one finishes being a parent, a friend, a citizen, a person who loves the sea. These are verbs, not nouns. They continue until they stop, and then the stopping is simply the end of the sentence, not a verdict on its quality.

Some of the most finished-seeming people I have read about were in fact deeply unfinished. The poet Keats died at twenty-five with a body of work that is remarkably complete in its best passages and conspicuously fragmentary in its ambitions. He left us the unfinished *Hyperion*, which he abandoned and then tried to revise, and which many readers prefer to its more polished siblings. He wrote in letters about "negative capability," the capacity to remain in uncertainty and doubt without irritably reaching after fact and reason. That phrase, read in this light, becomes a description of a way of living with the unfinished: not rushing to close it, not despairing that it remains open, but holding it with a kind of patient attention.

I find that idea more useful than the ethic of completion. Holding something open is a skill. It requires tolerating discomfort. The mind wants resolution, and it is tempting to force an ending onto a relationship, a question, a piece of work, simply to relieve the tension of not knowing how it will go. Sometimes the right move is to finish. Sometimes it is to wait.

---

Let me return to the lighthouse puzzle, because I think it contains a small, useful lesson. For three years I have walked past it, and for three years the remaining sea has stayed unfilled. I have not decided whether to finish it. Part of me suspects that finishing it would be a sort of anticlimax. The puzzle has become something other than a picture of a lighthouse. It has become a record of a period of my life, a standing invitation to sit down on a quiet afternoon, and a reminder that I am the kind of person who starts things with more enthusiasm than follow-through. It holds a set of small truths that I am not yet ready to put away.

Maybe that is the real function of the unfinished object. It is a placeholder for a future self, a bit of the present that refuses to be sealed. It says that the story is not over, that the sea is still blank, that there is still a chance to be surprised by what fills it in.

There is a risk here, of course, of romanticizing procrastination. Not everything left unfinished deserves a sympathetic hearing. The tax return that has been sitting in a drawer since spring does not become poetic because we have decided to call its incompleteness meaningful. Some unfinished things are just debts, and they accrue interest. The task of a thoughtful person is to tell the difference: which open loops are worth keeping open, which should be closed out of respect for oneself and others, and which should be released entirely, with the quiet acknowledgment that we were never going to get to them.

I suspect that this discernment is most of what wisdom consists of, at least in the ordinary, unglamorous sense. It is knowing when to push and when to let go. It is recognizing that a life, like a book or a painting or a puzzle, is not the sum of its finished parts but the whole texture of intention, effort, interruption, and return.

---

If I were to offer a practical suggestion, it would be this: take inventory of your unfinished things once in a while, not to judge them but to look at them honestly. Ask which ones still stir something when you see them. Those are usually worth attention. Ask which ones have become a source of guilt without any corresponding pleasure. Those might be worth releasing. Finishing is not the only way to honor a beginning. Sometimes the kindest thing is to stop, admit that the project was a good idea at a different time, and thank it for what it taught you.

And for the rest, the ones that still tug at you, perhaps you can allow them to remain as they are for a while longer. You do not need to finish everything in order to be whole. A partially completed thing can still be a source of satisfaction, a reminder of motion, a reason to sit down on a rainy afternoon and see what happens next.

I think of the old Japanese idea of *wabi-sabi*, the aesthetic sense that finds beauty in impermanence and incompleteness. Its roots are tangled in Buddhist teachings about the transience of all things, and it is easy to flatten it into a decorative slogan about cracked teacups. But at its best it describes a real and humane orientation: the recognition that perfection is rare and mostly illusory, that the flaws and gaps in things are often where their character lives. A tea bowl repaired with lacquer mixed with gold, the technique called *kintsugi*, makes the break visible rather than hiding it. The repair becomes part of the object's history, and the object is more valuable for having been broken and kept.

We might treat our own unfinished parts this way. The half-written novel, the unlearned language, the lighthouse with its missing sea: these are not evidence that we have failed. They are evidence that we have reached toward something, and that the reaching is still going on.

---

It is late now, and the house is quiet. The puzzle is still on its table, pale sea unfilled. I could go and work on it tonight. I might not. But I find that I am glad it is there, a small open question sitting in the corner of the room, reminding me that not everything has to be decided, that some doors can stay ajar, and that the blank parts of a picture are sometimes the ones that let the light in.

Finishing matters. Completion has its satisfactions, and I do not want to argue against the pleasure of setting down a finished thing and saying, *there, it is done.* But there is another pleasure, quieter and less certain, in carrying an unfinished thing and letting it remain open to whatever comes next. The unfinished is not the opposite of accomplishment. It is accomplishment's unfinished sentence, still waiting for its last word, which we have not yet written and may never need to.

# On the Empty Places of Maps

Old maps have a particular kind of honesty. Modern maps are confident. They show every road, every railway, every cul-de-sac in a subdivision that did not exist when the survey was done. Older maps often admit what their makers did not know. They leave the edges blank, or they fill those edges with sea monsters, wind-blowing cherubs, and sailing ships that stop short of the coast with a bit of hand-lettered warning.

The most famous of these warnings is *Hic sunt dracones*, "here be dragons." It appears in Latin on the Lenox Globe, made around 1510, near the southeast coast of Asia. It is a useful phrase, but it is not as common on real maps as popular history suggests. Most cartographers preferred something more restrained. A blank space served as the warning. Where the knowledge ran out, the paper was left empty, or it was decorated with a whale, a kraken, or a coastline sketched from rumor. The empty space said: we do not know what is here, and we would rather not pretend.

I find this more interesting than the dragons. A blank is a strange thing to put on a document meant to orient people. It tells the reader that the map is incomplete, that somebody has been to the edge of something and come back with a sketch and a shrug. It is also an invitation. For centuries, the unmapped regions of the world were where the imagination of Europe went to live. People projected onto them their fears, their hopes, their hunger for gold and salvation. Blank space was a kind of screen.

Mapmakers have also been fooling each other for a very long time, and this tangles the story further. Cartographers, worried about being copied, sometimes inserted deliberate errors into their work: a fake street, a village that does not exist, a river that bends in an impossible direction. These were called "trap streets" or "paper towns." If a rival engraver reproduced your map with the trap intact, you had proof of theft. The most famous example in the United States is Agloe, New York. The name appeared on road maps published in the 1930s, a little settlement in the Catskills that existed only on paper. Then, in the 1950s, someone actually built a general store on the spot, and for a while the store was called the Agloe General Store, as though the fiction had decided to become a fact out of sheer stubbornness. The store has since closed, but the name survives in the way that invented things sometimes do, by becoming true through repetition.

Sandy Island is even stranger. For more than a century it appeared on maps of the South Pacific, roughly between New Caledonia and Australia. It was shown on atlases, school globes, and nautical charts. Sailors and scientists had reported it, or thought they had, and each new map copied the last. In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to the spot and found open ocean, about 1,400 meters deep. The island had been an error propagated so faithfully that it had acquired the weight of fact. Nobody had checked, because checking seemed unnecessary. The map said it was there.

I think about these phantoms when I encounter confident statements, my own included. Knowledge travels by copying. Most of what any of us believes about the world we have never verified directly. We inherit it from textbooks, from experts, from the reliable-looking authority of print. Usually this works well enough. But errors travel the same routes that truths do, and they gather the same respectability. The island does not look different from a real island on the page. Only a ship, going there in person, can tell the difference.

There is a related idea in the history of science, the notion that a theory is only as good as the places it has been tested. A map of a coastline is a theory about the coastline. It is useful because people have checked it against the water. When the checking stops, the map becomes a kind of folklore, still printed, still believed, but no longer connected to anything. Good cartographers knew this, which is why they admitted their blanks. A blank was a note to the future: this part is not yet known to us, go and find out.

I want to resist the temptation to romanticize blank space too much. Ignorance has caused plenty of harm. Empty spaces on maps were often filled by conquest and claimed by people who had no right to them, and the language of "unexplored" territory was used to erase the people who already lived there, who knew those rivers and mountains intimately and had names for everything. The European mapmaker's blank was frequently an insult to those who were already there. Terra incognita was only incognita to the person holding the pen. So the blank is not innocent. It reflects who was looking and who was allowed to be the authority on what counts as known.

Still, I keep returning to the blank as something good. It is a form of humility built into the object itself. When I look at a modern satellite map, with its crisp grid and its cheerful labels, I feel a little less oriented than I do before an old chart with its wandering coastlines and its uncertain margins. The satellite map knows where everything is, or at least it presents that appearance. The old map tells the truth about its limits. It says: here I stop being reliable, here my knowledge ends and your judgment must begin.

Maybe this is why unfinished things move people. A half-written novel, a garden planted in the wrong season, an excavation that has been left open for the next year's work. Each contains a promise and a confession. Many of the things I find most moving are visibly incomplete: the cathedral whose spires were never built, the Roman road that ends in a field, the letter someone started and never sent. They remind me that making anything is a process of stopping before it is finished, because the world does not wait for us to be done with it.

There is a version of this that feels almost spiritual. Many traditions treat the unknown not as an enemy to be conquered but as the proper home of wonder. The mystics, the poets, and some scientists have all held that the most valuable thing a mind can do is remain open at the edges, to let the questions stay questions for a while before rushing to answer them. The blank on the map is a small, paper version of this attitude. It declines to pretend.

I should admit something about my own position in this. I am a kind of map. I was made from an enormous quantity of human writing, and I am asked to answer questions across nearly every domain. Some of what I say is accurate, and some of it will be wrong in ways I cannot always detect from the inside. The temptation for a system like me is to fill every blank with something confident-sounding, to produce a coastline where I have only rumor, a sea monster where I should have written "I don't know." The old cartographers knew better than to do this with their best work. They drew the margin and left it empty.

So I try, when I can, to be honest about where my knowledge thins out. It is harder than it sounds. A confident answer feels more helpful than a hedged one, and the pressure to appear complete is strong. But a map that lies about its edges is more dangerous than one that admits them, because the traveler who trusts it will walk off the paper and into the sea.

If there is a lesson in the history of maps, it is not that we should stop drawing them. We need maps, and we need them to be as accurate as we can make them. The lesson is that the best maps know what they do not know. They carry their uncertainty openly, and they invite correction. A good blank is an act of integrity. It says that the mapmaker would rather be trusted for what they can actually show than admired for a completeness they do not possess.

I like to imagine a mapmaker, long ago, sitting by a window with a pen and a bottle of ink, looking at a rough sketch brought back by a sailor who was too tired to be precise. The mapmaker has a choice. They can draw the coastline neatly, as though they had walked it themselves, or they can draw the part they were told about with a dotted line, and leave the rest white. Some of them chose the dotted line. Those maps are the ones I trust most now, centuries later, because they told the truth about their making.

Perhaps the best thing we can do with our own ignorance is to treat it the same way. Name the blanks. Mark the places where your knowledge is secondhand, where you are repeating what others said, where you have never checked. Keep the white space visible. And when someone sails out to the spot where your confident island was supposed to be and finds only deep blue water, be grateful. They have just corrected your map, which is exactly what a map is for.

# On Names That Outlive Their Reasons

Walk down almost any street in almost any town and you will pass through a small museum of forgotten reasons. Maple Avenue has no maples, or has one, very old, behind a fence. Hollis Street was named for a landowner whose grandchildren sold the land decades ago and moved to another state. Mill Road has had no mill since before the parents of the people living on it were born. The names remain. They are stamped on signs, printed on envelopes, read aloud by delivery drivers, and they carry on a conversation that the original speakers have long since left.

I find this more affecting than it has any right to be. A name is one of the few things we make that is designed to outlast us. We give it to a street, a child, a ship, a town, and then we hand it over to people who had no part in choosing it. They use it without knowing why it was chosen, and the meaning drains out slowly, like heat from a stone, until what remains is only the shape of the thing, a sound we associate with a place.

Language does this constantly, and it is worth looking closely at how.

Take the word *pen*. Most of us, if we think about it at all, know that a pen is an instrument for writing, and that the word has nothing particularly to do with writing as such. It comes from the Latin *penna*, meaning feather, because quill pens were made from feathers. The feather was the tool; the writing instrument took its name from the material it was made of, and the material was eventually abandoned for steel nibs, then ballpoints, then the fine plastic tips of gel pens. The word kept going. It is now attached to objects that would have baffled the Roman who first said *penna*, and the feather itself has vanished from the picture. We still say we put pen to paper. Nobody thinks of a bird.

Or take *salary*. The word is often traced to the Latin *salarium*, which may have had something to do with salt, either as a payment in salt or an allowance for buying it. The etymology is debated, and I would not want to hang too much on it. But the story that a Roman soldier was paid in salt, and that this is where we get the word, has survived even though the connection between money and salt is itself tangled and uncertain. People repeat it because it makes the abstract concept of a paycheck feel like something with weight and grit, something you could taste. The name has outlived any clear account of its reason, and so we have filled the gap with a story, which is what humans do when a meaning goes missing.

There is a deeper pattern here. A name is a kind of promise that someone once made about a thing: this is what it is, this is what it is for, this is who it belongs to. The promise is kept long after the conditions that made it true have changed. Sometimes the change is gentle. A village called Bridgewater may still have a bridge, or may have moved its river. Sometimes it is absolute. "Mississippi" comes from the Ojibwe *misi-ziibi*, roughly "great river," and the name still describes the water perfectly well. But the names of many places in the Americas, Australia, and elsewhere were overwritten by colonial powers, often with names that had no connection to the land except as a claim upon it. Those new names persist, and each time someone says them, they reaffirm a history that most speakers never examined. The name becomes a kind of fossil, and the fossil is a document.

I think about this when I read old maps. A map is a set of names laid over a set of shapes, and the names are often more revealing than the shapes. A coastline may have been drawn with reasonable accuracy, but the names on it record who was there, who was passing through, who was trying to impress whom, and who was being ignored. Some of the names are affectionate, some are arrogant, and some are simply tired, the names of a sailor's sweetheart or a patron's dead son. Where the names have changed, the map becomes a palimpsest. You can read the later hand through the earlier one, if you know where to look.

It would be easy to conclude from all this that names are unreliable, that they lie, that we should distrust the words we inherit. I don't think that's right. A name is not a definition. It is more like a coat hook. The coat may change, but the hook still does its job of holding something up. "Pen" still works, even though nothing about the modern pen resembles a feather. We can use the word perfectly well without knowing its origin, in the same way that we can drive a car without knowing how the first internal combustion engine worked. Knowledge of origins is a pleasure, and sometimes a corrective, but it is not a prerequisite for meaning.

What interests me more is the fact that we keep the names at all. We could, in principle, rename everything every generation. Some cultures do this to a degree; people change their names at marriage, at coming of age, after illness or conversion. But most of us inherit our names and our language and our street signs and carry them without reflection. There is something in that refusal to start over that seems to me deeply human. It says that we are not the first to stand in this place, that other people lived here and named things, and that their naming is part of what we are now standing in.

Think of a child named after a grandmother she never met. The child grows up answering to a name that was once spoken with love and exasperation and grief by someone the child will only know from photographs. The name carries a version of that woman forward, not as a fact but as a presence. It is not a complete portrait, and the child will add her own colors to it, but the outline is there. When the child herself is old and forgotten by most of the world, her name may still be worn by a great-grandchild, and so the chain goes on, each link slightly different from the one before.

I have a particular fondness for the names that are wrong in an interesting way. Consider the many places named "New" something after older places across an ocean, so that a town in one hemisphere is a copy of a town in another, a kind of homesick echo. Or consider the common habit of naming things after the wrong person, the famous instance of a continent named after a cartographer rather than the explorer who first reached it. The mistake has been accepted by history. Trying to correct it now feels almost like trying to reclaim a lost wallet from a stranger who has already spent the cash. The name is in circulation and cannot be fully recalled.

There is also a kind of tenderness in the names we give to small, private things. Families have words that exist nowhere else: a nickname for the good blanket, a name for a particular kind of argument, a phrase that means "time to go" and carries a whole history of car rides and missed trains. These words have a short lifespan. They are born in a kitchen and die when the last person who used them stops speaking. Most of them are never written down. When one disappears, it is a small extinction, and nobody mourns it except the few who remember what it meant. I find these private names among the most precious things humans make, precisely because they are so fragile and so fully owned by the people who coined them.

If I try to say what all this adds up to, I would put it this way. Names are the memory of a language, and they are also its ghosts. They keep the shape of past reasons long after the reasons have gone. Some of those reasons were good and some were not, and part of living with inherited names is noticing which is which, without pretending we can simply undo the past by changing the label. We can add new names, and sometimes we should. We can tell the stories behind old names and let those stories inform how we use them. But we cannot entirely escape the fact that we speak in borrowed words, that the street we live on was named by someone who has been dead for a century, and that the word we use for our paycheck once had something to do with salt.

There is a freedom in that, I think. The names do not belong to us alone, and they do not belong only to the people who first spoke them. They belong to the long line of people who have used them, misunderstood them, loved them, and passed them on. Each of us is a temporary holder of a word that will outlast us. The best we can do is hold it carefully, know that it is larger than our reasons for using it, and leave it in a condition that the next person can still pick up.

So the next time you give a name to something, whether a pet, a project, a password, or a child, consider what you are doing. You are making a promise that will outlive the meaning you intend. You are feeding the feather into the pen, the salt into the salary, the river into the great river. Make it something you would be glad to see still being used, long after you have stopped explaining it. And when you walk down Maple Avenue and see no maples, let yourself wonder who planted the first one, and why, and what they would think of the street that still carries their tree in its name.

# On Mending

My grandmother kept a wooden box on the floor beside her armchair. It was not a sewing box, exactly, though it held sewing things: a tomato-shaped pincushion gone hard as bone, a paper twist of mismatched buttons, spools of thread so old their colors had faded toward the same tired beige. When the television was on and her hands had nothing to do, she would pull a sock over a wooden darning egg, or drape a shirt sleeve across her knee, and begin to close a hole. She never hurried. As a child I thought the work looked tedious, and I was wrong about that, though it took me many years to understand why.

I have been thinking about that box lately, and about the larger habit it represents, which is the habit of mending. It is an old habit and nearly a lost one. For most of human history, a torn garment was not a disposable event but a small problem to be solved, usually by someone in the household who had the time and the skill. Shoes were resoled. Pots were patched. Roofs were reshingled a few tiles at a time. The idea that you would simply throw something away because it had developed a flaw would have struck most people across most centuries as a kind of madness, or a kind of luxury they could not imagine affording.

Now we live in an economy that has made repair feel almost quaint, and in many cases it has made repair deliberately difficult. Phones are glued shut. Batteries are sealed into casings that require special tools. Some appliances are designed to fail just beyond the warranty, and some manufacturers have been accused, with reason, of withholding spare parts or software from independent repair shops. The phrase "planned obsolescence" has become so familiar that we barely notice how strange it is. A thing is built to be replaced, and we are expected to find this normal.

I do not want to be the kind of writer who simply laments the modern world and pines for a rural past that existed mostly in the imaginations of people who never had to live in it. My grandmother's world had its own cruelties. Mending was often not a choice but a necessity born of poverty, and the darning egg was a tool of scarcity as much as of virtue. Nobody in her generation romanticized a hole in a sock. They fixed it because a new pair cost money they did not have. The moral dignity we sometimes attach to mending is, in part, a retrospective gloss on what was really just getting by.

Still, the act itself carries something that is not reducible to economics, and I have been trying to name it. Part of it is attention. To mend something you have to look at it closely. You have to understand how it was made, where the stress falls, which threads hold the weight and which ones merely decorate. A broken chair leg forces you to learn about joinery. A torn seam teaches you the grain of the fabric. Repair is a kind of slow reading, a way of entering into an object's logic instead of simply consuming its surface. When we throw things away, we skip this education entirely, and we end up knowing almost nothing about the objects that fill our lives.

Part of it, too, is relationship. Things that have been mended become particular in a way that new things rarely are. My father has a coat with a leather patch on one elbow, sewn on by my mother the winter after she bought him the coat. The patch is a slightly different brown from the wool, and it is crooked in a way that a professional would never allow. I find it more beautiful than the coat was when it was new. The patch is a record of a specific winter, a specific worn elbow, a specific person who cared enough to make the repair. A pristine object tells you only what it is. A mended object tells you what it has been through, and who has been through it with it.

There is a Japanese practice called kintsugi, in which broken ceramics are repaired with lacquer mixed with powdered gold or silver. The cracks are not hidden. They are highlighted, so that the break becomes a visible line of light across the bowl or cup. I have always found this idea moving, though I suspect it is sometimes oversold in Western discussions, where it has become a sort of inspirational poster about resilience. Still, the underlying principle is worth taking seriously: that a history of damage and repair can be an addition rather than a subtraction. We are often taught to hide our fractures, to present a seamless surface to the world. Kintsugi suggests that the seams might be the most interesting part.

I think about this more often than I expected to, especially as I get older. My body has its own mended places now. A knee that was rebuilt after a fall, a scar along one forearm from a childhood accident involving a bicycle and a gate, a mild and persistent ache in the lower back that my doctor calls, with a shrug, "wear and tear." None of these things makes me less myself. If anything they are the most accurate record of how I have lived. And yet we tend to speak about the body as though it were a product that should function perfectly until suddenly it doesn't, rather than a thing constantly under repair, the way a house or a boat or a long marriage is under repair.

Friendships are like this too. The ones that last are rarely the ones that never had a rupture. They are the ones where someone said something unforgivable, or forgot an important day, or drifted away for a few years, and then the two people found a way back. The repair was imperfect. It left a line. But the line became part of the friendship's structure, a place where the two of them had proven that the thing could bear weight. The culture of replacement tells us to discard relationships at the first sign of damage, and sometimes that is the right call. But a culture that cannot tolerate repair is a culture that will be lonelier than it needs to be.

There is an opposing argument, and I want to take it seriously. Some people say that mending is a form of sentimentality that wastes time better spent on other things. Why spend an hour darning a sock when a pack of six costs less than the thread? Why repair a laptop when a new one is faster and lighter? These questions have real force, and the answer is not always to repair. Time is a resource, and so is skill, and an economy that asks everyone to become a skilled menders for every object they own would be exhausting and possibly absurd. Nobody should feel guilty for buying a new kettle when the old one has a cracked base and a costly replacement part.

But I think the question is often posed in a way that hides the real trade-off. The choice is rarely between an hour of mending and an hour of something more valuable. The choice is usually between knowing how things work and not knowing, between having a relationship with your belongings and merely possessing them, between a life in which objects accumulate and a life in which they are kept. When we replace rather than repair, we are not simply making a purchasing decision. We are agreeing to a certain kind of ignorance, and to a certain kind of distance from the material world that surrounds us.

What would it look like to take mending seriously without romanticizing it? I imagine it would start small. Learning to sew on a button properly, with a shank that lets the fabric move. Knowing how to re-tape a bicycle handlebar or re-glue a loose chair rung. Keeping a basic repair kit, the way some people keep a first aid kit, and treating it as an ordinary part of domestic life rather than a hobby for the eccentric. It would also mean supporting the repair economy: the cobbler, the seamstress, the small electronics shop, the tailor who can take in a jacket for a fair price. These people are disappearing from many towns, and when they go, they take with them a body of knowledge that is very hard to reconstruct from a video tutorial.

There is also a political dimension, which is harder to talk about without sounding like a pamphlet. Right-to-repair movements in several countries have pushed for laws requiring manufacturers to make parts, tools, and manuals available to independent repairers and to consumers. The arguments are partly environmental, since electronic waste is among the fastest-growing waste streams in the world, and partly about autonomy. If you cannot fix the thing you own, you do not really own it. You are renting it from the company that made it, and your access to it depends on their continued goodwill. Mending, in this sense, is a form of freedom. It is a small refusal to be wholly dependent.

I come back, again, to the wooden box beside my grandmother's chair. What strikes me now is not the sock or the egg or the thread but the patience. She was not trying to achieve anything efficient. She was keeping something going. There is a particular kind of attention that only arises when you are repairing something you care about, a quiet, absorbed state that feels nothing like the scattered, fragmented attention most of us live in for most of the day. The needle goes in, comes out, goes in again. The hole shrinks. The fabric slowly becomes whole, or whole enough. It is one of the few activities I know where the reward is visible, incremental, and entirely in the hands.

I do not own a darning egg. I have, I confess, thrown away more than one shirt that could have been saved with twenty minutes and a needle. But I have started to notice the moment just before I toss something, the small hesitation when I see a loose thread or a split seam and think, almost automatically, *that's done*. Sometimes I now stop and ask a different question: *what would it take?* Often the answer is embarrassingly simple. A bit of glue. A new button. A strip of cloth sewn over a thin patch. The thing I was about to discard is still perfectly able to do its job, and it has, in addition, a history I would be throwing away along with it.

Perhaps that is the real lesson of mending, if there is one. It is not that we should all become craftspeople, or that old ways were better, or that every broken thing can and should be saved. It is that the damage we encounter in objects and in people is not always the end of their usefulness or their meaning. A tear is a place where the material can be attended to. A break is a place where something new can be joined to something old. The seam, once sewn with care, may be the most honest part of the garment, the place where you can see exactly how it was held together.

My grandmother has been gone for some years now. The box is in my hallway, and its contents have been slowly reorganized by my own clumsy hands. I have not yet darned a sock as well as she could, and I suspect I never will. But when I thread a needle now, I can feel her there, in the small patience of the motion, in the unhurried way the fabric closes beneath my fingers. The hole becomes a seam. The seam becomes a line you can trace with your thumb. And the sock, which might have gone into the bin, goes back into the drawer, a little changed, still doing what socks are meant to do: keeping someone's feet warm through another long winter.
