# On Unfinished Things

Somewhere in my apartment there is a jigsaw puzzle that is missing eleven pieces. It has been missing them for about six years. The picture is a harbor town in Portugal, all blue doors and washing lines, and I have reached a state of peace with the gaps. Sometimes I walk past the card table where it sits, under a sheet of cardboard I never bothered to replace, and I notice that the sky is complete and the bottom-left corner is a fog of loose cardboard. I don't feel guilty about it anymore. I feel something closer to fondness, the way you might feel about a friend who never quite got around to becoming the person they planned to be.

I have been thinking about unfinished things for a while now, and I have come to suspect that they make up a much larger share of the world than we admit. Our houses are full of them: the half-painted wall, the drawer of cables for devices we no longer own, the cookbook with one recipe bookmarked and never attempted. Our inboxes hold drafts of replies. Our phones hold photographs of books we meant to read. Most of us carry around a private archive of abandoned intentions, and we rarely look at it directly, because looking at it feels like being scolded by a version of ourselves who had more time, more discipline, or simply more faith that tomorrow would be as available as today.

Yet the unfinished has its own strange dignity, and history is kinder to it than we are to ourselves.

Consider Franz Schubert's Symphony No. 8 in B minor, the one we call the *Unfinished*. He began it in 1822 and wrote two complete movements and a fragment of a third, a few dozen bars of scoring, and then he set it aside. He lived six more years and wrote a great deal of music in that time, including other symphonies, but he never returned to this one. Nobody knows exactly why. Perhaps he lost interest, perhaps he was ill, perhaps he sensed that the piece had said what it needed to say in those two movements. What we have is haunting precisely because it stops. The cello melody in the first movement rises and falls with a tenderness that seems to be asking a question, and the silence after the second movement feels less like an absence than a held breath. If Schubert had finished it, we would have a good symphony. Because he didn't, we have an object lesson in how beauty can live inside incompleteness.

Or consider Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família in Barcelona, which has been under construction since 1882 and is still not finished. Gaudí himself knew he would not see it done. When he died in 1926, struck by a tram while walking to a service, only a fraction of the structure existed. Architects and craftspeople have been working on it ever since, using digital models, computer-controlled stone cutting, and the original plaster models Gaudí left behind, some of which were damaged in the Spanish Civil War. The completion date keeps moving, now pegged loosely to the centenary of his death. Tourists queue for hours to walk through a building that is, by any ordinary definition, a ruin in progress. And yet nobody I have ever met has said the cathedral would be better if it were already done. The scaffolding is part of what it is. The cranes against the skyline are part of the story.

Japanese aesthetics have a name for this kind of value. Wabi-sabi is often translated as an appreciation of imperfection and impermanence, of things that are weathered, asymmetrical, incomplete. It is easy to turn it into a lifestyle slogan, a reason to buy rustic ceramics and feel virtuous about it, but at its root it is a fairly sober philosophy. Nothing lasts. Nothing is finished, because finishing is a fiction we tell ourselves on the way to the next thing. The tea bowl with a chip in its rim is not a failed tea bowl; it is a tea bowl that has been used, handled, lived with, and the chip is simply the record of that living.

There is an even more literal version of this idea in kintsugi, the practice of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold or silver. Rather than hiding the cracks, the repair makes them the most visible and luminous feature of the vessel. The break becomes part of the object's biography rather than a shameful secret to be disguised. I find this image almost painfully useful. So many of us treat our unfinished or broken parts as things to conceal, and we spend enormous energy maintaining a surface of completion. Kintsugi suggests a different strategy: let the seam show, and fill it with something precious.

I want to be careful here, because there is an easy sentimentality in all this, and I am not sure I trust it entirely. Plenty of unfinished things are simply unfinished because someone gave up, or was never capable of finishing, or was too afraid of the verdict that finishing would deliver. The novel that stays in a drawer for thirty years might be a masterpiece or might be mediocre, and the not-finishing protects the writer from knowing which. There is a particular kind of cowardice that dresses itself up as artistic openness. I have done this myself, many times. I have told people I was "still working on" something when what I was actually doing was avoiding the moment of judgment that would come when I showed it to anyone.

So the unfinished can be a refuge as well as a gift, and it is worth asking which one we are living in. Kafka famously asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts after his death. Brod did not, and we have *The Trial* and *The Castle* and the diaries, which are among the most important works of twentieth-century literature. We can be grateful for Brod's disobedience. But it is worth noticing that Kafka's own unfinished works were, in part, an expression of his self-doubt and his fear of exposure. The books he left incomplete carry a weight of anxiety that is inseparable from their power. Their brokenness is beautiful, but it is also a wound, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

Dickens died in 1870 with *The Mystery of Edwin Drood* only half complete. Scholars have spent more than a century arguing over who did it, how it would have ended, and whether the murder victim is actually dead. There are whole books, competing theories, even stage adaptations that choose different endings and invite the audience to vote. The unfinished novel has become a kind of parlor game, a puzzle with missing pieces that generations of readers have been happy to fill in with their own imaginations. In a way, Dickens gave us a gift he never intended: the chance to be co-authors of his last book, however unwillingly.

Maybe this is the real secret of the unfinished. When something is complete, it closes a door. It says: this is what it is, take it or leave it. When something is incomplete, it leaves the door ajar, and the person encountering it has to step through and participate. The half-finished song invites you to hum the rest. The gaps in the jigsaw puzzle make me look more closely at the pieces I do have, and at the blue doors and washing lines, and at the particular way the light falls on the harbor. The puzzle's incompleteness has made me a more attentive viewer of an image I would otherwise have glanced at and dismissed.

There is also the matter of time, which is the true reason most things are unfinished. We live with a finite number of hours, and we are constantly choosing among competing possibilities, most of which we will never pursue. Every unfinished project is a record of a choice, a decision to spend the afternoon on something else, or a realization, often painful, that the project was not the right one after all. The pile of abandoned hobbies in a closet is a map of who we tried to become and the paths we discovered were not ours. Seen this way, unfinished things are less like failures and more like sediment, layers of attempts that compose the strata of a life.

I think about my grandmother, who knitted constantly and never finished anything she didn't need. Her closet was full of half-made sweaters in colors that were out of fashion by the time she set them down, balls of yarn tied to needles with the stitches still on. My mother used to say it drove her crazy. But when my grandmother died, we found a half-finished blanket on the couch, its pattern a series of soft diagonal bands, and it was clear she had been working on it that same week. The blanket was not finished, and it was not meant to be finished in the sense of being sold or displayed. It was simply the next thing in a long sequence of next things, the working-out of an attention that lasted until it didn't. My mother kept it. It is unfinished, and I cannot imagine it any other way.

What, then, do we owe our unfinished things? I don't think we owe them completion. Some should be finished, and some should be quietly let go. The discipline lies in telling the difference. But I think we owe them honesty. We owe them the admission that we began them for reasons that mattered to us, that we are not always the people we were when we started, and that the gap between intention and execution is not a moral failing but a condition of being finite. We can keep the puzzle on the table, or we can tip the pieces back in the box. We can leave the symphony at two movements and treat the silence as its own kind of music.

I also think there is some freedom in accepting incompleteness as a general condition. The house is never finished. The career is never finished. Relationships are never finished, not in the sense of reaching a final state that requires no further attention. We are, all of us, perpetually under construction, like the cathedral in Barcelona with its cranes and its scaffolding and its endlessly postponed completion date. This can feel like a burden, but it can also feel like permission. You do not have to be done to be worthy of being looked at. You do not have to resolve every question before you are allowed to speak.

Schubert did not finish his eighth symphony, and it is one of the most loved pieces of music ever written. Gaudí did not finish his cathedral, and it is one of the most visited buildings in Europe. Kafka wanted his work burned and it survived anyway, partly because someone disobeyed him. Dickens died mid-sentence, so to speak, and generations of readers have been arguing about the ending ever since. None of these works is diminished by its incompleteness. If anything, the incompleteness is part of what makes them feel alive, because they still seem to be in motion, still open to the people who encounter them.

So I will leave the puzzle where it is, with its eleven missing pieces and its fog of loose cardboard in the corner. It is a small thing, a domestic failure of no consequence. But it has taught me to look at what is there rather than fixating on what is absent, and to find in the gaps a kind of invitation. Somewhere, I suppose, the eleven pieces are still in the world, under a couch cushion or in a neighbor's recycling or lodged in the vacuum cleaner. They may never turn up. The picture of the harbor town may remain forever a little bit broken, and I find I can live with that. Some things are better unfinished. Some things are only ever unfinished, which is not the same as being wrong.

# The Streets That Aren't There

Somewhere in the history of cartography, a mapmaker sat down and invented a street. He gave it a name, drew its curbs and its intersections, and placed it in a quiet corner of a city where no street had ever existed. He did this on purpose, and he hoped nobody would notice.

These invented streets are called trap streets, or copyright traps, and they are one of my favorite small deceptions in the history of human knowledge. The logic is simple. A mapmaker publishes a city guide. Rivals, who want to sell their own guides without paying for the surveying, copy the original. If the copier reproduces a street that appears nowhere else in the world, the copying is proven. The fake street is a fingerprint, a way of saying *this came from me*. Some of these phantom streets were absorbed so thoroughly into the maps that followed that they took on a second life. A fictional lane in one edition became a real address in the minds of people who lived nearby. In at least one famous case, a settlement was built on the name, and the village that grew there was called, roughly, "Agloe" after the made-up place on a map of New York State. It exists now as a tiny crossroads with a general store, and it is a town that began as a lie told to catch a thief.

I find this story irresistible, but I find it more irresistible the longer I think about it. A map is supposed to be a promise: here is the land, here is how it is arranged. We trust maps the way we trust few other documents. We fold them, mark them, hand them to strangers. And yet every map is a selection. It must leave out almost everything. A map of a city that showed every tree, every crack in the pavement, every person standing on every corner would be useless, a second city laid over the first, impossible to read. So the mapmaker decides, constantly, what matters, and what can be dropped. The trap street is the mapmaker's confession that the selection is a human act, that someone chose the lines, and that the lines can be false.

---

I have been thinking about maps lately partly because of how I learned to navigate as a child. My grandmother had a road atlas that lived in the glovebox of a car that smelled of peppermints and old upholstery. The atlas had been annotated over decades in three or four different pens. Some roads had been crossed out where highways had been rerouted. Some towns had circles drawn around them because they were where relatives lived, or where a particular diner was good, or where something had happened that nobody discussed. Reading that atlas was never just reading geography. It was reading a record of a woman's life, rendered in lines and marginalia. The official map was the skeleton, and her pen was the flesh.

This is, I think, the deeper truth behind the trap street. Every map is a collaboration between the authoritative and the personal. The printed lines claim to be objective, and in a sense they are; the rivers are where the rivers are. But the act of choosing what to draw, and what to name, and what to trust, is always partly a story. The mapmaker who invented a street was telling a story too, a story about the value of his own work and the fragility of other people's honesty.

---

There is a related idea in the way we handle information more generally. We tend to think of knowledge as a pile of facts that accumulate, each one either true or false, each one either attached to its source or floating free. But the trap street shows how fragile this picture is. Once a false thing enters the world, it does not stay where you put it. It gets copied, cited, printed in the next edition, asked about by a traveler who wants directions, and eventually it acquires the weight of reality simply through repetition. The fake street became a real place. The lie, once it had enough witnesses, became a fact on the ground.

I think about this when I encounter claims that seem obviously wrong but that have been repeated so often they feel familiar. Familiarity is a strange kind of evidence. We tend to believe things we have heard before, even when we cannot remember where we heard them. Psychologists have studied this under various names, the illusory truth effect among them: statements that are repeated become more credible, regardless of whether they are accurate. The mapmaker's trap worked on the same principle in reverse. He planted a fiction that was meant to be discovered as fiction, but the world's tendency to take in what it sees was stronger than his cleverness. The street survived because it looked like it belonged.

So what does it mean to be a careful reader of the world? Partly it means remembering that everything you know arrived through some channel, and that channels can carry things that are not there. Partly it means cultivating a gentle suspicion toward the too-convenient detail, the place name that sounds exactly like what you'd expect, the fact that confirms what you already hoped. Trap streets are often designed to sound plausible. They are named like real streets because their purpose is to be mistaken for real ones. The better the fake, the more it reveals about what we are willing to accept without checking.

---

I do not want to end on pure cynicism, though, because the trap street is also a kind of delight. Consider the people who found it. A surveyor in the field, perhaps, or a traveler with a map in one hand and a street sign in the other, looking for a road that was not there, and eventually concluding that the map was wrong. Or consider the copyists themselves, who must have felt a small thrill at seeing their own false street reproduced by a rival, and who perhaps did not realize until much later that they had been caught. Each of these moments is a tiny drama of discovery, the sudden reversal of trust.

And there is something almost tender about the mapmaker's invention. He had to imagine a place in complete detail, to decide what the street would be called, where it would bend, how wide it would be. He built a little world and then hid it inside the real one. In a sense, every novelist does this. Every map of an imagined country, every fictional town with its streets and churches and bakeries, is a kind of trap street that we agree to enter willingly. The difference is that the novelist tells us the street is invented. The mapmaker did not. The trap works only because the reader forgets to ask.

I like to think the best maps, and the best stories, are honest about their own incompleteness. Old maps sometimes carry the phrase "here be dragons" or simply leave the margins blank, an admission that the surveyor's knowledge had edges, that beyond a certain line the world was unknown. There is more honesty in a blank space than in a confidently drawn lie. A blank space says: I don't know. A trap street says: I know, and I am going to make sure you can't prove otherwise.

---

I have a habit, when I visit a new city, of trying to get lost on purpose. I put the map away and walk without a destination, turning down streets because they look interesting. Sometimes I end up somewhere I could never have planned for: a courtyard with a fountain nobody mentioned, a bookshop with a cat asleep on the counter, a row of houses that seem to lead nowhere. These discoveries feel like gifts precisely because the map did not promise them. The printed city is a starting point. The real city is what you find when you let the lines go slack.

Perhaps this is what the trap street ultimately teaches. Maps are useful, even necessary, but they are not the territory. A map is a model, a set of decisions made by someone with particular purposes and particular blind spots. The best use of a map is to hold it loosely, to check it against what you see, to notice when the world disagrees with it. And when the world disagrees, the right response is curiosity rather than certainty. Maybe the street is missing because the map is wrong. Maybe the street is missing because it was built after the map was printed. Maybe the street was never there at all, and someone wanted to see whether you would notice.

I think of Agloe, the little crossroads that began as a phantom. Today it has a store and people who live there and probably have no idea their town's name was a copyright joke. Its residents are not frauds. They are simply people living in a place that happens to exist, which is more than the original street could ever claim. There is a lesson in that, too: the things we invent can become real if enough people build their lives around them. This is both hopeful and a little alarming. It means that the stories we tell, the categories we draw, and the names we give things can shape the world in ways we did not intend. A map can make a town. A rumor can make a reputation. A repeated claim can make a fact.

So I try, when I can, to be the kind of reader who asks where a thing came from. Not because I expect every street to be a trap, but because the habit of asking keeps the world open. It keeps the blank spaces honest. It reminds me that the lines on any page were drawn by someone, and that I am allowed, even encouraged, to look up from the page and check.

---

If I were to draw my own map, I think it would have a few trap streets of its own. A lane named after a grudge I never quite let go of. A small square that exists only because I once wanted it to. A road that bends toward a house I have never visited but imagine often. These would be my inventions, and I would not be able to tell you which of my beliefs are surveyed and which are invented, since I have built so much of my understanding out of the same materials the mapmaker used: plausible names, confident lines, and the comfortable assumption that what is drawn must be there.

Perhaps that is the real subject of the trap street. It is not really about maps. It is about the gap between the drawing and the land, and about how much of human life happens in that gap. We live by our maps, and we are lost when they fail us. The mapmaker who invented a street was trying to protect his work, but he also created something more interesting: a small reminder that every representation of the world is also a choice, and that choices can be wrong, and that the most important thing a traveler can carry is not a perfect map but the willingness to notice when the road ahead does not match the page.

I hope, when I finally reach the end of my own journey, that I will have left behind more honest maps than I found. Maps with blank spaces where I did not know. Maps with pencil marks where I changed my mind. And, perhaps, a few clearly labeled traps, so that whoever comes after me can see exactly where I was fooling myself, and can walk past the phantom street and onto the real one, which was there all along, waiting to be found.

# The Rivers Under the Streets

Somewhere beneath the street where I buy my morning coffee, there is a river. I have never seen it, and neither has anyone who walks above it today. It was covered over in the nineteenth century, when the city wanted its waste carried away and its stench out of sight. The stream was given a brick vault, then a sewer, then a place in the municipal records, and then it was forgotten, the way most inconvenient things are forgotten once they stop being inconvenient. Now it flows in the dark at a depth no one thinks about, while people argue about parking and buy bread above it.

I find this idea hard to shake. A city is usually described as a set of surfaces: facades, intersections, storefronts, the bright lit parts we point to on maps. But every city is also a sediment of earlier decisions, and many of those decisions are buried. Old streams run beneath pavement. Former shorelines hide under landfill. The foundations of demolished churches sit beneath parking structures. Walk through almost any old European city and you are walking across layers of choices that were made by people who are now only names on plaques, if they are remembered at all.

I like to imagine the river as an argument that lost. Someone, a council or a committee or a single exasperated engineer, decided that the water should go underground. It seemed reasonable then. Open streams carried disease, smelled terrible in summer, flooded in spring, and got in the way of new roads and new buildings. The people who vaulted them over were not villains. They were solving a problem as they understood it, with the tools and values of their time. The river was simply the first casualty of a plan that expected progress to be clean and linear.

Yet the river did not vanish. It kept going, carrying rainwater and runoff and whatever else the city sent down into it. It still answers to gravity and to weather. After a heavy storm, it rises, and the drains on certain corners gurgle and push back. Engineers call this a capacity problem. I think of it as a reminder. The thing you buried is still there, still moving, still obeying the older logic of the land it once ran across.

---

I have come to believe that most of what matters in a human life has this same quality of being underground. The things we have covered over are not gone. They continue to flow in the dark and occasionally surface when pressure builds.

Consider grief. We are often told to bury it, to move on, to put it in its place and return to the business of living. Some people do this with real success. Many others find that the grief keeps moving through them, unseen, shaping their moods and reactions in ways they can't quite trace. A song in a grocery store can open a passage they didn't know was there. A particular smell, the sound of a certain voice in another room, and suddenly the water is high in the street.

Or consider the versions of ourselves we abandoned. Most of us had a childhood interest that we dropped because it wasn't practical, or a language we studied for a year and let slip, or a kind of person we meant to become before the years made that path seem closed. None of these things disappear entirely. They run underneath the pavement of our adult routines, feeding into who we are without asking permission. Sometimes I think that the restlessness many people feel in middle age is simply the sound of these buried streams becoming audible again.

I don't say this to suggest that we should dig up everything. A city that tore up its streets every time it rained would never get anything done. Some burial is necessary. We cannot carry every river on the surface of our lives. But there is a difference between burying something deliberately, with a map and a plan for where it goes, and simply forgetting it exists. The first is a kind of management. The second is a kind of loss, because the water keeps moving whether or not anyone is keeping track of it.

---

There is a practice in some cities, which I learned about by accident, of maintaining old maps alongside modern ones. Planners, historians, and sometimes ordinary residents keep records of where things used to be: the course of a creek, the position of a tannery, the boundary of a wall that came down two centuries ago. These maps are rarely useful for navigation. You cannot drive by a stream that no longer exists on the surface. What they offer instead is orientation in time. They tell you that the ground you stand on has a history, and that the familiar shape of your neighborhood was once something else.

I wish more people kept maps of their own interior lives in this way. Not diaries, exactly, though those can serve the purpose. I mean a kind of honest accounting of what was there before. What did you once believe that you no longer believe? What did you once want that you quietly gave up? Which losses are still active underground, and which have run dry? Such a map would not make life simpler. But it might make the sudden floods less mysterious, and it might help us see that the strange turns in our behavior are not random. They follow old channels.

I have noticed that people tend to treat their pasts in one of two ways. Some treat it as a museum, a set of finished exhibits they can visit but not change. Others treat it as a basement full of things they never intend to look at again. Both approaches have a certain comfort. But the river does not care which story we tell about it. It moves according to the shape of the land and the weight of the rain, regardless of whether we acknowledge it.

---

Water is patient in a way that human plans rarely are. A river will take the easiest path, and if you block that path, it will find another. Over decades, it will undermine the foundations of a wall you thought was permanent. It will seep into basements and soften the mortar of old bridges. It will wear down stone so slowly that no one notices until a sinkhole opens on a quiet afternoon. The city that buried its river did not destroy it. It only postponed the moment when the river would have to be reckoned with.

The same is true of unresolved things in a person. A suppressed anger does not disappear because we refuse to feel it. It finds other routes, sometimes subtle ones: a sharpness in our voice, a tendency to withdraw at the wrong moments, a habit of picking fights about small things that are really about large ones. A buried fear shows up as avoidance, or as a kind of over-preparation that exhausts everyone around us. None of this is a moral failure. It is simply hydrology. Water finds its way.

Engineers who work on old urban waterways often say that the most important skill is not building new infrastructure but understanding the existing flow. You have to know where the water wants to go before you can decide where it is allowed to go. I suspect the same is true of a life. The question is rarely whether there are buried rivers. The question is whether we know their course well enough to live with them, to route around them when necessary, and to open them up when it is safe and wise to do so.

---

I should say something about the sound. Above a buried stream in the city, you can sometimes hear it if you stand very still near a storm drain. It is not loud. It is a steady, almost conversational murmur, the sound of water talking to itself in a language built of stone and gravity. Most people walk past without noticing. A few stop and listen. I am one of the ones who stop, and I suspect that is why this idea has taken such hold of me.

I think there is something in us that wants to hear the buried things. We are curious creatures, and we sense, even when we don't articulate it, that the surface is not the whole story. Archaeologists dig because they are driven by a conviction that the ground holds meaning. Novelists write about families that carry old secrets. Children ask where the rain goes after it leaves the gutter, and the answer, if you follow it, leads you underground into a network of pipes and channels that most adults have never considered.

It is worth remembering, too, that buried rivers are not only problems. They are also sources. Many cities drew their first water from springs and streams that later went underground, and some still depend on aquifers that move slowly through rock far below the streets. The river that was covered for convenience may still be the reason the city can drink. Its burial did not end its usefulness. It changed the terms on which it served us.

Perhaps the same is true of the parts of ourselves we set aside. The ambition that became too painful to pursue directly might later inform the way we raise our children or mentor a younger colleague. The grief we could not speak aloud might eventually become a kind of tenderness toward others who are suffering. The buried thing keeps working, changing form, still part of the water even when it is no longer visible.

---

On my walk to get coffee, I sometimes pause at the corner where the storm drain sits, and I try to hear the river. Most days I cannot. The traffic is too loud, or the wind is wrong, or I am simply not paying close enough attention. But on quiet mornings, after rain has fallen overnight, I can sometimes catch it: a faint, persistent sound rising from the grate, as though the city had a hidden voice that only speaks when the conditions are right.

I think of this as a kind of invitation. The world is layered, and the layers are not all visible. The streets we walk every day rest on older streets, and the buildings we take for granted were raised on the ruins of others. Our own lives are similar. We are built on foundations we did not design and cannot fully see, and the water that once ran through our early years continues to move beneath us, shaping the ground.

So I try, when I can, to stop and listen. To notice when the surface gets soft and the old channels show themselves. To remember that the river I cannot see is still a river, and that its course tells me something true about where I have been. The city will go on burying what it finds inconvenient, and I will go on forgetting certain things too. But every so often, standing at a corner with a paper cup warming my hands, I hear the water moving underneath, patient and unbothered, carrying what was put beneath it toward a sea none of us will ever see.

# The Honesty of Blank Spaces

Some of my favorite objects are maps that lie, or rather, maps that tell the truth in a way their makers didn't intend. Take Sandy Island. For well over a century it sat in the Coral Sea, east of Australia, drawn in neat outline on charts and atlases. Its location was recorded in 1876 by a whaling ship, and later cartographers copied it, and copied it again. Google Maps showed it. Schoolchildren were taught its name. Then, in 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to the spot and found nothing but deep blue water, about 1,400 meters down. The island had never existed. It had survived for generations on the strength of other people's confidence.

I find it hard not to be charmed by this. Sandy Island is a small monument to how we come to know things. Most of what any of us believes about the world, we did not verify ourselves. We inherited it, the way a mapmaker inherits a coastline from the last mapmaker. Each copy carries a little of the authority of the one before it, and after enough copies, the claim stops looking like a claim at all and starts looking like geography.

Mapmakers have a name for the deliberate version of this trick: the trap street. Cartographers sometimes insert a fictional road, town, or landmark into their work, so that if a rival copies the map, the invention exposes the theft. The most famous example is Agloe, New York, a settlement that appeared on maps published by the General Drafting Company in the 1930s. It had no houses and no people. It was a set of letters on a page waiting to be caught. Then, at some point, someone decided to open a general store at the spot where the phantom town was supposed to be, and the Agloe General Store did in fact come into being, a real building for a fictional place. The store eventually closed, but the name entered the lore of the mapping world, and the story now serves as a reminder that the line between the invented and the real is thinner than we like to think.

---

What strikes me most about old maps, though, is not the invented islands but the blank spaces. Before the nineteenth century, and in many ways well into it, the edges of known territory were drawn with a kind of shrugging honesty. Where explorers had not gone, mapmakers left empty parchment, or they filled it with monsters, sea serpents, and sketches of strange peoples. The phrase *hic sunt dracones*, "here be dragons," is often cited as if it appeared routinely on old maps. In reality it is rare; the best-known example is on the Hunt-Lenox Globe, dating to around 1510. But the impulse behind the phrase was common. Where knowledge ran out, imagination moved in.

We tend to read those blank spaces as embarrassing, a sign of ignorance that later, better science corrected. I think that's a mistake. A blank space is a form of honesty. It says: *we do not know this*. It refuses to pretend. A modern map, by contrast, can look seamless and complete even when it is full of gaps. Satellite imagery and tidy color gradients give an impression of total knowledge. The ocean floor, which we have mapped in far less detail than the surface of Mars, is still often shown as a smooth, confident blue.

Consider the island of California. For a long time it was drawn as an island, separated from the mainland by a strait, and the notion persisted for decades after Spanish explorers had reason to suspect otherwise. The Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino spent years in the region around 1700 and provided evidence that it was a peninsula, though the idea of the island lingered on some maps for a while longer. Here the error was not an empty space but a confident line, a false coastline drawn with the same ink as true ones. Blank spaces admit ignorance. Confident errors hide it.

I sometimes think about this when I read things written with great authority. The most dangerous claims are often not the obviously wild ones, which invite skepticism, but the calm, plausible ones that fit neatly into a picture everyone already holds. Sandy Island was not dangerous, of course, but it shows how a plausible error can travel very far because each person who repeats it adds a little credibility and no one feels obliged to go and look.

---

I should be careful not to romanticize the old mapmakers too much. Many of them had commercial reasons to project confidence. A chart that admitted it was guessing was less saleable than one that looked finished, and sea captains who relied on a faulty map could be killed by it. There is a reason sailors developed a deep suspicion of anything they had not sounded themselves, and why navigational charts in later centuries were so often annotated with the phrase "position doubtful" or "reported." Those small annotations are, to my mind, some of the most intellectually admirable marks in the history of cartography. They are the mapmaker saying, in effect: *here is what we think, and here is how much to trust it.*

Maps like these were not perfect, but they were built on a discipline of distinguishing observation from inference. A reported island is different from a surveyed coastline, and a surveyed coastline is different from one that a ship's captain sketched in a fog. That distinction is worth remembering in a world where every fact arrives looking identical, sitting on the same bright screen beside the rest.

---

There is another reason blank spaces move me. They imply that the world is bigger than what we have seen. An unmapped coast or unexplored sea is a kind of promise. For most of human history, a traveler could stand at the edge of the known and feel the pull of what lay beyond. The ocean was not just water but an invitation.

Today there are very few true blank spaces left on the surface of the earth. Almost every mountain range, river, and reef has been photographed, measured, and entered into some database. Even the deepest trenches have been sonar-scanned, though only a small fraction of the seafloor has been mapped at high resolution. We have, in a sense, run out of places to be ignorant in the old, geographic way. The blank spaces have migrated elsewhere: into the human body, into the microbial communities of soil, into the three-pound universe of the brain, into questions about how the deep ocean's food webs actually function or what dark matter is. We have not eliminated the unknown. We have only moved it inward, to places that are harder to draw.

I find that encouraging, actually. A map of the unknown would be a strange and beautiful thing. Imagine a chart in which every region was shaded according to how well it was understood, with the sharp edges of settled knowledge fading into a soft gray where guesses begin, and the unmapped regions left pale and open. Such a map would not look as impressive as a modern atlas. It would look more like a conversation, a record of what we have checked, what we have assumed, and what we have simply not reached.

---

Sometimes I think the ideal attitude toward knowledge is something like the attitude of a good cartographer on the edge of a coast. You draw what you have seen. You mark what you have heard from others with a note of how you heard it. You leave space where you have no information and you do not fill it with dragons unless you are clearly labeling them as stories. And you accept that someday a ship will sail to your confident island and find only water, and that this will not be a humiliation but simply the ordinary way that a map gets better.

The trouble is that this is hard to do with our own beliefs. We are far more comfortable with the sure outline than with the honest blank. Most of us carry around a private atlas full of islands we have never visited, drawn in by people we trusted, and we rarely check the coordinates. It is worth asking, now and then, which parts of our picture of the world we have actually sounded, and which we have only copied from someone else's chart.

I do not think this calls for constant doubt. You cannot live as a permanent skeptic. You would never cross a street or trust a friend. But there is a difference between provisional trust and blind repetition, and a good map-reader knows the difference. She holds her charts loosely, uses them to navigate, and watches the water for signs that the chart has drifted from the truth.

---

Sandy Island has a strange afterlife. Even after its nonexistence was established, it lingered in the minds of people who had learned it as a fact. Some were irritated, some were amused, and a few insisted they had seen it on a map as children. The island was gone, but the memory of its confident presence persisted, which is perhaps the most human thing about it. We do not give up our certainties easily, even when the evidence is clear. We feel the loss of the island almost as much as we would feel the loss of a real place.

I like to think that the discovery of its absence was a kind of gift. It was a moment when a whole structure of inherited confidence was tested against the physical world and found wanting, and the world, in the form of deep blue water, simply stayed where it was. There was no argument to win. The sea had already answered.

So here is my small wish, for mapmakers and for the rest of us. May we leave room on the page for what we do not know. May we mark our guesses as guesses. May we be the sort of people who, when the ship comes back with a sounding of 1,400 meters where we had drawn an island, say, "Ah," and pick up the pen to correct the chart. The blank spaces are not the failure of the map. They are where the map stays honest, and where the next voyage begins.

samples.result:
# The Honest Blank Space

Somewhere in the back of a drawer, most people have a map they no longer need. It might be a road atlas with cracked spine creases, a tourist map of a city they visited once, or a laminated trail guide from a park they meant to return to. These objects have a peculiar quality. They are at once extremely useful and almost entirely false, and I think their falseness is the source of their charm.

Every map lies, and the lie is not a flaw. A map is a decision about what to leave out. The moment you decide that a road matters and a footpath does not, that a river deserves a blue line and a stream does not, that the distance between two towns should be measured in straight lines rather than in the winding actual miles a traveler would walk, you have begun to abstract the world. Abstraction is what makes maps readable. A map that contained everything would be as large as the territory it described and about as useful. Jorge Luis Borges made this point in a single paragraph of a short story about an empire whose cartographers grew so ambitious that they produced a map at a scale of one to one. It covered the entire province, and eventually it was abandoned to the weather, its tattered fragments still standing in the western deserts as the only relics of the discipline. The fable is funny, but it is also a careful argument. Representation works precisely because it throws things away.

Consider the London Underground map. In 1931, Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman working part-time, drew a diagram of the railway lines that bears almost no resemblance to the physical city above it. Beck was not interested in where things were. He was interested in how they connected. He straightened the lines into horizontal, vertical, and forty-five-degree segments, spaced the stations evenly, and let the Thames wiggle into a strange, unbothered shape that tells you nothing about its actual meandering. Geographers initially disliked the design because it seemed to abandon accuracy. Passengers, however, found it immediately intuitive, and the design has been copied by subway systems around the world. Beck's map is a lie in service of a truth: a passenger does not need to know that Notting Hill and Bayswater are separated by a few hundred meters of street. The passenger needs to know which train to take and where to change. The distortion is a kindness.

What interests me is that the best maps are honest about their distortions, even when they look precise. The old cartographers understood this better than we do. Medieval mappaemundi, the circular world maps of the Christian Middle Ages, placed Jerusalem at the center and filled the margins with monsters, Gog and Magog, and creatures with heads in their chests. Modern readers often treat these as quaint errors, but many of them were doing something subtle. They marked the edges of what the mapmaker knew and gave those edges a visual vocabulary. The phrase "here be dragons," which appears on some early globes and charts, is frequently cited as evidence of medieval ignorance, but the historical record is thin. The phrase is more often a later invention or a flourish than a standard practice. Still, the idea it evokes is valuable. A blank space on a map can be an honest admission that no one has been there yet, and a map that admits its blank spaces is more trustworthy than one that paints them in with false confidence.

Our contemporary maps have largely lost this honesty. A modern navigation application presents the world as seamless and complete. The blue line of the route glows with authority. Every intersection is labeled, every restaurant is pinned, every street is rendered in crisp type. Yet this completeness is itself a kind of distortion, because the app is not showing you the world; it is showing you a model of the world that is constantly being updated, and it has been optimized for a particular purpose, which is getting you from point A to point B with a minimum of thought. It does not tell you that the shortcut through the alley is unlit, that the bridge floods in spring, or that the building on the corner was demolished two years ago and the database hasn't caught up.

There is growing evidence that this kind of navigation changes how we think about space. A few studies have suggested that people who rely heavily on turn-by-turn directions build weaker mental representations of the places they travel through. In one often-cited 2020 study, researchers found that habitual GPS users showed poorer spatial memory and less activity in brain regions associated with wayfinding, although the findings are debated and the causal story is far from settled. Still, the intuition behind them is familiar to anyone who has followed a voice instructing them through a neighborhood they have visited a dozen times without ever learning its shape. The app gets you there. You do not know where you are.

Psychologists have a term for the internal version of this: the cognitive map. In the 1940s, Edward Tolman ran experiments with rats in mazes and noticed that they did not simply memorize sequences of turns. When a familiar route was blocked, they could often find an alternative path they had never taken, which suggested they were building some kind of spatial model of the environment. Tolman's idea was controversial in his time, and the details of how the brain represents space have since become far more complicated. We now know that the hippocampus contains place cells, neurons that fire when an animal is in a particular location, and grid cells, which seem to provide a kind of coordinate system. But the basic insight holds. We do not carry the world around in our heads as a photograph. We carry a rough, active, constantly revised map, full of landmarks and distortions, and we use it to think about where we are and where we might go.

The memory palace, an ancient mnemonic technique attributed to the Greek poet Simonides, depends on exactly this capacity. You imagine a building you know well, walk through its rooms in your mind, and place the things you want to remember in specific locations along the way. To recall them, you retrace the route. The method works because human memory is far better at holding spatial and narrative structure than abstract lists. Simonides supposedly discovered the technique after a banquet hall collapsed and he was able to identify the guests by remembering where each had been sitting. Whether or not the story is true, it captures something essential. We remember places, and we remember ourselves as moving through places.

I find myself wondering whether we are also maps of ourselves, and whether we tell ourselves the same kind of useful lies. When someone asks you to describe yourself, you do not list every thought, every moment of doubt, every forgotten promise or half-finished project. You select. You say you are a teacher, or a person who loves the sea, or someone who is bad with money, and each of these labels is a simplification that makes the self legible to others and to yourself. Like Beck's diagram, the self-description straightens some lines and suppresses others. It gets you through the conversation. It is not the territory.

The danger is the same as with the navigation app. A self-map can become so complete and so confident that it stops admitting its blank spaces. We stop noticing the parts of ourselves that do not fit the diagram. We decide, early on, that we are not a creative person or not a patient one, and the map hardens into a fact. The remedy, I think, is something like the old cartographers' honesty. Keep the monsters in the margins. Admit the unexplored regions. Let the map be a working document rather than a monument.

There is also a more practical argument for leaving some blank space, and it concerns the pleasure of getting lost. Walking without a map in an unfamiliar city is one of the few reliable ways to make the world feel large again. You turn down a street because it looks interesting, and you discover a square you did not know existed, a bakery with a line out the door, a mural that someone painted over an old advertisement. You are forced to pay attention because you have no script telling you what to notice. The disorientation, at first mildly anxious, becomes a kind of attentiveness. You start to build your own map, and that map is different from anyone else's, because it is made of your particular wrong turns and accidental discoveries.

I do not want to romanticize inefficiency. Maps are enormously useful, and the people who made them, from ancient surveyors to the engineers who built satellite positioning systems, accomplished things that deserve admiration. Nobody should have to wander lost through a hospital parking structure to prove a point about attentiveness. But there is a difference between using a map and surrendering to one. The first keeps you in the position of a person who knows that the map is a tool made by people with particular purposes. The second turns you into a passenger, carried along by a model you never think to question.

So perhaps the best thing to do with the old maps in the drawer is to look at them not as broken instruments but as portraits of their makers' attention. Each fold and crease records a moment when someone needed to get somewhere and tried to make sense of the world well enough to do it. The roads that were drawn, the lakes that were colored in, the empty spaces left white for lack of knowledge: all of these are evidence of a particular relationship between a person and a place. The map is a conversation, and like any conversation it is partial, shaped by who is speaking and why.

I think of the cartographers in Borges's story, the ones who made the map as large as the empire and then watched it crumble. Their folly was the desire for a representation that would contain everything and therefore replace the world. The sensible alternative is to accept the limits of representation and to find delight in them. A good map tells you where to go and then steps aside. It trusts you to look up from the paper, to notice the light on the water, to ask a stranger for directions and learn something unexpected in the answer.

The blank spaces, then, are not failures. They are invitations. They mark the places where your knowledge ends and your experience must begin. Every traveler, every reader, every person trying to understand themselves eventually arrives at one of these edges. What matters is what you do next: whether you draw a dragon there and move on, or walk closer, slowly, and start making a map of your own.

# The Coastline Problem, and Other Things Maps Leave Out

Measure the coast of Britain and you will get a different answer depending on how you measure it. Use a ruler a hundred kilometers long and you skip over the small bays, the estuaries, the shingle spits, and the rocky fingers that jut into the sea. The total comes out shorter. Shrink the ruler to ten kilometers and it bends into more of the detail, and the total grows. Shrink it to one kilometer, then to a hundred meters, then to the length of a boot, and the coastline keeps getting longer. Each finer measurement reveals inlets that the coarser one could not see. In the limit, the coast has no definite length at all.

Lewis Fry Richardson, a meteorologist and pacifist who was also an odd and original thinker about conflict, noticed this in the 1950s while studying the borders of countries. Benoit Mandelbrot later gave the problem a name and a theory, and it became the starting point for fractal geometry. But the observation is older than either man, and it does not require any mathematics to feel. Stand on a beach and you know that the line between land and water is not a line at all. It is a negotiation, a fringe, a zone of wet sand and tangled kelp that moves with every tide.

I keep returning to this puzzle because it exposes something about maps in general. A map is a decision about what to keep. Every map is a compression, and compression always means loss. The cartographer must choose a scale, and the scale determines which details survive. A road atlas drops the footpaths. A nautical chart drops the farmhouses but keeps the shoals. A map of a city for tourists shows the cathedral and the river and omits the three-story laundromat where the old men play chess in the afternoons. None of these choices is wrong. They are the price of being useful. But they also mean that a map is never a neutral picture of the world. It is an argument about what matters.

---

Consider the history of maps as a history of changing priorities. Early European world maps, the mappae mundi of the medieval period, were not concerned with accurate distances. Jerusalem sat at the center, and the shape of the known world was arranged according to theology more than geography. Monsters and marvels filled the blank edges. Sometimes the cartographers wrote in the margins that beyond this point lay unknown lands full of dangers, and sometimes they simply left the parchment empty or decorated it with a sea serpent. We look at these maps and smile at their confusion, but they were honest in a way that many modern maps are not. They showed what their makers believed was important, and they did not pretend to be a mirror.

The modern map aspires to be a mirror. It uses projections, datums, and coordinate systems to pretend that the spherical Earth can be flattened without distortion. This cannot be done. Any flat representation of a globe must sacrifice something: area, shape, distance, or direction. The Mercator projection, which made navigation easier by keeping lines of constant compass bearing straight, inflates Greenland until it looks roughly as large as Africa, when in fact Africa is about fourteen times bigger. Schoolchildren who grew up with that map carried a quiet falsehood in their heads for generations. The falsehood was not malicious. It was simply the cost of a particular purpose, and the purpose was getting ships across oceans without the navigator needing trigonometry at every turn.

What interests me is that we rarely remember the sacrifice. We see the map and believe the map. The lines look authoritative. The colors look objective. A surveyed boundary feels like a fact of nature rather than the result of a dispute settled in an office, sometimes by men who had never visited the land they were dividing. Richardson's coastline paradox has a political cousin: the length of a border depends on the scale at which people agree to look at it, and borders are usually drawn with a ruler at a scale no one lives at.

---

There is a second kind of omission that interests me more, and it is the one that happens in the mind rather than on the page. Most of us carry around maps of our own lives, and these maps are compressed in the same way. We remember the big events and the landmarks: the wedding, the move to a new city, the year of the illness, the job we left. Between these points lies an enormous amount of unrecorded territory. Ordinary Tuesdays. The walk to the bus stop. The particular way a friend laughed at something stupid in a parking lot in 2009. These things are the fine-grained coastline of experience, and most of them vanish when we compress our memories into stories.

Oddly, we often feel the loss most when we return to a place we once knew well. You drive back to the town where you grew up and the road is the same but the shop on the corner is gone, replaced by something with a different name. Your memory had reduced the town to a few streets and a feeling, and now the detail has come back, unfamiliar and insistent. The town was never the map you carried. It was always the finer, longer, messier thing, and the map was a small mercy that let you live without remembering everything at once.

I think this is why nostalgia has such a strange texture. It is nostalgia for detail that we did not know we were losing. We remember the outline and forget the grain, and then we are stunned to discover how much grain there was. Proust understood this when he wrote about the madeleine dipped in tea, which dissolved a whole childhood into a single taste. The taste was a kind of key that unlocked compressed territory. The entire village of Combray came back, not as a map but as a fractal, every corner revealing another corner.

---

If maps always omit, then the question becomes how to live with that omission gracefully. One answer is to remember that the map is not the territory, which is a line so often repeated that it has become a cliché. But clichés persist because they point at something true and difficult. The map is useful precisely because it is not the territory. You cannot drive from Lisbon to Porto using a map at a one-to-one scale; the map would be as large as the country and as useless as the country itself. Abstraction is a tool, and tools are good. The trouble comes only when we forget that we made the abstraction and begin to take its outlines for the real shape of things.

Another answer is to go looking for the fine grain deliberately. Walk the coast rather than driving past it. Stop at the tide pool. Learn the names of the birds that live in the reeds at the edge of the lake. Most of us will never map a coastline or a continent, but we can practice a kind of attention that refuses to accept the first simplification. When you slow down, the world stops being a diagram and becomes a place with a texture you cannot fully summarize. A single hillside in late autumn can contain more information than any atlas. The moss on the north side of a stone, the way the light falls through a row of birches, the small bright beetle walking across a leaf: none of this will ever appear on a map, and none of it is trivial.

I find this practice steadying, perhaps because it reminds me that the world is larger than any of the representations I use to think about it. It is a kind of humility that does not require giving up on knowledge. We still need maps. We still need to summarize, to generalize, to say that a river runs from the mountains to the sea. But we can hold those summaries loosely, aware that behind each one lies a coastline that keeps growing as we look closer.

---

There is also an ethical dimension to what maps omit, and it is worth taking seriously. Whoever decides what appears on a map is exercising a kind of power. Colonial maps often erased existing place names and replaced them with the names of the surveyors' patrons. Some regions appeared as empty because no one who drew the maps bothered to ask who lived there. Indigenous communities have spent decades working to get their own place names, territorial claims, and knowledge recognized on official maps, and in many cases the fight is still ongoing. A blank space on a map is rarely blank to the people who live in it. It is blank only to the person holding the pen.

This matters for everyday life too. Digital maps now guide most of our movements, and they are remarkably good at what they do. But they also shape what we notice. A navigation app optimizes for efficiency, which means it routes us along the fastest path, past the places that are most convenient for traffic and least likely to surprise us. Over time, we may find that we have stopped wandering. We know how to get from A to B without knowing anything about the neighborhoods in between. The map has made the territory invisible. I do not think this is a catastrophe, but I think it is a loss worth naming, the way one might mention the disappearance of a species from a forest that still looks green from the highway.

Perhaps the healthiest relationship with maps is a kind of playful skepticism. Look at a map and ask what it has chosen to show. Who made it, and for what purpose? What would it look like at a different scale? Which place is missing, and why? These questions turn a passive viewing into an active reading. They also make the map more interesting, because it becomes a document of human choices rather than an oracle.

---

I want to end somewhere less analytical, because the coastline keeps reminding me that there is joy in the irreducible. Richardson's paradox is, at bottom, a delightful fact. A coastline is infinitely complicated, and no ruler can capture it. This is not a failure of measurement. It is a sign that the world has more structure than our instruments were designed to hold. Mandelbrot later showed that the same kind of self-similar complexity appears in clouds, mountains, river networks, the branching of trees, the veins of a leaf, and even the arrangement of blood vessels in the body. The rough edge repeats at every scale. Zoom in and you find the same kind of ruggedness you saw from farther away.

There is something consoling in this. It suggests that the world does not run out. However closely we look, there is more to see, and the seeing does not exhaust the thing. A map can only give you a finite number of points, but the territory keeps offering new ones. Each time you return to a familiar beach, the tide has rearranged the sand, a different piece of driftwood has washed up, and the water has gone out farther than it did last week. The coast is always being redrawn, and that redrawing is not a defect of the coast. It is what coasts do.

So I think the lesson of the coastline is not that maps are bad. It is that they are a beginning. They give us a way into a place, a rough sketch that lets us find our way, and then the place takes over and surprises us. The map gets us to the shore. The shore does the rest. We walk along the edge of the water, noticing the things no one thought to draw, and we discover that the line between land and sea is less a boundary than an invitation. It asks us to come closer, and then closer still, and it never quite finishes telling us what it is.

# On Getting Lost

Some of my clearest memories are of being lost. I don't mean the dramatic kind, stranded in a desert or missing a flight. I mean the small, pleasant disorientation of realizing you have walked a few streets past the place you meant to be, and that the city has quietly rearranged itself around you. The street names are unfamiliar. The light is different. A bakery you've never noticed smells of cardamom and burnt sugar, and for a few minutes the world feels larger than the version you had been carrying around.

We have made getting lost very hard to do. Phones tell us where we are with a blue dot that never wavers, and they tell us where to turn before we have finished wondering whether we should. This is useful. I use it constantly. But I have started to suspect that something gets lost in the bargain, and that the thing is not just the inconvenience of wrong turns but a particular way of paying attention to the world.

Consider what navigation used to require. Before satellites, a person moving through unfamiliar territory had to build a mental model of the place from scratch. You noticed that the river bent to the east, that the church spire was visible from two different hills, that the road climbed gently after the second bridge. You kept track of how long you had been walking and in what direction, and you adjusted your sense of where you were as you went. Cognitive scientists sometimes call this path integration, and some animals are astonishingly good at it. Desert ants returning to their nests after a long meandering foraging trip can head back in an almost straight line, having tallied their steps and turns the whole way. They are not reading a map. They are constantly updating an internal sense of where home is relative to where they are.

Humans can do this too, though we tend to be worse at it, partly because we rely on landmarks and partly because we rarely practice. Some researchers have found that people who navigate by memorized routes, turning left at the gas station and right at the school, often develop weaker overall spatial models than those who navigate by orientation, who know roughly where north is at all times. The GPS user, in this light, is a bit like a passenger who has memorized a bus timetable without ever seeing the city. The turns are handled. The geography stays vague.

I don't want to sound like a nostalgist about this. I have no wish to abandon the map in my pocket, and I'm not going to pretend that a paper atlas is inherently more honest than a screen. Maps have always been arguments. They choose what to show and what to leave out, which roads get thick lines and which become dotted ones, which neighborhoods are drawn at the scale of a tourist's wandering and which are reduced to a gray smudge. The old maps of the sea, with their sea monsters and their confident coastlines drawn from hearsay, were no more faithful than ours. They were just more visibly human about their uncertainty. Sometimes a mapmaker would write *here be dragons* at the edge of what he did not know, and that phrase still carries a kind of courage. It admits the limit.

Modern maps rarely admit limits. They render everything with the same crisp authority, and this is a subtle form of persuasion. When a route is drawn as a single bright line, we forget that it is one option among many, chosen by an algorithm optimizing for distance or time or traffic. We forget that the street we are being sent down might be quieter and more beautiful than the one we would have chosen, or that the shortcut through the alley runs past a wall covered in faded murals no one would have seen on the main road. Efficiency is a value, but it is not the only one, and it has a way of crowding out the others without announcing itself.

Getting lost, in the good sense, is a way of relaxing that efficiency. It forces you to look. When you don't know where you are, you start reading signs you would otherwise skim. You notice the shape of the roofs, the kinds of trees, the way people greet each other on the sidewalk. You begin to make guesses and test them. "That hill must be the one I saw from the square, so the river should be on my left." Sometimes you are right, and the small satisfaction of it is out of proportion to its importance. Sometimes you are wrong, and you end up somewhere unexpected, which is often the more memorable outcome.

I think there is something here about attention more generally. Attention is not just a matter of how much of it we have but of what it is directed toward and how it is shaped. Being lost pulls attention outward. Knowing exactly where you are and where you're going tends to pull it inward, toward the destination, toward the next notification, toward the small private anxieties that travel with us everywhere. The Japanese poet Bashō wrote about walking through the countryside with a kind of open receptivity, letting the road set the rhythm of his thoughts. He was not lost in any practical sense; he had a route and a purpose. But he had also cultivated a way of moving through space that let the world into the poem. Being a little lost is one way to make room for that.

Lostness also has a social dimension that I find oddly moving. When you are lost in a city where you don't speak the language well, you have to ask people for help, and that asking creates small connections. A woman with a shopping bag points you toward the metro and tells you, unprompted, about the closure on the line you were about to take. A teenager on a bicycle walks his bike two blocks with you because the street you're looking for is hard to find. A shopkeeper draws a crude map on the back of a receipt, and the map is wrong in one important way, but his kindness is not. These moments are fragile and easy to skip when a screen can answer the question silently. They are also, I think, among the most reliable ways we encounter strangers as people rather than as obstacles or background.

None of this means we should throw our phones into the river. It means we might choose lostness deliberately, the way some people choose to fast or to sleep without an alarm. Leave the map closed for one walk a week. Pick a direction and go, and when you come to a fork, pick the path you have not taken before. Accept that you will sometimes circle back to a place you recognize and feel faintly foolish. The foolishness is part of the point. It keeps you honest about how little you actually know about the place where you live.

There is also a deeper version of getting lost that has nothing to do with streets. Most of us have had the experience of finding ourselves in the middle of a life we did not plan, with the landmarks we relied on gone or unrecognizable. A job ends, a relationship dissolves, a body changes in ways no one warned us about, and suddenly the internal map that once told us where we were no longer fits the terrain. This kind of lostness is not pleasant in the way a wrong turn in a foreign city can be pleasant. It is frightening, and it can last a long time. But it has something in common with the smaller version. You are forced to pay attention to what is actually in front of you, because the stories you were using to navigate have stopped working. You start noticing things. You ask people for directions, sometimes literally and sometimes figuratively, and you discover that others have been lost in similar ways and are willing to say so.

I have come to think that the ability to tolerate being lost, even to enjoy it a little, is a form of maturity. It means being able to sit with not knowing without immediately reaching for the nearest answer. In a culture that treats uncertainty as a problem to be solved as quickly as possible, this is a difficult discipline. Every gap in our knowledge seems to call for a search, a query, a quick confirmation. But some gaps are worth leaving open for a while. Some questions get better when you walk around them.

The ants, I suppose, are not troubled by being lost. They do not experience the nest as a destination to be reached quickly. They simply keep track of where they have been and where home lies, and they trust the accumulated sense they have built. There is a lesson there that is almost too obvious to state: we are constantly building an internal sense of where we are, and that sense can be strengthened or allowed to atrophy depending on how we move through the world. If we let the blue dot do all the work, we may arrive at many places without ever quite knowing where we have been.

So I will keep using my phone, and I will keep being grateful for it when I'm running late in an unfamiliar city. But I will also keep a small habit of wandering. I will take the street that looks interesting even when it adds ten minutes. I will ask the old man on the bench which way the river is, and I will listen to his answer even when it sends me in the wrong direction first. I will let myself be a little lost, not as a failure of planning but as a kind of permission. The world is larger than my map of it, and I would rather remember that than forget it in the name of arriving on time.

The best wrong turns I have taken did not get me anywhere I intended to go. They got me somewhere better: a courtyard I would never have found, a conversation I would never have had, a view over rooftops that made me stop and simply look. Getting lost, it turns out, is one of the few ways left to be surprised by a place you thought you already knew. I think that is worth a few minutes of uncertainty. I think it may be worth quite a lot more than that.
