# On the Honesty of Blank Spaces

Old maps are beautiful in a way that newer ones often aren't. Their coastlines curl like the edges of burnt paper. Sea monsters coil in the corners, compass roses bloom with winds that have names, and little ships with bellies full of sail drift over water rendered in tiny engraved waves. But what I keep coming back to is the blankness. Across the interior of a continent, or in the middle of an ocean, the cartographer simply left the paper empty, or wrote a few words in the margin and let the rest be silence. Sometimes the phrase was *terra incognita*, unknown land. Sometimes it was nothing at all.

I find that blankness more honest than most of what we now call information.

---

Consider the logic of a map. It is a deliberate act of selection. No map can show everything. A map of a city at true scale, with every stone and blade of grass, would be the size of the city, and therefore useless. So the mapmaker must choose: this road matters, that alley does not; this river gets a blue line, that creek is dropped entirely. Every map is a set of decisions about what to keep and what to discard. The most important thing a map can do is tell you what it has decided to leave out, and most maps do this poorly, or not at all.

The old cartographers, working with the reports of sailors and merchants, often knew exactly where their knowledge ended. A coast was sketched from one voyage, so its outline was tentative and dotted. An interior was guessed at from rumor, so it was left blank or filled with decorative beasts that were, in a sense, a confession: *here we do not know, and we would rather draw a lion than pretend.* The blank space was a kind of truthfulness. It said, plainly, that the knowledge stopped here.

Modern maps tend to hide their edges. A satellite image of the earth is seamless, sharp, and apparently complete, and so we assume it is. We rarely ask how old the imagery is, what clouds obscured it, what was interpolated, what was guessed by an algorithm stitching together fragments. The surface looks finished. The uncertainty has been smoothed away, and with it, the reminder that someone made choices.

---

I think this matters beyond cartography. We live in an age of apparent completeness. Search a question and an answer appears, fluent and confident, in a tone that rarely wavers. Scroll a feed and the world seems to arrive pre-assembled, every event labeled and every opinion sorted into a neat column. The texture of uncertainty, the dotted coastlines and the blank interiors, has been flattened. We are handed a map without margins.

This is not entirely the fault of technology, though technology has accelerated it. There has always been a human pull toward the finished picture. Nobody wants to hear "we don't know yet" when they are frightened or confused. Experts are tempted to round off their doubts for the sake of clarity. Politicians discover that certainty wins elections. Journalists learn that a headline with a question mark gets fewer clicks than one with a verdict. Over time, a culture can forget how to tolerate the blank space at all, and begins to experience any gap as a failure rather than a fact.

But a blank space is not a failure. It is a boundary marker. It tells you where to be careful, where to walk slowly, where to send someone to look. The sailor who knew the chart was incomplete sailed closer to the shore with a leadsman calling depths. The sailor who trusted a confident but wrong map ran aground.

---

There is a particular kind of intellectual humility that I have come to admire, and it looks a lot like those old maps. It says: *this is what I know, and this is how I know it, and here is where it runs out.* It does not apologize for the edges. It does not pretend the edges aren't there. It draws the coastline in a firm line where the evidence is strong and in a dotted line where it is weak, and it has the nerve to leave the interior empty when it has nothing reliable to say.

That kind of honesty is rarer than it should be, partly because it is less satisfying in the moment. A blank space offers no story. A dotted coastline gives you no comfort. But over the long run, honesty about limits is what makes a map trustworthy at all. If a map shows you a river everywhere, you have no way of knowing which rivers are real. If it marks its uncertainties, then its confident lines become meaningful. The blank space is what gives the drawn lines their weight.

I think this applies to people too. The friends I trust most are the ones who can say "I don't know" without flinching, and who can say "I was wrong about that" without elaborate self-defense. Their confidence means something precisely because it is not automatic. When they tell me something firmly, I believe them, because I have seen them mark the places where they were unsure.

---

It is worth noting that a blank space on a map is also an invitation. For centuries, the empty interiors of continents drew explorers. The question "what is out there?" is one of the most powerful motivators humans have ever known. Much of what we now know about the world was learned by people who started with a blank page and decided to go look. The emptiness was not just a limit of knowledge; it was a kind of promise.

There is something lovely in this. A blank space says that the world is larger than what we have yet seen. It leaves room for surprise. A map with no blank spaces, if such a thing could exist, would be a map of a world with nothing left to discover, and I find that a rather lonely idea. The incomplete map keeps the future open.

So perhaps the best response to a blank space is neither dread nor the urge to fill it with something false. It is curiosity, tempered by care. Look at the edge. Ask what lies beyond it. Go closer carefully, marking what you find as you go, and leave the new lines honest about their own uncertainty.

---

I want to say something about the sea monsters, because they are often mocked as the childish decorations of a superstitious age. But I don't think they were simply foolish. A cartographer who drew a sea serpent in an unknown ocean was doing something subtle. He was marking danger, or at least the feeling of danger, and he was marking it as *unknown* rather than *known to be safe.* The monster said: here be things we cannot account for. It was a warning dressed as art.

Modern maps have mostly dispensed with monsters, which is in many ways progress. We understand the oceans better now. But we have also lost the habit of marking the unknown as unknown. A contemporary map might show a seabed in precise topographic detail that was in fact interpolated from sparse soundings, and nothing on the map tells you that. The sea monster has been replaced by false precision, which is in some ways more dangerous, because it does not look like a warning at all.

I sometimes wish we had a more honest visual language for uncertainty: a faint hatching, a fade, a question mark drawn into the landscape. Some scientific maps already do this, with confidence intervals and shaded error zones. These are good developments. But they are rarely the ones that reach the public, and they are rarely the ones we absorb when we are glancing at a screen on the way somewhere else.

---

There is a practical lesson here, and I suspect it generalizes. When you encounter a claim, a map, a summary, or an explanation, it helps to ask: where are the blank spaces? What is this source not saying? Where does its knowledge run out, and does it tell me so? A source that never admits any edge is not necessarily lying, but it is asking for more trust than it has earned. A source that marks its limits, even imperfectly, is giving you the tools to judge it.

This does not mean becoming a cynic who distrusts everything. Cynicism is just another way of refusing to read the map. The old navigators did not stop sailing because the charts were incomplete. They sailed carefully, consulted multiple sources, took soundings, watched the birds and the color of the water, and adjusted as they learned. They trusted the charts enough to use them and doubted them enough to survive. That balance is hard, and it is the real skill.

---

I keep thinking about the moment when a cartographer, having finished a coastline from a sailor's account, looked at the vast empty space beyond it and decided not to fill it. It would have been easy to fill. Paint an island, sketch a mountain range, add a river that flows nicely toward the sea. The paper would look more complete. The client might be pleased. But that would have been a small betrayal, a promise the mapmaker could not keep. Leaving the space blank was a form of integrity.

I like to imagine that cartographer as a kind of patron saint of honest uncertainty. Not someone who knew everything, but someone who knew where their knowledge stopped and had the courage to say so on the page. In a world eager for finished pictures, that courage seems more valuable than ever.

---

So if you ever find yourself with a blank page, whether it is a literal map, a research question, a conversation with someone you are trying to understand, or a decision about your own life, consider leaving the empty places empty for a while. Resist the urge to fill them with the first plausible thing. Draw the coastlines you can actually see. Mark the dotted lines honestly. Write, if you must, a few words in the margin: *here we do not yet know.*

That sentence is not a defeat. It is the beginning of a voyage. Every map that now hangs on a wall was once a blank space that someone chose to approach with care instead of fear, and to leave honest instead of pretty.

The old maps still have a lot to teach us. They show us that the most useful thing a picture of the world can do is tell the truth about its own edges. And they remind us that somewhere beyond the last drawn line, there is still a great deal we have not seen, and that this is not a problem to be solved so much as a country to be explored, slowly, with a lead line in hand and a willingness to be surprised.

# The Drawer of Unknown Cables

Every household has one. Mine is the second drawer down in the kitchen, to the left of the stove, and it is where the cables go to wait. There are phone chargers for phones I no longer own, a coil of thin white wire with a plug at one end and nothing at the other, two adapters whose purpose I can only guess at, a tangle of rubber-sheathed cords that might power a printer or a long-dead desk lamp. Occasionally I open the drawer looking for a specific cable, fail to find it, and close the drawer again with the vague sense that I have just consulted a record of decisions I never quite made.

I have come to think of that drawer as a small archive of intentions. Each cable was once attached to something I needed, and I kept it because I assumed I would need it again. Keeping a cable is a bet on the future, a low-stakes wager that the device will return, or that I will someday buy another device that requires the same odd connector. Most of these bets have lost. The devices are in landfills or in other people's closets. But the cables persist, because discarding them requires a small act of faith that I will not need them, and faith of that kind is harder to muster than it sounds.

There is something quietly moving about this. Nobody sits down and decides to become a person with a drawer full of obsolete wires. It accumulates, one reasonable decision at a time. Each individual choice to keep a cable is defensible. The total is absurd. That gap between the logic of each moment and the shape of the whole is, I suspect, a fairly accurate description of a human life.

---

Archaeologists have long understood that the most revealing objects are often the mundane ones. Pottery shards tell us more about daily diet than royal tombs do. Trash middens, those heaps of discarded bones and broken tools, are sometimes more honest than the monuments built to commemorate a civilization's ideals. People write their official histories with great care, but they throw away their junk without thinking, and the junk is candid in a way that deliberate records rarely are.

A junk drawer is a midden in miniature. If some future historian were to excavate my kitchen, she would learn that I owned devices I no longer used, that I expected to need things I never needed, that I was, on balance, more hopeful than efficient. She would learn that I lived in a world saturated with small electronic objects, each requiring its own particular connector, a world designed so that nothing quite fits anything else. She might conclude that my household was organized around a promise of compatibility that was never fully kept.

I find this funny, and also a little sad, which is how I feel about most things that reveal us without meaning to.

---

There is a philosophical tradition, mostly associated with the Stoics and their descendants, that counsels us to distinguish between what is in our control and what is not. The cable drawer seems to be an exercise in the opposite direction. It is a place where I store things I cannot control, in anticipation of circumstances I cannot foresee. The future devices I might one day own are, by definition, beyond my reach. Keeping their possible connectors is a way of preparing for a world I have no real power to shape.

And yet I do not think this is simply foolishness. Preparation is one of the oldest human virtues. Grain stored in autumn, wood split before winter, a spare key hidden under a stone: these are all bets on an uncertain future, and most of them pay off often enough to justify the effort. The cable drawer is a degenerate version of that impulse, the way a sourdough starter kept alive for a decade might be a degenerate version of food storage. It has lost its connection to necessity, but it has kept the shape of care.

Perhaps that is the real function of the drawer. It is not really about cables. It is about the refusal to assume that the present is the final state of things. Keeping the old connector says, in effect, that the world might change in ways I cannot predict, and I would rather not be caught without a way to adapt. It is a small, stubborn optimism, and optimism of that kind is rarely rational in the narrow sense, but it has a function in a life. It keeps the door slightly open.

---

I have tried, over the years, to clean out the drawer. I have done it the way people are advised to do it, by sorting into piles: keep, recycle, donate, throw away. The keep pile has never been empty. When I hold a cable up to the light and ask whether I will ever use it, the honest answer is almost always no, and yet my hand returns it to the drawer. I have started to suspect that the question I am asking is the wrong one. I am not really asking whether I will use the cable. I am asking whether I am willing to let go of the version of myself who might have.

That version is oddly specific. He is someone who owns the old camera, who still has the laptop from college, who will need to charge a device that has not yet been invented but will, he assumes, use a connector that resembles this one. He is more organized than I am, and more prepared, and in his imagined life there is always a cable for every occasion. When I throw away a charger, I feel I am disappointing him slightly. This is absurd, because he does not exist, but absurdity has never been much of a barrier to feeling things.

I suspect many of our attachments work this way. We keep old identities alive in drawers, closets, and folders: the instrument we once meant to learn, the language we planned to speak, the running shoes that imply a self who runs. These objects are less about their function than about the futures they hold open. Discarding them feels like closing a door, and most of us are reluctant to close doors even when the rooms behind them have long since been dismantled.

---

Minimalism has become a fashionable response to this problem. Its advocates describe lives stripped of excess, rooms with clear surfaces, closets containing only what is used. There is wisdom in this, and I admire people who manage it. But I have always found something slightly suspicious about the aesthetic of emptiness, the implicit claim that the ideal self is one who needs nothing held in reserve. A life with no spare cables is a life that has committed fully to the present, which is admirable, but it is also a life with no archive, no evidence of having once expected something else.

Human beings are not very good at living entirely in the present, and I am not sure we should be. We are creatures who remember and anticipate, who build monuments and keep letters and save voicemails from people who have died. The cable drawer is a minor, almost comic version of these impulses, but it belongs to the same family. A person who keeps nothing is not necessarily more free than one who keeps too much. Sometimes the person who keeps too much is simply more attached to the possibility that things will connect again.

Still, I would like the drawer to be smaller. I have resolved, more than once, to empty it entirely. I have not yet managed to do so, and I am beginning to think I may never fully succeed. Perhaps the drawer will simply continue to grow, a record of my hopes and my failures to act on them, until someday a stranger opens it and finds a coil of white wire with a plug on one end and nothing on the other, and wonders, as I do, what it was meant to connect.

---

There is a line I half remember from some essay or poem, something about how we are made of the things we refuse to throw away. I am not sure it is true, and I am not sure who wrote it, which is itself a little telling. Memory is leaky. What survives is often what we happen to have kept, and what we keep is often a matter of habit more than conviction. The drawer is not a theory of the self, but it is a kind of evidence, and evidence, unlike theory, tends to be honest about our contradictions. I want to be efficient, and I keep the cables. I want to live in the present, and I keep the past in a kitchen drawer. I want to trust the future, and I keep a connector for a device I will never buy.

Maybe the sensible response is not to empty the drawer but to make peace with it. I could treat it as a small museum of my own uncertainty, a place to visit when I need to remember that I have always been, in some modest way, a person who hedges against the unknown. The cables are not failures so much as attempts at a conversation with a future I cannot see. Most of those attempts went nowhere, but they were made in good faith, and there is something to be said for good faith even when it produces clutter.

I think, on reflection, that I will keep the drawer. Not forever, perhaps. Someday I may move house, or downsize, or simply be forced by circumstance to decide what matters. But for now, the drawer stays where it is, to the left of the stove, holding its small collection of possible futures. When I open it looking for something I cannot find, I will remember that the search itself is not entirely pointless. Somewhere in that tangle is the evidence of a person who believed that things might one day connect again, and I find I am not quite ready to disprove him.

# The Drawer

Every kitchen has one, and every household pretends not to. It is usually the drawer nearest the stove or the sink, the one that sticks a little when you pull it and then gives all at once, as if it has been waiting for you to make a mistake. Mine holds a rubber band ball the size of a walnut, two dead AA batteries that I have never been able to bring myself to throw away, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed years ago, a single chopstick, a tangle of twist ties, a small brass key with no tag, and another small brass key with no tag, which is slightly different from the first.

I have been thinking about this drawer for weeks, mostly because I opened it looking for a screwdriver and came away with nothing but a question I could not answer. What are these keys for? I do not know. I have tried every lock in the apartment and several in the building's laundry room. I have no idea whose they are or what they once opened. Some previous version of my life, some apartment or car or filing cabinet or diary, was secured by these objects, and then the lock went away or I did, and the keys stayed behind, faithfully, in the dark.

I find that moving in a way I cannot fully justify.

---

The junk drawer is a peculiar institution. Nobody decides to create one. It accumulates through a kind of geological process, a slow sedimentation of things that were too useful to discard and too useless to place. Each object enters the drawer with a small act of deferral. *I'll deal with this later.* The battery might still have a charge. The menu might be needed if the delivery app goes down. The key might belong to something important that I will eventually remember. The chopstick is simply waiting for its pair, which will never return, but the chopstick does not know that, and neither, quite, do I.

The drawer is a monument to the future tense. Everything in it is a promise that has not been cancelled. It is the most optimistic place in the house, and also, in a gentle way, the most melancholy, because the promises are mostly not going to be kept.

I think this is why tidying it feels so fraught. When you empty a junk drawer, you are forced to make decisions about hypothetical futures, and most of them are decisions to forgo a version of yourself who might one day need a spare key to a building you no longer live in. There is a small but real grief in throwing away the dead battery, because throwing it away admits that the future it was meant for is over. The battery is not really about power. It is about the afternoon, years ago, when you thought you might need a flashlight in a power cut, and you were a different person who believed in power cuts.

---

Keys in particular carry an unusual weight. Of all the objects a person accumulates, keys are the most purely symbolic. A key has no value except in relation to a lock. It is a question that only has meaning when it meets the right answer. Stripped of its lock, a key is a sentence with its subject missing, a promise of access to a room that has been demolished or rebuilt or sold.

The history of the key is ancient and tells us something about why we keep them. The earliest keys were wooden, pin-tumbler mechanisms of the kind still used in some rural parts of the world, and archaeologists have found them in the ruins of Egyptian and Mesopotamian settlements. The Romans made bronze keys that were often worn as rings, a habit that linked the key to the body and to status. A key was a sign that you had something worth protecting, and that you were trusted with the protection. To carry keys was to carry a portion of someone else's confidence, or your own.

There is something of that old feeling in the junk drawer. The keys in it are not operational, but they are still, in some sense, trusted. I have not thrown them out because throwing out a key feels like a small betrayal of a bargain I no longer remember making. Perhaps one of them opened the front door of a flat where I once lived with someone I no longer see. Perhaps the other opened a bicycle lock that was stolen in a city I have not visited in a decade. I have no way of checking, and so the keys stay, sealed inside their uncertainty, neither useful nor disposable.

---

Archaeologists have a useful habit when confronted with a site they do not understand. They catalogue everything, including the things that seem trivial, because the trivial things are often the most revealing. A broken clay pipe or a button or a piece of worn glass tells you how people actually lived, as opposed to how they described themselves in official records. The grand temple gets the attention, but the midden, the refuse heap behind the house, is where the daily life is preserved.

The junk drawer is a midden in miniature, and I sometimes imagine an archaeologist of the future excavating it. She would find the twist ties and conclude, correctly, that the household bought bread in plastic bags and had a habit of securing them. She would find the takeout menu and learn that the neighbourhood once had a restaurant specialising in something, though she could not be sure what. She would find the batteries and assume a certain dependence on portable electronics, and the keys would puzzle her. Multiple keys, no locks, no label. She might write a paper about them. She would be as wrong and as right as any reader of ruins usually is.

What would she miss? She would miss the feeling of the drawer being pulled open in a hurry on a Tuesday night, the particular sound of rubber bands sliding over each other, the way the menu has a faint grease stain shaped like a country I have never visited. She would miss the reasons. Archaeology can recover objects, but it struggles to recover the intentions that once surrounded them. The key is there, but the reason it was kept, and the reason it was never thrown away, is gone.

---

There is a current of thought, popular in recent years, that holds the cluttered house to be a kind of moral failure. The most famous advocate of this view is probably a tidying consultant whose books urge readers to hold each object in their hands and ask whether it sparks joy. I admire the clarity of this approach and I have, in fact, emptied several drawers under its influence. There is a real pleasure in a cleared surface, in a cupboard you can close without leaning on it, in the sense that your possessions are a chosen set rather than an accident.

But I have never been able to ask the joy question of the keys. They do not spark joy. They spark a low, persistent uncertainty, a hum at the edge of attention, like a radio left on in another room. Yet I suspect that they are doing some kind of work. They are a record, however incomplete, of places I have been, people I have lived near, and locks that once were important enough to require a key. Discarding them would be tidy, but it would also be a small act of forgetting, and I am not sure I want to forget as efficiently as I might like.

Maybe this is simply sentimentality, and maybe sentimentality is underrated. A certain amount of it is necessary for a life to feel like a life rather than a series of transactions. We are, after all, made of the accumulated residue of our attachments. The keys are residue. The batteries are residue. The chopstick, orphaned from its pair, is residue in the most literal sense: what remains after a larger thing has dissolved.

---

I do not want to romanticise the junk drawer too much. It is also, quite plainly, a problem. It is hard to find the thing you need in it. It is cluttered and occasionally sharp. The batteries are probably leaking. The rubber bands are perishing into a sticky mess. I know that, if I were a better organised person, I would sort the drawer into compartments, label the keys, test the batteries, and recycle the menu. I would have a drawer of tools and a drawer of cutlery and a drawer of things I actually use. It would be efficient and perhaps, in its way, beautiful.

And yet I suspect I would also be sad. The disorder is not just disorder. It is a tolerance for not knowing. The drawer says, in effect, that not everything in a life needs to be explained or justified or accounted for. Some things can simply be kept, in the dark, on the chance that they might matter someday, even if that someday never arrives. There is a generosity in that, a refusal to assume that the past is worthless merely because it has stopped being useful.

I think about the people who might have owned these keys. They are probably not thinking about me. They have their own drawers, their own accumulations, their own small uncertainties about which thing belongs to which life. The world is full of these unlabelled objects, these partial stories, and most of them will never be pieced together. A stranger might one day find my drawer after I am gone, and see the twist ties and the keys and the menu and try to guess at the person who kept them. The guess will be wrong in most particulars and perhaps right in one or two. That seems about the most any of us can hope for, from the people who come after: a partial and affectionate error.

---

So the drawer stays, for now. I will not clean it today, though I might tidy the batteries into a bag and take them to the appropriate bin when I remember. The keys will keep their secrets, and I will keep my ignorance of them, which is its own kind of intimacy. I have decided that not knowing what a key opens is not the same as failing to understand my life. It is simply one of the ways that life exceeds my understanding, leaving remnants I cannot fully account for and do not need to.

There is a larger lesson here, I think, though I hesitate to make it too neat. Every household, every mind, every life, contains a drawer like this. Some are literal, filled with rubber bands and dead batteries. Others are figurative: old grievances, unfinished projects, half-remembered friendships, passions that once burned and now sit quietly in the dark. We keep them because we cannot bear to decide, in one stroke, that they no longer count. We keep them because they remind us that we were once someone who believed in power cuts, or in keys, or in the future enough to save a chopstick for its pair.

The skilled tidier will tell you that you can let all of that go, and perhaps for some people in some circumstances that is true and even liberating. But I am not sure it is true for everything. Some objects, like some memories, are worth keeping precisely because they cannot be fully explained. They sit at the edge of the known, asking quiet questions, and the questions are a kind of company.

I push the drawer shut. It sticks halfway, then gives, the way it always does, as though it has been waiting for me to make a decision and has decided, kindly, to let me off this time. The keys stay where they are. Tomorrow I will still not know what they open. Some nights that bothers me, and some nights it does not, and I have come to think the difference between those nights is most of what it means to live with a past you cannot fully recover, and with a future that is, like the drawer itself, mostly full of things we have not yet learned how to use.

# On the Things Maps Leave Out

Every map is a kind of lie told in order to be useful. A map of a city shrinks the city to the size of a tablecloth and then pretends that the shrinking is faithful. It draws the river as a single blue line when the river is actually a churning, silted, seasonal thing that floods a neighborhood every spring. It draws the streets as thin black threads, though each one has a smell, a slope, a particular crack in the pavement where someone once lost a tooth. The map is honest about what it chooses to include and silent about everything else, and that silence is the part I find most interesting.

I have been thinking about maps lately, partly because I have been thinking about gaps. Maps have always been places where people admit, or fail to admit, what they do not know. The early European cartographers faced a peculiar problem. The known world was smaller than the world they had to draw. Their charts ended at the edges of sailors' reports, and beyond those edges lay what they called *terra incognita*, unknown land. Some mapmakers simply left the space blank. Others filled it with ornament: sea monsters curling through the water, wind-blowing cherubs in the corners, the occasional tribe of men with their heads beneath their shoulders. The blank and the monstrous were two ways of saying the same thing. We do not know what is here.

What strikes me is that the monsters were often more honest than the blanks. A blank space looks like nothing. It suggests an empty ocean or a land without inhabitants, and a reader could easily assume that what isn't marked is simply absent. A drawing of a sea serpent says something different. It says *here there is something we cannot describe, and we would rather you know that than think there is nothing here.* The illustrator was marking the boundary of his own ignorance, which is one of the more difficult things for any person to do in public.

There is a stranger category still, which is the invented place. Cartographers, worried that competitors were copying their work, sometimes placed fictional towns, rivers, or islands on their maps. If a rival reproduced the map faithfully, the phantom would appear on the rival's version too, and the original mapmaker could prove the theft. These were called paper towns, or trap streets, and a few of them managed to escape the paper and enter the world. A settlement called Agloe, in New York's Catskill Mountains, was a famous example. It appeared on a map published by a company in the 1930s, and when people began to ask about it, they discovered that it did not exist. Eventually someone opened a general store there, named it the Agloe General Store, and the store became a real place with a real address. The fiction had been adopted by the world it was meant to protect itself against.

I like this story more than I can easily justify. It suggests that the line between what is and what is written down is thinner than we pretend. A map is supposed to follow the land, but sometimes the land follows the map. Roads get built where the planners drew them. Borders harden into fences along lines that were once only ink. A town that exists only on paper can, under the right conditions, acquire a post office and a grudge.

Maps also leave out people, which is perhaps the most consequential omission of all. The standard street map shows where the roads go but not who walks them, who is afraid to walk them after dark, who has been pushed out of the neighborhood by rents that rose faster than the pavement was repaired. Some modern maps try to fix this. Heat maps show where ambulances go most often. Maps of redlining, the old practice of marking certain neighborhoods as hazardous for lending, reveal how institutions once drew invisible lines through cities and then acted as if the lines were natural features of the terrain. Reading those maps is unsettling because they are so precise. Someone sat down with a pen and decided, in effect, which blocks were worth saving. The map did not just describe a city; it helped decide the city's future.

So a map is never neutral. It is a decision about what matters enough to be drawn, made by someone with particular purposes, usually for someone else's use. This is not a scandal. It is simply what maps are. The problem arises when we forget that a map is a choice and begin to treat it as a window.

I think about this in relation to myself, too. Each of us carries a private map of ourselves, and it is drawn at a similar scale of usefulness. We mark the landmarks we are proud of: the job, the degree, the house, the sensible decision we made at twenty-six that turned out well. We draw the rivers of our childhood as single lines. We leave large areas blank because we do not have the words for them, or because we are ashamed of what the words would reveal. And when people meet us, they see the map we show them, and they often take it for the territory.

What would an honest self-map look like? It would probably need to include the sea monsters: the fears we cannot describe, the appetites we would rather not name, the places in our history where we simply do not know what happened or why we responded as we did. It would need the paper towns too, the pieces of self-description we invented to protect ourselves from being copied or judged, which have since become so real that we forget they were invented at all. Some of us have a whole town of this kind. We say we are the sort of person who is not bothered by criticism, or who has always known what we wanted, and after years of repetition the claim has acquired a post office.

I do not mean that we should abandon the simplified map. We could not function without it. Nobody can walk through life while attending to every river and every hidden cellar. Reduction is how the mind copes with complexity, and the map's selectivity is a kindness as much as a limitation. A map that showed everything would be as useless as the territory itself, which is too large and too detailed to hold in one glance. The art lies in knowing which things were left out and being willing to go back and check.

This is the lesson I wish I had learned earlier. When I look at a map now, I try to ask what it has omitted and why. Who decided this road was important and that alley was not? Whose names are missing? What does the blank space conceal, and who benefits from the concealment? These questions do not make the map worthless. They make it readable. They turn it from a set of instructions into an argument, and an argument can be answered, revised, and improved.

The same questions can be applied to the maps we carry in our heads. When I notice that I have described myself in a particular way for a long time, I can ask whether the description is accurate or merely convenient. When I find a blank area in my understanding of someone I love, I can resist the temptation to fill it with a confident drawing. Sometimes the honest move is to draw a small sea serpent and write beside it: *here be something I do not understand yet.*

There is something almost tender in the old mapmakers' sea monsters. They were not sophisticated, and they were often wrong, but they were modest in a way that the cleanest modern charts sometimes are not. They admitted that the sea was bigger than their knowledge of it. They left room for surprise. A sailor who looked at one of those maps knew that the coast he was approaching might contain things nobody had recorded, and he would have to keep his eyes open.

Perhaps that is the best attitude to take toward any map, including the ones we make of ourselves and each other. Use them, because they are necessary and often beautiful. Trust them enough to navigate by them. But keep an eye on the margins, where the ink thins out and the monsters are waiting. Expect the territory to be stranger than the drawing. And when you reach a place the map did not predict, do not insist that it is not there. Stop, look, and start drawing again.

# On Noticing

For most of my life I have walked the same few blocks to the same places, and for most of that time I saw almost none of them. The route from the front door to the bus stop, the bus stop to the office, the office back again: I could make the trip with my eyes half closed, and often I did. Then one October morning I left my phone in my pocket, took the long way around, and discovered that the street I had walked perhaps two thousand times had been quietly changing the whole while.

There was a fern growing out of a crack in the sidewalk, just beside the curb, its fronds curled like the top of a violin. I have no idea how long it had been there. Weeks, probably. Maybe years. A fig tree had leaned its branches over a brick garden wall, and someone had tied a strip of blue ribbon to the iron gate, faded almost to gray. A window that I had always assumed was painted shut was open, and a cat was sitting on the sill watching the street with the complete seriousness of a magistrate.

None of this was new. It had all been there. What was new was me, or at least the part of me that was paying attention.

I think a great deal of ordinary life is lived in this half-sleep. Our minds are efficient, and efficiency means discarding what seems already known. The brain builds a model of the world and then, to save energy, stops checking the model against reality. We see the shape we expect rather than the thing in front of us. This is useful. Nobody could cross a busy intersection if they had to re-examine every object from scratch. But the cost is that the familiar becomes invisible, and invisibility is a kind of absence. We can live for years in a city, a marriage, a job, or a body without really looking at any of them.

The poet Mary Oliver wrote, more or less, that attention is the beginning of devotion. I have always found that phrase a little grand, but I understand the impulse behind it. To attend to something is to grant it existence in a fuller way. When I stopped to look at the fern, it stopped being background and became a particular thing with its own history and its own stubborn will to live in a crack that had no business supporting it.

Attention is also, I have come to believe, a form of respect, and perhaps of love. People who have spent decades with one landscape, a farmer who knows which corner of the field floods in spring or a fisherman who can read the color of the water, seem to me to possess a kind of wealth that cannot be easily measured. They have noticed. Their knowledge is not abstract. It is made of thousands of small observations, each one a moment of paying attention rather than assuming.

I do not want to romanticize this too much. Attention is tiring, and the world does not always deserve it. Some streets are ugly, and some days are merely gray. There is a version of mindfulness that becomes a kind of self-improvement project, a checklist of gratitudes to be ticked off before breakfast, and I find that version as wearying as the autopilot it claims to cure. Noticing is not a performance. It does not need to produce a feeling of joy. Sometimes it simply reveals that a building needs painting, or that the bus is late again, and that is information too.

Still, there is a particular pleasure in the discovery of the already-known. It resembles the feeling of finding a letter you forgot you had written, or hearing a song from childhood and remembering all the words. The world is not hiding from us. It is simply waiting, patiently, for us to lift our heads.

I have been trying, since that October morning, to take the long way more often. Not every day, and not with any grand resolution, but enough to keep the habit alive. I have learned that the bus stop has a bench with a small brass plaque I had never read, honoring someone who loved this neighborhood. I have learned that the bakery on the corner changes its window display with the seasons and that the baker, a silver-haired man who never seems to sit down, hums while he works. I have learned that the fern is still there, though it has grown a little larger, and that somebody has begun to water it.

That last detail delights me most. Someone else has noticed too. Perhaps it was a neighbor, or a child on the way to school, or a passerby with time to spare and a bottle of water in a bag. Attention, it turns out, is contagious in the gentlest way. One person looks closely at a small green thing and then another person does too, and a street that was merely a route becomes a place.

I do not know how much of my life I have passed without seeing. I suspect the answer is a great deal. But I am no longer convinced that the loss is final. The fern was there all along, waiting for me to bend down and look. Most of what matters, I suspect, is like that: already present, already growing in the cracks, asking only for a little of our slow and deliberate regard.

# On Listening to the House

Every house has a voice, and most of us stopped hearing it years ago. The refrigerator hums in a particular key. The old radiator knocks twice before it warms up, like someone asking permission to come in. The stairs complain under a certain weight, so that a family member's footsteps can be identified from the bedroom without looking. We live inside these sounds the way we live inside the color of the walls, noticing them only when they change.

I've been thinking about this because of a small event. For about a week, the house went quiet in a way I didn't expect. The refrigerator had been replaced, and the new one runs without the low drone the old one made. At first I kept waiting for a sound that wasn't coming. I'd walk into the kitchen and pause, the way you pause on a staircase when you've miscounted a step. Only after several days did I realize how much of my sense of home had been built out of that hum. The absence felt like a missing word in a sentence I knew by heart.

This is strange, because we tend to think of home as something visual or spatial. We describe it by its rooms, its square footage, the view from the kitchen window. But when I try to remember the places I've lived, the first things that return are sounds. The particular cough of a furnace in a rented apartment in a city I no longer live in. The screen door in my grandmother's house, which had a double-note squeal, one high and one low, as it closed. A neighbor's dog that barked at the same hour every evening, so reliably that it became a kind of clock. None of these were beautiful, exactly. But they were mine, and they carried a weight that photographs don't.

Sound is also peculiarly tied to time. A photograph freezes a moment, but a sound is always happening. It requires duration. You can't hear a single instant of rain; you hear the rain falling for a while, and the longer it falls, the more it becomes a container for everything else you were doing. Rain on a metal roof is a different experience from rain on shingles, and rain on a window is different again, more intimate, close to the body. People who grew up with a certain kind of rain carry it with them for life. I suspect that's why so many of us find rain soothing even when we have no memory of a specific storm. We're recognizing something older than memory, a rhythm our bodies learned before we had words.

There's a larger lesson here about attention. We live in an age that is loud in some ways and oddly numb in others. We are surrounded by notifications, music piped into elevators, engines idling outside, and yet we rarely listen. Listening is different from hearing. Hearing is passive; sound simply arrives. Listening requires a decision to turn toward something, to let it occupy you for a moment. It is a small act of respect. When you listen to a person, you give them your time and your quiet. When you listen to a house, you learn where its tensions are, which pipes are failing, which windows let in the wind.

I've started doing a small exercise, which I'd recommend to anyone. Once a day, I sit somewhere in my home with my eyes closed and try to name every sound I can hear, from the nearest to the most distant. The list usually begins with obvious things: a voice, a car, the tick of a clock. Then it grows stranger. The faint whine of a laptop fan. The hush of air moving through a vent. Water settling in a pipe after someone flushed a toilet two floors up. Birds I can't see. The creak of a chair as I shift my weight. Within a few minutes, a room that felt empty is full. It's as if the house, which I'd thought of as a static object, reveals itself to be a busy, breathing thing.

Of course, not every sound is welcome. Some are reminders of things that need fixing, or of noise from neighbors that wears on the nerves. There's a difference between the sounds that make a place feel like home and the ones that make it feel like a burden. But even the unwelcome sounds teach something. The buzzing light in the hallway tells you that a bulb is failing. The faucet's drip, which keeps you awake, reminds you that a small thing can take up a great deal of space if you let it.

Perhaps this is what it means to be at home somewhere: to know its sounds so well that their absence feels like a loss, and their presence feels like company. We can't choose every sound around us, but we can choose to notice them. And when we do, we discover that the places we live are not silent backdrops to our lives. They are constantly speaking, in low voices and small creaks, and if we listen carefully, they tell us that we are still here, still in the middle of something, still being held.

The new refrigerator, I should say, has become familiar now. I no longer wait for the hum that isn't there. Instead, I've started noticing the faint click it makes when its cycle changes, a sound I'd never heard before because the old machine was too loud to let it through. It's a small new note in the house's song. I'm learning it, the way you learn a new friend's laugh, one ordinary moment at a time.

# On the Blank Spaces

Old maps often had their most interesting features in the empty places. Cartographers who did not know what lay beyond the coastline sometimes wrote a warning in the margin, *here be dragons*, or drew a sea serpent curling through the water. Some left the interior of a continent white and unlabeled, a polite admission of ignorance. I find these blank spaces more honest than the detailed maps that came after them. They say plainly: we have not been here, and we do not know.

Modern maps have mostly filled those gaps. Satellites photograph every ridge and river. You can zoom in on a street in a city you will never visit and see the cracks in the pavement. Yet something has been lost along the way. The blank space did more than mark ignorance. It was an invitation. It asked the reader to imagine, to wonder, and perhaps to go and see for themselves.

I have a soft spot for the people who drew those early maps. They were working from travelers' accounts, which were often exaggerated, sometimes confused, and occasionally invented outright. A sailor who had been blown off course might describe an island that did not exist, and a cartographer would faithfully ink it onto the chart. Phantom islands persisted for centuries. Some were still appearing on maps in the nineteenth century, because no one had sailed back to check. There is something touching in that stubbornness, the way a rumor could outlive its evidence simply because nobody had disproved it yet.

Blank spaces also exist in our own lives, though we rarely draw them. There are years we cannot account for, friendships that drifted without an ending, and questions we never thought to ask our parents until they were gone. We tend to treat these gaps as failures, things to be ashamed of or hurried past. But perhaps they could be treated the way old cartographers treated the unknown interior, as a place to acknowledge honestly and approach with curiosity rather than dread.

I think about this when I consider how much certainty people feel they need. We are uncomfortable saying "I don't know," and in conversation we often reach for a confident answer even when our knowledge is thin. Politicians do it, experts do it, and so do ordinary people at dinner parties who would rather sound informed than admit they have only heard a half-remembered story. The early mapmakers were, in a sense, more disciplined than we are. When they did not know, they left the space empty, or they wrote down exactly what they had been told and noted its source.

There is an argument that the blank spaces were not really honest, since a sea monster on a map is not an admission of ignorance but a kind of decoration, a way of making the unknown look charming. Perhaps. But even decoration tells us something. A map drawn in the sixteenth century reveals what its makers feared, hoped for, and found beautiful. Looking at one now, we see not only the coastline but the imagination of the people who drew it, their assumptions about the world and their sense of its wildness.

I wonder what our maps will reveal to future readers. Our current ones look so complete, with every road named and every building outlined, but they hide their own blank spaces in less visible ways: the oceans we have barely sampled, the deep soil beneath our feet that remains mostly uncharted, the inner lives of creatures we share the planet with. We have filled the margins with data, and the data gives an impression of thoroughness. Someday someone may look back and see how much we did not know, and smile at our confidence the way we smile at the phantom islands.

Still, I do not think the answer is to go back to drawing dragons. The impulse behind those drawings was not foolish. It was a recognition that the world is larger than our knowledge of it, and that this is worth remembering. The best explorers I have read about carried that recognition with them. They wrote carefully about what they saw, marked clearly what they could not confirm, and treated the edge of the known as a beginning rather than a wall.

So when I look at a modern map now, I try to look past the tidy grid of streets and find the places where the information thins out: the mountain range with only a few spot elevations, the coastline sketched from a distance, the region labeled simply "unsurveyed." Those places still hold the old invitation. They remind me that there is more to learn, and that the most honest thing I can say about much of the world is that I have not yet been there.

# On Unfinished Things

Somewhere in my house there is a half-finished crossword, folded into a drawer. It has been there for about two years. Most of the squares are filled in, and a handful of clues still sit open, waiting for a word I never found. I think of it sometimes, the way you think about a friend you lost touch with. It isn't a tragedy. It's just unfinished, and I've come to suspect that unfinished things make up a larger share of the world than finished ones.

Consider the cathedrals. Many of the great ones were begun by people who knew they would never see them completed. Masons carved stones for towers that wouldn't rise until their grandchildren's time, and some spires were never built at all. Look at the facade of a cathedral in Milan or the unfinished towers of some Gothic churches in Europe and you see a building that is also a kind of argument: the people who built it believed in a future they wouldn't inhabit. There is something moving about that faith. It requires you to care about a result you will never claim.

We are less comfortable with that now. We live in an age of completion metrics. Progress bars fill, notifications clear, inboxes are emptied and celebrated. The unfinished has come to feel like a failure of discipline. But I've started to think this is a distortion. Much of what gives life its texture is precisely what remains open: the conversation that ended before the argument was settled, the friendship that drifted into a warm, uncertain distance, the language you were learning and then stopped learning, still able to say *good morning* and *where is the bathroom* and not much else.

Think about music. Schubert left his Symphony No. 8 with two complete movements and a fragment of a third, and it has been known for more than a century as the "Unfinished." Nobody hears it and thinks, *what a shame*. We hear it and feel the strange ache of something cut off mid-sentence, and that ache is part of the beauty. The silence after the second movement is not an absence so much as a question, and we carry it with us. Had Schubert finished the symphony in the conventional way, we would have a pleasant piece of music. Instead we have a door left ajar.

There is also a practical wisdom in leaving things unfinished. Painters have long known that a canvas can be overworked. The sketch has a looseness, a confidence in its gestures, that the polished final version sometimes loses. Writers talk about the first draft as a kind of permission: a place where you are allowed to be wrong because nobody is grading you yet. Unfinished work is honest about its own process. It shows its seams. It tells you that someone was thinking here, and then thinking moved on.

I suspect part of our anxiety about the unfinished comes from mortality. Every project left incomplete is a small reminder that our time is limited, that someone else will have to sort out our drawers and our half-written letters and our draft novels stored on old hard drives. The Latin phrase *memento mori* is usually taken as a call to gloom, but it can also be an invitation to lightness. If nothing is ever fully finished, then nothing has to be perfect to matter. The crossword does not need to be completed for the afternoons I spent with it to have been worth something.

My grandmother kept a garden she never considered finished. Every spring she moved a bed, replanted a row, tried a new climbing rose against a fence that was already crowded. When visitors praised it, she waved them off. "It's never done," she'd say, with a satisfaction that was hard to mistake for regret. I didn't understand her then. I think I do now. For her, the garden was not a product to be delivered. It was a relationship, and relationships don't get finished. They get tended.

Maybe that is the real lesson of the unfinished. It asks us to shift from the question "Is it done?" to the question "Is it alive?" A living thing is always in some state of becoming. A tree is never finished growing, and neither is a city, a language, a person. We are all, in a sense, the unfinished symphony: a few movements played with conviction, a few passages still waiting for their resolution, and a silence at the end that we will not get to hear from the inside.

So I am leaving the crossword in its drawer. Maybe someday I'll pull it out, find the word that eluded me, and feel the small click of completion. Or maybe I won't, and it will stay there as a reminder that I once cared enough about a stray clue to carry it for two years. Either way, it has done its work. It was a place where I was curious, stubborn, and a little bit hopeful, and those things do not require a finished grid to be real.

# On Unfinished Things

There is a kind of comfort in leaving things unfinished. I don't mean the work that piles up and makes us anxious. I mean the half-read book face-down on the nightstand, the sweater with one sleeve knit and the other still on the needles, the letter that has been "almost done" for three weeks. These objects sit in our lives like open doors, and I have come to think they are some of the most honest things we own.

Finished things ask nothing of us. A completed painting hangs on the wall and tells you what it is. A novel, once you reach the last page, is closed for good, its ending fixed like a stone in a riverbed. That permanence has its own dignity, but it also has a kind of silence. Unfinished things keep talking. The unfinished sweater says, *you were once someone who wanted to make this for another person.* The bookmark says, *the story is still waiting, and so is the version of you who was enjoying it.*

I have a notebook filled with beginnings. Some are only a line long: a woman who keeps bees in a city apartment, a man who writes letters to a lighthouse keeper who died in 1911, a sentence about the smell of wet pennies that I wrote on a train and have never been able to continue. When I flip through it, I feel no shame at the abandoned pages. Instead I feel a strange sort of company. Each beginning is a small argument I once had with the world, and I am glad that some of those arguments were never settled, because an unsettled argument leaves room for later.

We live in a culture that prizes completion. We measure ourselves by output, by the number of projects shipped and goals crossed off. There is a particular modern anxiety in seeing a list with too many open items, as though each one were a debt. But I suspect much of what makes a life rich is precisely the amount of it that remains open. A person who has finished everything has, in a sense, run out of reasons to continue. The unfinished is the reserve, the place where curiosity lives.

Consider how gardens work. A garden is never finished. Even the most meticulous gardener is always in the middle of something: pruning, planting, waiting for the clematis to climb the fence it hasn't yet reached. The garden is valuable precisely because it is in process, because each season revises the last. Nobody walks through a garden and wishes it were complete. We walk through it wanting to see what it becomes.

Relationships work this way too. The best conversations with old friends never fully conclude. You pick up a thread from a decade ago and find it still tugging at something in both of you. Marriages that last are rarely built on a single moment of resolution; they are built on a thousand small continuations, on the daily decision to keep going with someone whose story is still being written. To finish a person, to decide you understand them entirely, is to close a door that should have stayed ajar.

Of course, there is a flip side. Some unfinished things are simply abandoned, and abandonment is not the same as openness. The unpaid bill, the apology never offered, the dream we stopped feeding because it felt too hard: these carry weight, and pretending otherwise is a kind of self-deception. The task, I think, is to learn the difference between what is waiting and what is wilting. A waiting thing still gets a glance now and then, still tugs at the attention. A wilting thing has become a reproach, and maybe the honest move is to let it go with some gratitude for what it taught.

I try, lately, to keep a few things deliberately open. I leave a chapter of a book unread for a month. I start a drawing I know I won't finish this week. I let the question stay a question instead of rushing it toward an answer. This feels less like laziness than like keeping faith with the possibility that I will be different later, that the person who returns to the sweater in spring will have learned something the person who began it did not.

There is also humility in the unfinished. It admits that we don't know how things will turn out, that our understanding is provisional, that the next page might change everything we thought we knew about the story. A finished life, if such a thing exists, is available only in retrospect, and even then only to others. From the inside, we are always mid-sentence.

So I have made a small peace with my clutter of incomplete things. The stacked books, the half-written letters, the seedlings that never quite became plants: they are evidence that I kept wanting things, kept starting, kept believing there would be time. That belief, however often it has been tested, seems to me one of the more hopeful habits a person can have.

Tonight I will probably not finish the book on my nightstand. I will read a few pages, put it face-down again, and turn off the lamp. In the morning it will still be there, open at the same place, waiting for me to come back and see what happens next. I find I am grateful for that. Some doors should stay open a little longer.

Every house I've lived in has a drawer that nobody opens on purpose. It's usually the one nearest the kitchen door or beside the bed, and it holds the things we decided, at some earlier moment, were too useful to throw away. Rubber bands from newspapers that no longer arrive. A tangle of twist ties. Three keys whose locks I can't name. Batteries of uncertain charge. A church bulletin from a wedding in 2014. Half a roll of masking tape, the good kind.

I've been thinking about why we keep these things, and I don't think the answer is simply thrift or laziness, though it is sometimes both. Keeping a rubber band is a small bet on the future. It says: there will be a moment when I need to bind something together, and on that day I will be glad I didn't let this go. Most of the time the bet loses. The rubber band sits for years, slowly drying into a brittle ring, and then one day it snaps when you touch it, and you feel a faint embarrassment at how long you were guarding it.

But every so often the bet pays off, and that payoff keeps the whole habit alive. The stray key fits the lockbox nobody could open. The orphaned screw is exactly the size the cabinet hinge needed. The lone twist tie closes the bread bag in a moment when nothing else would. These wins are so satisfying because they're rare, and because they feel like the drawer has been vindicated. Its clutter becomes an archive of possibilities, each item a question the future might someday ask.

There's something quietly hopeful in this. Keeping the drawer is a way of refusing to believe that a moment is finished. Modern life tries hard to tell us otherwise. We're encouraged to declutter, to keep only what sparks joy, to admire the minimal and the curated. Those ideas have merit. A house buried in paper is genuinely oppressive, and I have felt that weight. But the drawer of useless useful things resists the logic of the purchase. It reminds me that most objects aren't really commodities to us. They're fragments of situations we once lived in and of futures we once imagined.

Think about the keys in particular. Each was cut for a specific door, and someone once needed it every day: the apartment where you lived at twenty-three, a car you sold, an office you left behind. The key has outlasted the relevance of its door. Holding it is a way of holding that former life, and though you couldn't tell anyone which lock it belonged to, you know it belonged to something. The key has become pure memory, detached from function, which may be the most a physical object can become.

The same is true of the small envelope of spare buttons, each one labeled in your mother's handwriting, or in your own, years ago, with the name of a coat that may no longer exist. Buttons are a particularly honest kind of keepsake. They promise repair, and repair implies that you intend to go on wearing things, mending them, and staying in the same shape long enough for the shape to need mending. A spare button is a small vote for continuity.

Of course there is a limit. Hoarding is real suffering, and the line between a useful drawer and a sealed room of unopened boxes is not always easy to see from inside. I think the healthy version of the habit has a particular shape: it is small, bounded, and occasionally consulted. The drawer has walls. When it overflows, you sort it, and the sorting is its own quiet ritual, a moment of admitting that most of the bets have lost and letting those go, while keeping a handful that still feel alive. The discipline is not in keeping nothing. It's in keeping on purpose.

I sometimes imagine a future archaeologist excavating the drawer of a typical house and trying to reconstruct the people who lived there. What would she conclude? That they were careful, perhaps, and a little anxious about being unprepared. That they believed in second chances for objects, and in the eventual arrival of a need. That they wrote phone numbers on the backs of receipts and never quite trusted anything to hold information for them. She would be right about some of it, and wrong about the rest, because she would be missing the feeling behind the clutter, which is hard to dig up: a sense that the future would ask for something, and that it was worth being ready.

I like to think the drawer is one of the few places in a home where we keep faith with the unknown. We never know what we'll need. We rarely do. The rubber band, the key, the spare button are our small way of saying we expect to keep living, that the world will keep handing us problems, and that with luck we'll be able to solve them with whatever happened to be lying around. Most of the time we won't need any of it. But on the one occasion we do, the drawer will be waiting, a little crowded and a little ridiculous, and it will have been right to be there all along.

# On the Blank Spaces of Old Maps

There is a particular kind of map I have always loved: the old ones, drawn before satellites and before anyone could fly over a coastline and photograph it. They are beautiful in a way that modern maps rarely are, and not only because of the ink and the lettering, the sea monsters curled in the corners, or the compass roses that look like they could bloom. What moves me most is how honest they are about what they don't know.

Consider a sixteenth-century chart of the Atlantic. The coast of West Africa is drawn with some confidence, because Portuguese sailors had been creeping down it for generations, logging every bay and sandbar. But the interior is often a blank, or filled with vague notations: *here are lions*, *here is a great river*, *here the people are said to be giants*. Farther out, the ocean is simply empty, or decorated with ships and wind-blowing faces. The mapmaker did not pretend. The gaps were left as gaps, or dressed in stories that everyone understood to be stories.

Modern maps have erased that honesty. Open any navigation app and the world looks finished. Every road is labeled, every river traced, every building outlined in soft gray. Even the places no one has visited are rendered with the same crisp certainty as your own street. The blank spaces have been filled, often by algorithms, sometimes by guesswork that has hardened into fact. I do not think this is simply a loss. Accuracy is a gift. But something gets lost when uncertainty disappears from view entirely, because uncertainty is where curiosity lives.

I think about this often in terms of my own life. I carry a kind of internal map, and it has more blank space than I would like to admit. There are whole regions of my understanding, of my family's history, of my own mind, that I have never bothered to survey. I used to feel embarrassed about this, as if a competent adult should have every coastline charted by now. But the old cartographers suggest a different attitude. A blank is not a failure. It is an invitation, and sometimes a warning. *Here be dragons* was not a joke so much as a note to the reader: proceed with care, and do not assume you know what you are looking at.

There is also a generosity in old maps that I find moving. They were made by people who knew they would be wrong in places, and who expected later travelers to correct them. Coastlines were redrawn, islands that had been imagined were erased, and rivers were discovered to bend in ways no one had guessed. The map was never a final verdict. It was a conversation between the people who had gone out and the people who would come after. Each correction was a small act of humility and a larger act of trust in the next sailor.

I wonder what a map of our present era would look like if drawn with that same spirit. Perhaps the margins would be full of notes in different hands: *surveyed in 1987, probably outdated*, *reported by a traveler, unconfirmed*, *the locals say this is different now*. Perhaps the blank spaces would be marked not with monsters but with question marks, which seem to me a more honest decoration than a whale or a compass rose. A question mark tells the reader that the world is still being explored, that the people who came before were not fools, and that the people who come after are welcome to add their own lines.

Maybe that is what I love most about the old maps. They remember that knowledge is a process. Every line on them is the residue of someone's journey, someone's risk, someone's willingness to sail toward an edge they could not see. The mapmakers were not omniscient. They were brave, and sometimes wrong, and always in the middle of the work.

I keep a reproduction of one such map on my wall, a rough chart of a coastline from about 1550. The paper has yellowed to the color of weak tea. In one corner, a small note in faded brown ink says something I have never been able to translate fully, though I have tried. Some words are clear; others have bled into the fibers of the page. I find that I don't mind. It reminds me that even the record of what we know is partial, and that the most interesting parts of any map are often the parts that have not yet been written down.

So I try, now, to hold my own understanding more loosely. When I meet someone I think I know, or a place I assume I have figured out, I try to remember the sixteenth-century cartographer, sketching the edge of a continent from secondhand reports and hopeful guesses. I try to leave a little blank space, and to be glad of it. The world is larger than my chart of it, and that is not a disappointment. It is the whole reason to keep sailing.

# On Half-Read Books

Almost everyone has a bookmark stuck somewhere in the middle of a book they stopped reading. Mine is in a paperback about the history of lighthouses, lodged around page 140, where the author begins describing the engineering of a Scottish reef light. I put it down one evening three years ago and never picked it up again. The bookmark is a receipt from a coffee shop that has since closed. Every time I walk past the shelf, the book reminds me that I once meant to finish it.

I have come to think the half-read book is one of the more honest objects we own. A finished book is a closed case. It has a verdict: I liked it, or I didn't, or it changed me a little. A half-read book has no verdict. It sits in an uncertain state, neither rejected nor embraced, holding whatever version of me was interested at the time. It is a record of a particular moment's attention, and attention is something most of us spend badly and rarely account for.

There's a common assumption that finishing things is a virtue and abandoning them a weakness. Some of that is true. A novel you've committed to deserves the courtesy of its last chapter, and quitting a job or a friendship or a hard conversation can be a way of avoiding the discomfort that finishing requires. But I've also noticed that the impulse to finish everything can make reading feel like homework. We push through dull passages because we feel we owe the author, or because we've already invested two hundred pages and sunk-cost logic whispers that the investment must pay off. Often it doesn't, and the honest move is to stop.

Still, I find myself drawn back to the unfinished ones. There's a particular pull in a book you abandoned at the exact point where the story was about to turn. I know a novel I put down during the chapter where a character decides to leave her marriage. I stopped, I think, because the book was making me uncomfortable in a way I wasn't ready to examine. Years later I can't say whether I stopped because the prose was dull or because the story was too close to something in my own life. The unfinished book holds that ambiguity for me. It asks a question I never answered.

Writers have long been fascinated by incomplete things. Schubert left his Symphony No. 8 in B minor with two complete movements and a fragment of a third, and it has become one of the most beloved pieces in the orchestral repertoire, partly because of its incompleteness. Listeners fill the silence with their own longing. Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts, and Brod, thankfully, didn't. The Aeneid was nearly destroyed because Virgil wanted to revise it, and he died before he could. We remember these works in part because they stopped short of the perfection their makers intended, and the gaps give us room to step into.

Maybe that is what a half-read book offers. It is an invitation I never accepted, a door I opened and walked away from. Returning to it means meeting the earlier version of myself who was reading it, and deciding whether to continue the conversation or let it rest. Some books I finish years later and find them transformed, as if the intervening life supplied the context they needed. Others I open again, read a page, and close with relief, confirming that I was right to stop.

I suspect there's a broader lesson in this, one that extends beyond paperbacks. We accumulate a lot of unfinished things: projects, languages we meant to learn, letters we began and never sent, a half-painted room, a plan to visit a town we keep meaning to see. We often feel guilty about them, as if each represents a failure of character. But many of them are simply evidence that our interests shift, that we're curious about more things than we have time for, that we keep trying. An unfinished life is not necessarily a wasted one. It might just be a life that kept opening doors.

So I'm going to leave the lighthouse book where it is for now. Maybe I'll finish it next winter, when the weather turns and the light comes in low through the window. Or maybe the bookmark will simply stay where it is, a small flag marking the place where I stopped to look at something else. Either way, the book has done its job. It reminded me, every time I passed it, that attention is finite and precious, and that the things we set down are not always lost. Sometimes they're just waiting for us to come back and see what we've become.
