# On the Value of Waiting

There was a time when you could not know something right away. If you wanted to know whether a friend across the ocean had received your news, you wrote a letter, sealed it, carried it to a post box, and then waited. The letter crossed oceans in ships, sat in sacks on trains, and was sorted by hands you would never see. Weeks passed. Then, sometimes, a reply arrived, written in a different season from the one you were living in. The waiting was built into the correspondence itself. You could not hurry it, so you learned to live alongside it.

I find myself thinking about that gap a great deal lately, mostly because it has nearly disappeared. Almost everything now arrives the moment we reach for it. A question becomes an answer in the time it takes to type it. A photograph of a sunset from a stranger's balcony appears before the sun has fully set in my own sky. This is marvelous in many ways, and I would not give it back entirely. But I wonder what we lose when no interval remains between wanting and receiving.

Waiting does something to desire. When you have to wait for a thing, you have time to imagine it. You build it in your head, usually larger and more detailed than the reality will turn out to be, and then the reality arrives and either fulfills the picture or quietly corrects it. Both outcomes teach you something. Instant access skips that rehearsal. We get the thing before we have had the chance to want it properly, and so wanting becomes thinner, a reflex instead of a relationship.

Consider the kettle. Anyone who has waited for water to boil knows the peculiar stillness of it. You stand in the kitchen with nothing to do, listening for the first tick of metal and the rising hiss. Some people reach for their phones in those minutes. Others simply stand there, watching the window fog or the light move across the counter. I have come to think of those unplanned minutes as a kind of small gift, a permission to do nothing that the day rarely grants. Nobody schedules them. They happen because the physics of heating water refuses to be rushed.

Patience, I suspect, is less a virtue than a byproduct of living in a world where things take the time they take. A seed does not sprout because you wished hard enough. Bread needs to rise for as long as it needs. A friendship deepens across years of ordinary Tuesdays, not in bursts of intensity. When everything is accelerated, we begin to misjudge which things actually need time, and we grow impatient with the people and processes that cannot be compressed. A person who takes a day to answer a message is not necessarily ignoring you. They may be thinking, or busy, or simply living at a human pace. Our expectations have drifted so far from that pace that we experience ordinary delay as rejection.

I do not want to romanticize the past too much. Waiting was often miserable. People died before letters reached them. News of disasters came too late to help. Impatience has driven real progress, and nobody sensible wants to return to a world without medicine that works quickly or information that moves freely. The point is not that delay is good in itself. The point is that delay was a kind of texture, and texture gave experience its depth. It allowed for anticipation, for memory, for the slow ripening of a thought.

Perhaps the practical question is not how to abolish instant access but how to reintroduce small, deliberate intervals into our days. Some people write letters by hand again, not to be quaint but because the slowness changes what they say. Others leave a question unanswered overnight before deciding what they think. Some take walks without headphones, letting their minds wander to unfinished problems and eventually produce something unexpected. These are modest acts, but they restore a sense of proportion. They remind us that not every thought needs an immediate reply, and that some of the best things arrive only after we have stopped demanding them.

There is also an unexpected kindness in waiting. When you must wait for someone, you extend them a kind of faith. You assume they are coming, that the letter is in transit, that the silence means something other than abandonment. Instant communication has made that faith harder to sustain, because every absence now feels like a choice. Maybe part of growing up is relearning how to trust the interval, to believe that what is meant for you will find its way, even if it takes longer than you would like.

The kettle has finally started to sing. I will pour the water, let the tea steep for the three minutes the box recommends, and sit by the window while it cools. Nothing urgent will happen in that time, and I find, to my surprise, that I am grateful for it.

# On Keeping Things

Somewhere in my kitchen drawer there is a rubber band that has been stretched so many times it no longer snaps back. It is brittle and faintly yellow, and it is not useful for anything. I have moved it through four apartments, and I could not tell you why. It isn't sentimental. I don't remember where it came from. It just never seemed like the right moment to throw it away, and the moment never arrived, and so it stayed, and now it has become one of those objects that belong to the drawer the way the drawer belongs to the kitchen.

I think most people have a drawer like this, or a shoebox, or a corner of a closet where the things they can't quite discard collect like sediment. Old keys to locks that no longer exist. Batteries of uncertain charge. Takeout menus from restaurants that have closed. Cables for devices we no longer own. We keep them on the theory that they might matter someday, and we are almost always wrong about that, but the theory is so reassuring that we keep paying for it in drawer space.

There is something quietly hopeful about this habit. To keep a thing is to bet on a future in which you will need it, or at least a future in which you will be the kind of person who might. The rubber band is a small wager that the world will continue to produce situations requiring a loop of elastic, and that I will be standing there, prepared. It is a bet I have never collected on, and yet I keep placing it.

The opposite impulse is equally human, and it is the one that shows up in the cleaning frenzy before a move or after a death. Suddenly every object is interrogated. Do you spark joy? Will you use this? When did you last touch it? The answers are often unflattering. We discover that we own four identical spatulas, eleven hotel soaps, and a box of greeting cards for occasions that have already passed. Keeping and discarding turn out to be two ways of negotiating with time, one looking forward and one looking back, and most of us oscillate between them without much awareness.

What interests me is how objects accumulate meaning that has little to do with their function. A mug from a conference I attended a decade ago is, practically speaking, identical to any other mug. It holds coffee. But it also holds a memory of a rainy hotel, a conversation in a hallway, a version of myself who believed certain things about his career. When I drink from it, the coffee is incidental. The mug is a kind of container for the past, and the past leaks out a little each morning.

Historians of material culture have long argued that objects are not inert. A well-worn doorstep, a pilgrim's stone, a church bell with a crack in it: these carry the marks of use and of the hands that used them. The wear is a record. Archaeologists read potsherds the way others read letters, inferring trade routes and cooking habits and grief from the shape of a broken bowl. Our own junk drawers are, in this sense, tiny archives, badly catalogued and unread, but archives nonetheless.

There is a particular melancholy in finding an object you had forgotten. You open a book and a bookmark falls out, a receipt from a city you no longer live in, dated to a week you can barely reconstruct. For a moment the past is not a story you tell yourself but a physical thing in your hand, insisting on its own reality. Then the moment passes, you put the receipt back, and the past returns to the shelf of things you half remember.

Perhaps this is why I can't throw away the rubber band. It is not really about elastic. It is about the reluctance to let any small piece of the past be declared worthless. Every object we keep is a refusal to fully settle the account with our previous selves. We are, in a sense, still negotiating with them, still letting them have a say in what occupies our space.

I don't think the answer is to become a minimalist monk with a single bowl and a single spoon, though there is a certain elegance to that life. I suspect the healthier approach is to keep things consciously. To ask, now and then, why a particular object is still here. Sometimes the answer will be that it is beautiful, or useful, or that it carries a story worth remembering. Sometimes the answer will be that I am afraid of the small finality of letting go. Both answers are worth knowing.

The rubber band will probably outlast me in that drawer, becoming ever more brittle until it crumbles into dust that someone else will eventually sweep away. For now, though, I leave it where it is. It is a small, stubborn reminder that I have been many places, that I have lived many versions of my ordinary days, and that some of those days have left behind nothing but a faintly yellow loop of rubber, waiting patiently for a use that will likely never come.

# Small Oceans, Left Behind

There is a particular kind of afternoon I find myself thinking about: the low tide, when the sea pulls back farther than seems reasonable and leaves behind a scatter of small worlds. Tide pools are sometimes described as miniature oceans, but that undersells them. An ocean is too big to notice. A tide pool is a place where the ocean has been reduced to something you can kneel beside and see whole.

Each one is a kind of accident of geography. A dip in the rock holds a little seawater, and the sea, when it withdraws, leaves that dip behind like a note on a table. Inside, a community has to make do. The water warms in the sun and cools at night. Its salt concentration can climb as the water evaporates or drop when rain falls into it. Sometimes a pool becomes so hot or so fresh that the creatures living in it simply cannot continue, and sometimes they endure conditions that would kill almost anything else. Sea anemones pull themselves tight against the air. Hermit crabs trade shells with the patience of people furnishing a house they cannot afford. Limpets clamp to the rock and wait, sealed against the drying wind, as if they had decided long ago that the best strategy was to become a small, stubborn part of the stone.

What strikes me most is how much of life depends on timing. The pools exist only in the gap between tides. For a few hours, a boundary is open, and then the sea returns and the whole arrangement is reset. Everything in a tide pool lives inside a clock it did not choose. The animals there have evolved to read that clock in their bodies, closing shells and slowing metabolisms when the water recedes, opening and feeding when it comes back. It is a rhythm so old that it is written into their tissues.

I suspect part of my fascination comes from the way tide pools resist being summarized. You can say "the intertidal zone is a harsh environment," and that is true, but it flattens something more interesting. Harshness is a relative term. To a barnacle, a sunny afternoon at low tide might be a kind of misery, but the same barnacle is perfectly suited to a life that a fish would find unbearable. Every organism in a pool is a specialist in a narrow band of conditions, and the pool itself is a patchwork of such bands, layered within a few feet of rock. The high edges dry out, the middle stays damp, the deep corners hold water longest. A creature's address determines its whole biography.

There is also something about the act of looking that changes me. To see a tide pool well, you have to slow down. You crouch, you hold still, and after a while the still water begins to show you things. A shrimp you had mistaken for a shadow reveals itself. A sculpin, camouflaged so thoroughly it might be a pebble with ambitions, flicks away. Fronds of algae that looked like decoration begin to look like forests, and the spaces between them look like streets. Attention works like a lens that gradually focuses. The pool does not get more interesting over time, exactly; I just get better at noticing.

I think this is one reason I value small, bounded places generally. A library carrel, a garden bed, a single room where someone has spent decades arranging things: these are tide pools of human life. They are contained enough that you can understand them, and rich enough that understanding them takes a long time. Big landscapes overwhelm the eye, but a small one invites a kind of respect. You begin to care about the particular creatures, their particular struggles, the way one season's storm rearranges a whole community of stones.

There is a melancholy in it too, which I do not mind. A tide pool is temporary by design. The sea will come back and take the warm water and the careful balance with it, and the animals will either retreat to deeper water or hold on until the next low tide. Nothing about this is tragic from the animals' point of view; it is simply how their world works. But from my side of the rock, the knowledge that the pool will be gone soon makes the looking more precious. I notice more because I know I will be leaving.

Maybe that is the real lesson of tide pools, if they have one. Abundance does not always announce itself. Sometimes it waits in a shallow hollow, between one tide and the next, asking only that you kneel down, be quiet, and let the small ocean show you what it contains. Then the water rises, the boundary closes, and you walk back up the beach carrying nothing but the memory of a world you were lucky enough to see.

# In the Margins

Some of my favorite things are the things other people left behind without meaning to leave them. A pressed flower in a paperback. A grocery receipt used as a bookmark, its items listing a life: eggs, lemons, a bottle of wine, batteries. And, most of all, the pencil marks in secondhand books.

I have a copy of a dog-eared poetry anthology from a church rummage sale. Someone, years ago, underlined a line in a poem by Mary Oliver, the one about paying attention being the beginning of devotion. Beside it, in a different pen, someone else had written "yes" with an exclamation point, as though answering a question the poem had asked them directly. Further on, a stanza has been crossed out, not violently, just a neat single line through it, as if the reader had changed their mind about it and wanted that known. I don't know who these people were. I don't know whether the first was the same person as the second, or whether the book passed through five hands before it reached the rummage table. But I feel I've been in a conversation I wasn't invited to, and it's one of the warmest conversations I've ever overheard.

There's something tender about marginalia. Writing in a book is an act of claiming, but it's also an act of offering. You're telling the next reader, whoever they are, *this is where I stopped and felt something.* Most of us are taught that writing in books is a kind of vandalism, and libraries certainly discourage it. Yet the scholars who annotate Montaigne, Shakespeare, and Darwin have made their margins into archives. Coleridge filled the borders of the books he read with long, frantic arguments with their authors. Those notes are now studied as seriously as the texts. He was, in a sense, thinking out loud for posterity, and posterity has been grateful.

I think what draws me in is the evidence of a body. A person held this book. They had a pencil, or a pen that was running low. They sat somewhere, maybe at a kitchen table, maybe on a train, maybe in a hospital waiting room, and something caught them. We can't recover the exact moment, but the mark persists. A little dent in the paper where the pencil pressed harder when the feeling was strongest. Handwriting that slants more sharply when the reader was tired or excited. These are small traces, but they're almost unbearably human.

We live in an age when so much of our reading leaves no trace. E-readers keep our highlights in the cloud, and while I'm sure someone could aggregate them and learn what passages readers love most, nobody holds the device and feels the weight of another person's attention. Digital annotations are tidy and searchable, but they lack the particular texture of a physical mark: the smudge of a thumb, the coffee ring that happened to fall on the page just as someone was rereading a sentence about grief. A book that has been lived with accumulates these accidents, and they become part of its meaning.

I wonder sometimes what my own books will say after I'm gone, if they outlast me. Will someone find my faint pencil check beside a sentence I thought was clever at twenty and found embarrassing at thirty? Will they see the question mark I put beside a claim I never resolved? I hope the marks I've left are honest. I hope I wrote down the moments when I was genuinely moved and not only the moments I thought I should be. There's a particular vulnerability in admitting, through a pencil line, that a sentence got to you.

Perhaps this is why I'm reluctant to clean up my own marginalia, or to erase the old pencil in a book I've acquired. Erasing feels like silencing a voice. A previous reader's enthusiasm, bluntness, or confusion is a piece of their history, and I'd rather live alongside it than scrub it away. When I read the "yes!" beside Mary Oliver, I don't feel like I'm reading a stranger's notes. I feel like I'm sitting beside them on a bench, both of us nodding at the same sentence, decades apart.

There's a broader lesson in this, I think, about how meaning is made. A text by itself is only a set of possibilities. It becomes something real when someone meets it, and those meetings leave residue. Every book is a palimpsest of readers, layered one over another. Even the copy you buy new has been touched by the hands of the warehouse workers, the bookseller, the person who chose it for a gift. We're always in the margins of something, and always leaving our own.

So I'll keep buying secondhand books with their stray notes and mysterious underlines. I'll keep leaving my own small marks, even knowing they might puzzle or amuse someone later. And when I find a line in a stranger's handwriting that makes me stop and say *yes* out loud to an empty room, I'll remember that the best thing a reader can do is pass the feeling along, however imperfectly, to whoever comes next.

# On Darning, and Other Quiet Acts of Staying

My grandmother kept a wooden egg in her sewing basket. It was smooth, pale, and about the size of a plum, and she used it to darn socks. You slid the egg inside the heel or the toe, stretched the fabric tight over its curve, and then wove new threads back and forth across the hole until the gap closed into a patch of slightly denser cloth. The result was never invisible. You could always tell where the hole had been. But the sock went back on, and it kept doing its job, and nobody had to buy a new pair.

I think about that egg more than I expected to. It represents a whole category of human effort that has mostly vanished from daily life: the small, unglamorous work of keeping things going. Mending a hem, resoling a shoe, re-caning a chair, patching a bicycle tube on the kitchen floor with the wheel upside down. None of these acts make the news. None of them produce anything new in the world. They simply prevent something from ending too soon.

There is a particular satisfaction in this kind of work, and I don't think it is only nostalgia. Mending asks you to pay attention to a thing as it actually is, not as it was sold to you. You have to understand how the fabric is constructed, where the stress falls, why the seam gave way. A broken thing becomes a puzzle with a physical answer. And when the repair holds, you get a small, specific pleasure that a purchase rarely provides. Buying something says that the world owes you a replacement. Repairing something says that the world is worth tending.

Economists would describe this in terms of cost. A new sock is cheaper than an hour of a person's time, so the rational choice is to throw the old one away. That arithmetic is correct in a narrow sense, but it leaves out a lot. It leaves out the fact that most of the value of an object is not in its material but in its history. The sweater your aunt knitted, the jacket that has been to three countries, the mug with the chip you've been meaning to fix for a decade. These things accumulate meaning the way a riverbank accumulates silt, slowly and without anyone deciding it should happen. Discarding them is easy precisely because we have stopped noticing that they were ever more than objects.

I don't want to romanticize the past. My grandmother's generation darned socks partly because they had no alternative, and the labor of mending fell heavily on women who were also doing a dozen other jobs. Scarcity is not a virtue. But the opposite condition, an abundance so total that nothing is worth keeping, has its own kind of poverty. When everything is disposable, nothing is particularly precious, including the people and relationships we treat the same way: quickly replaced, rarely repaired.

Maybe that is why the Japanese practice of kintsugi moves me so much. A broken bowl is mended with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, so the cracks become visible, bright seams running through the ceramic. The bowl is not hidden as having been damaged. Its breaking becomes part of its beauty. I find this a generous idea. It suggests that the scars of an object, or of a life, need not be shameful. They can be the most interesting part of the thing.

Of course, the wooden egg and the golden seam are both rare now. Most of us own clothes we cannot repair, phones with sealed batteries, furniture held together by glue and optimism. The tools have changed, and so has the expectation that a person might know how to fix anything. I do not think we can or should return entirely to the world of the darning egg. But I wonder whether we might carry a little of its attitude forward: a habit of asking, before we discard something, whether it can be made to last another season.

This is a small thing to ask. It will not solve climate change or fix the economy. But small habits shape large attitudes. A person who learns to mend a sock may come to see a torn friendship, a broken promise, or a failing institution as something that can also be worked on, patiently, with the right tools and enough attention. Repair is a kind of faith that the future can be built on what already exists.

I still have my grandmother's egg. It sits on a shelf above my desk now, a little yellowed, and I have never used it. I have no socks that need it. But I keep it there because it reminds me of something I don't want to forget: that holding onto things, and mending them when they tear, is one of the quietest and most honest forms of care we have. Somewhere, a thread is waiting to be pulled through a hole, and the work of keeping something whole is still worth doing.

There is a strange fact I keep turning over: we have better maps of the surface of Mars than of the floor of our own oceans. Mars has been photographed in fine detail by orbiters for decades, and the Moon has been mapped down to craters a few meters wide. The seafloor, which covers most of the planet and sits directly beneath the ships that cross it, remains mostly a blur. Estimates vary, but only about a quarter of it has been charted at high resolution. The rest is guesswork, interpolated from satellite measurements of gravity and a scattering of soundings taken by ships that were going somewhere else.

I find this thrilling in a way I can't fully justify. It means that somewhere below the surface of a sea I could drive to in an afternoon, there are mountain ranges I have never seen, canyons deeper than the Grand Canyon is wide, and volcanoes that nobody has photographed. Some of them probably have names now, given by the people who first mapped them, and most of those names are plain and practical. Ridges get named after research vessels. Seamounts get named after the ships that found them, or after whoever signed the paperwork. Once in a while someone gets poetic and names a feature after a myth or a lost sailor, and those names feel like small lights in the dark.

The sonar itself is a kind of miracle of patience. A ship sends sound pulses downward and listens for the echoes. The time it takes for the echo to return gives the depth, and a long line of these measurements, stitched together, gives a profile of the bottom. It is slow work. A ship mapping a patch of seafloor moves back and forth in tight lines, like someone mowing a lawn in the dark, and the resulting image is built one ping at a time. Nothing about it is instant. You cannot look down and see the bottom the way you look at a hill. You have to trust the arithmetic and wait.

I suspect that is part of why the subject moves me. Most of what matters in a life is unseen in exactly this way. A friendship that has run quietly for thirty years is mapped mostly by its echoes: a letter, a phone call, a sentence that lands precisely because the other person remembers something you said long ago. A person's character is less a visible surface than a bathymetry, the shape of what they have carried and where they have been pushed. We glimpse the peaks, the moments of obvious drama, and we infer the rest, and we are often wrong about the rest in ways we only discover when the sonar finally passes over a part we had assumed was flat.

There is also something humbling about the pressure down there. At the deepest points of the ocean, the water above weighs enough to crush most of the equipment we send. Creatures that live there have adapted to a world without sunlight, where the food arrives as slow drifts of dead matter from the surface, and where some animals produce their own light to find each other. I like to imagine that these animals have their own unmapped lives, their own rivalries and courtships and routines, going on with no witnesses at all. The fact that they are not observed does not make them less real. It only makes them private.

I think we are drawn to maps partly because they promise that nothing will be lost. A map says: this is here, and you can go back to it. But the seafloor reminds me that the most important territories often resist that promise. You can measure them, you can name them, and still they stay largely dark. Perhaps this is fine. Perhaps some parts of the world are meant to remain approximate, so that we keep a sense of wonder about what we have not yet touched.

I am not sure what I would do with a perfect map of the ocean floor, if one existed tomorrow. I suspect I would spend hours tracing the ridges with a fingertip, and then I would close the file and feel slightly disappointed, the way you feel when a mystery is solved and the solution is ordinary. The mystery was the good part. The not-knowing was a kind of room to think in.

So I find myself hoping the mapping goes slowly. I hope the ships keep sweeping back and forth, the pings keep returning, and the blurry parts gradually sharpen without ever quite finishing. There is something comforting about a world that still has depths we have not sounded, and about the idea that for every confident line on a chart, there is a dark valley somewhere that has not yet been named, going about its business under a great weight of water, waiting for someone to listen for the echo.

# On Keeping Small Things

Somewhere in my kitchen there is a drawer that has never been fully emptied. It holds rubber bands that have gone brittle, a dead AA battery, three keys whose locks I can no longer identify, a takeout menu from a restaurant that has since closed, and a small brass bell with no clapper. I've opened that drawer a hundred times and never once cleared it out. When I do open it, I feel a flicker of something between guilt and affection, as if I've stumbled on a room in my own house I'd forgotten existed.

I've been thinking about why we keep things like this. Most of the objects in that drawer are useless. The keys open nothing I own. The bell makes no sound. Yet I can't bring myself to throw them away, and I suspect many people have a drawer, box, or shelf like mine. We are a species that hoards the meaningless, and I've come to think this is less a flaw than a clue about how memory and attention actually work.

A key that once opened a front door is a tiny archive. It's a reminder of an apartment I lived in for six years, of the particular stiffness of its lock, of the morning I stood on the landing fumbling with it while carrying groceries and a bag of library books. The key itself doesn't contain that memory, of course. It's more like a hook. Pick it up and the whole scene comes back, half-formed and slightly blurred, the way a song from childhood can drop you back into a afternoon you hadn't thought about in decades.

Our minds are not filing cabinets. Psychologists who study memory have spent a long time showing that remembering is a reconstruction, not a playback. Each time we recall something, we rebuild it from fragments, and the fragments we use are often external: a photograph, a smell, a melody, an object worn smooth by years of handling. The brass bell in my drawer probably came from a trip or a gift or a shop I've forgotten. I can't reconstruct the day it entered my life. But I can feel that it belongs to a larger story I once lived, and that feeling is a kind of knowledge too.

There's something faintly absurd about all this, and I don't mind the absurdity. Modern life pushes us toward efficiency and minimalism. We're told to tidy up, to keep only what sparks joy, to digitize our photos and donate our books. There is wisdom in those impulses. Clutter is real, and so is the weight of owning too much. But there's also a danger in treating every object as if its only value were its function. A world stripped of purposeless things would be a world with fewer reminders, fewer accidental doorways into the past.

Consider how much of what we love is useless in the narrow sense. Nobody needs a chipped teacup, a pressed flower, a letter folded into quarters and softened by rereading. A grandmother's ring doesn't do anything a plain band wouldn't. Yet these things hold meaning precisely because they are not interchangeable. Replace a childhood stuffed animal with an identical one and something essential is lost, even though no information has changed. The particularity is the point.

I think this is why I find old buildings and old cities so moving. A church with worn stone steps, where generations have pressed their feet into the same shallow dips, tells you something no history book can. The wear is evidence of repetition, of countless ordinary moments: people hurrying to services, children running up to be scolded, old men sitting down to rest. Nobody set out to make those dips. They are the residue of ordinary life accumulating over time, and to walk across them is to feel briefly connected to a chain of human presence stretching backward.

Perhaps that's what the drawer is for. It is a small, private museum of a life, arranged without curation. It contains no masterpieces, only the debris of ordinary days that happened to matter. Someday, I suppose, someone will open it after I'm gone and wonder what the keys opened and why the bell was kept. They'll invent stories to fill the gaps, which is what we all do with other people's relics. Those invented stories will be wrong in details and perhaps right in spirit.

I don't want to romanticize clutter. I do still intend to clean out that drawer, probably this spring, when the light is better and I'm feeling brisk. But I suspect I'll keep the bell. I'll keep at least one of the keys. And when I close the drawer again, I'll feel the same small pang of recognition, the sense that the past is not entirely gone so long as a few of its objects survive in the dark, waiting for someone to pick them up and remember.

# The Honest Blank

Old maps have a habit I find endlessly charming. Where a cartographer didn't know what lay beyond the coastline, he often wrote something like *hic sunt dracones*, or drew a whale with its mouth open, or coiled a sea serpent in the corner of the Atlantic. Sometimes he left the space alone, a field of parchment with nothing on it. I have always liked those blank patches best, or at least I like what they admit. They say: our knowledge stops here. Past this line we are guessing, or we are not even guessing.

Modern maps rarely confess anything. Satellite imagery has filled nearly every square kilometer with roads, contour lines, and little icons for pharmacies and parking garages. The world has been rendered so completely that it is easy to forget how recently most of it was unknown. Within living memory, large parts of the Amazon basin, the interior of Greenland, and the highlands of New Guinea were being walked for the first time by people carrying notebooks, mules, and considerable optimism. Some of those explorers came back with maps that were wrong in charming ways. Others came back with nothing, or didn't come back at all.

I find myself thinking about this because I realize how little I know about the place I live. I could draw the route from my front door to the grocery store, the post office, and the train station with reasonable accuracy. I could tell you where the potholes are and which intersection floods after a heavy rain. But ask me to sketch the streets two blocks east of my house and I would produce a mess of guesses, a few landmarks, and a large blank space where a whole neighborhood sits. I walk past those streets sometimes. I have simply never had a reason to go into them.

This is how most of us know most places: as a set of routes. We have a map of our habits, not of the land. The town becomes a corridor between the places we need to be, and everything off the corridor fades into a kind of tactful white. There is nothing wrong with this, exactly. Attention is finite, and no one can hold the whole world in mind. But I suspect we lose something when the blank spaces disappear entirely, not because we need more dragons, but because the blank is an invitation. It says that the world is larger than what we have looked at, and that looking is still possible.

There is a difference between knowing a place and having a map of it, and the difference is mostly time. A map can be bought in an afternoon. Knowing a place takes years of small repeated encounters: learning which bakery opens early, which bench gets the afternoon sun, which tree drops its blossoms in May and makes the sidewalk pink. You cannot download that. It accumulates the way sediment does, one ordinary day at a time. The people who know a city best are rarely the ones with the most sophisticated navigation apps. They are the ones who once got lost there on purpose.

I think about the old cartographers' dragons with a certain fondness now. They were not simply ignorant. Many of them were careful, and when they knew something, they drew it precisely. The monsters were a way of marking the edge of what could be verified, a sort of footnote in ink. *Here our evidence runs out.* That is a useful thing for any mind to be able to write down. We are much worse at it than we used to be, perhaps because uncertainty has come to feel like a failure rather than a boundary. Confident mapmaking is attractive. A world with no blank spaces looks finished, and finished things are easier to trust, even when they are not true.

Still, the blanks are not gone. They have only moved. The deep ocean floor is still less thoroughly mapped than the surface of Mars, a fact that surprises most people. Much of the human interior, the private landscape of other people's grief or ambition or humor, remains unsurveyed no matter how many messages we exchange. Our own pasts are full of places we visited once and never returned to, their details dissolving into a pale wash. These blanks are not defects. They are simply the honest shape of finite lives.

So I have made a small resolution, the kind that is easy to make and harder to keep. Once in a while I want to walk down one of the streets I have never entered and let it remain unknown for a few minutes, with no destination and no phone open. I want to notice what I don't yet understand and let the notice be enough. Maybe I'll find a bakery I didn't know existed. Maybe I'll find only a row of houses with peeling paint and a dog asleep on a porch. Either way, I will have turned a white space into a line of ink, one step at a time, and I will know that the map was never the territory, only a promise to keep looking.

Somewhere, I suspect, a cartographer is still drawing a small sea monster in the margin of a page nobody will read. I hope he is enjoying himself. The honest blank deserves that much care.

# On the Blank Spaces of Maps

Old maps have a habit I find endlessly appealing. Along the edges of the known world, where the cartographer's knowledge ran out, they often wrote something like *hic sunt dracones*, "here be dragons," or simply left the paper empty. Sometimes they drew sea monsters curling through the unsurveyed water, or a sketch of a strange animal with no clear source. These decorations were not always meant as jokes. They were admissions. The mapmaker was saying: this is where I stopped knowing.

I like that honesty. Most of the things we make to represent the world are built to look complete. A modern road atlas or a phone's navigation screen presents itself as a finished truth, every street labeled, every route calculated to the second. Nothing on the screen tells you what it has left out, what was guessed, what was copied from a survey done in 1962 and never updated. The old maps at least showed their seams. Their blank regions were a kind of confession, and the monsters were the confession's way of being entertaining about it.

There is a famous story, possibly apocryphal, about a mapmaker who inserted a fictitious town into his map to catch anyone who copied his work. If a rival later published a map with that town, it would prove theft. The trap is a small piece of wit, but it also reveals something true about maps: they are made of decisions, and every decision leaves a trace. A map is never just a picture of land. It is a record of who surveyed, who paid, who wanted what, and what they were willing to get wrong.

Maps also taught people to imagine. Before satellites, a blank space on the chart was an invitation. Sailors told stories about the coasts they had glimpsed through fog. Explorers vanished into the interior and returned with descriptions that other people redrew, and the redrawn versions sometimes produced new rivers and mountains that existed only in the hope of the person drawing them. Some of those hopes were true. Others were misremembered, and some were simply invented by men who wanted patrons to keep funding them. Imagination and error were tangled together, and the results still shaped where people went.

I find myself thinking about blank spaces outside of geography, too. Every person carries a map of their own life, and it has its own unsurveyed regions. There are years we barely remember, friendships that drifted without a clear ending, parts of our character we have never explored because we were never tested in them. We do not usually write *here be dragons* in those places. We tend to pretend the map is complete, that we know ourselves well enough to give directions. But a more honest map would have a few empty patches, and maybe a few monsters drawn in the margins to mark the spots where we are still afraid to look.

There is something freeing in admitting that. A cartographer who marks the edge of their knowledge is not weaker for it. In fact, the marks make the rest of the map more trustworthy. When a surveyor says "coastline uncertain," you believe the coastline everywhere else. When someone admits they do not know something, you tend to believe what they do claim to know. Confidence is cheap. Calibrated honesty about one's limits is rarer and more valuable.

Modern cartography has, in many ways, eliminated the blank spaces. Satellite imagery has filled in most of the planet's surface. Nearly every road, river, and building is recorded. Yet the blanks have not disappeared so much as moved. They now live in the data itself: in the coverage gaps of a mapping service, in the neighborhoods that were never surveyed in detail, in the places where the labels are wrong because nobody has bothered to check. Maps still lie by omission. They just do it more quietly.

Perhaps the best thing a map can do is to leave a little room for wonder. There is a particular pleasure in standing at the edge of something you do not yet understand, whether it is an unnamed coastline or an unfamiliar idea. The old mapmakers, with their dragons and sea serpents, seemed to understand that the unknown is not just a gap to be closed. It is also a place where the mind gets to play.

So I would like to keep a little of that spirit. When I reach the edge of what I know, I want to say so plainly, and then perhaps sketch something small and strange in the margin. Not as a substitute for knowledge, but as a reminder that the world is larger than any chart, and that the most honest thing a maker can do is mark the place where the paper ends and the real territory begins.

There is a particular kind of quiet that exists only in old libraries, and I have been thinking about it lately, though I could not tell you exactly why. It is not the absence of sound. Somewhere a radiator ticks, a page turns, a chair scrapes against the floor. It is more like the quiet of a room where a great many people have agreed, over a long time, to be patient with one another. The books hold their breath. Nothing is in a hurry.

I was thinking about that quiet while reading about color, which is an odd thing to be thinking about in a library, but libraries are where my mind tends to wander. For a long time there was a famous observation, made in the nineteenth century by a British statesman who was also an amateur classicist, that Homer's Greek seemed to lack a word for blue. The sea was "wine-dark," the sky was bronze or iron, honey was green, and sheep, strangely, were violet. Gladstone, peering at these descriptions, concluded that the ancient Greeks had a limited or underdeveloped sense of color. Later scholars argued about this for generations. Some pointed out that Greek did have words for dark and light, for shining and dull, and that Homer's palette was organized around brightness rather than hue. Others suggested that the Greeks saw the world perfectly well and simply sorted it differently. Still others noticed that many languages around the world have words for black and white and red, and only later acquire a word for blue, as if blue were a late arrival at the party.

I find this fascinating not because I think the Greeks were colorblind, which they almost certainly were not, but because it reminds me how much of what we perceive depends on what we have learned to name. We tend to assume that our categories are simply the shape of reality, that the sky is blue the way a stone is hard. But the sky is only blue because we have decided, collectively and over centuries, to carve a particular band of light and call it that. A child learns the word and then, suddenly, sees blue everywhere: in shadows, in the flicker of a flame, in the edges of clouds. The world did not change. The attention did.

That is one of the stranger powers of language. It is not only a way of describing what we notice; it is a way of deciding what is worth noticing in the first place. Every word is a small lamp, and it lights one corner of a room while leaving the rest in shadow. A culture that has many words for snow will see distinctions among snowfalls that outsiders miss. A person who has learned the vocabulary of birds starts hearing a dozen species in a single morning chorus where before there was only noise. Attention is partly a skill, and skills are passed down through words, through teachers, through people who bother to point and say, "Look, there."

I think this is why I love the old libraries and the old books in them. A book from two hundred years ago is a record of a mind looking at the world with a different set of lamps. Its author sees things I cannot see and misses things I take for granted. Reading such a book is a bit like walking through a house whose former residents left their furniture arranged in ways that make no sense until you sit down in their chairs. Suddenly the angle of the window makes sense, and you understand why they wanted the light from the east.

There is also something humbling in it. We are all, in our own time, making confident claims about what is real and what is merely imagined, what matters and what is trivial. Some of those claims will look as strange to our great-grandchildren as Gladstone's theory of Homeric color looks to us. We will have sorted the world into categories that seemed natural and inevitable, and they will have turned out to be one way among many of seeing. This is not a reason for despair. It is a reason for a certain looseness of grip, a willingness to hold our categories lightly enough that we can still learn from people who divided the world differently.

I do not want to make too much of a small historical squabble. Homer was not a poor painter. The sea in the Odyssey is vivid and alive, and I can see the wine-dark water as clearly as anything I have ever read. Perhaps the lesson is simply that vividness does not require our vocabulary. The Greeks managed to make the sea gleam for three thousand years without the word we now use to describe it, and we make our own sky blue with words that a future reader might find curious.

Outside the library window, the afternoon has turned the particular gray-gold of early autumn, and I am trying to see it without reaching for the familiar label. It is harder than I expected. There is the brown of the bricks, the rust of a fence, a green so yellowed it borders on something else entirely. I can name none of it precisely. What I can do is look a little longer, and let the colors arrive before the words do. That, I suspect, is the closest I will get to the Greeks' sea: a moment of seeing before the sorting begins, when the world is still wider than the language I have for it.

# On Blank Spaces

Old maps have a habit I find endlessly appealing: they admit what they don't know. Along the margins of sixteenth-century charts, sea monsters curl through water that no sailor had crossed. Interiors of continents are filled with mountains drawn from rumor, or left empty, or labeled with a confident name for a place nobody had visited. Sometimes a cartographer simply wrote *terra incognita* and moved on. I have a soft spot for these gaps. A blank space on a map is a kind of honesty, a refusal to pretend that the world is fully known.

We don't make maps like that anymore. A modern satellite image has no blank spaces, or at least none that matter. Every coastline is traced, every road numbered, every building given a pin. The unknown has been pushed so far to the edges that most of us never encounter it. When I open a map application on my phone, it shows me my position as a blue dot with the quiet assurance of a thing that has always been there. The dot never hesitates. It never says, *here there be dragons*.

I'm not sure this is an improvement, at least not in every respect. Maps don't just record the world; they shape how we attend to it. A blank space invites curiosity. It says that someone should go look. A fully rendered space says that looking has already been done, and the job now is simply to navigate through it. The difference between those two attitudes is the difference between exploring and commuting.

There is a related habit in how we think about knowledge in general. We tend to treat understanding as a finished product, a body of settled facts, when much of what we actually know is provisional and patchy. Think of how often a confident explanation turns out to have a hole in it, a place where the cartographer guessed. The people who made the old maps knew they were guessing, and some of them drew the guesses beautifully. The sea serpents were a way of saying, *we are not sure what is out there, but something probably is.*

I think there is wisdom in keeping some of that posture. It's useful to be able to say, plainly, that I don't know a thing, and to leave the space on the page unfilled until I have a reason to fill it. This is harder than it sounds. Silence feels like failure, and a blank invites the question of why I haven't done better. But a mind that can tolerate blank spaces is also a mind that can still be surprised.

Surprise is perhaps the thing we lose most easily as we get older. Childhood is full of it, because everything is a blank space. A child who sees a snail for the first time is mapping a territory no one has described to her. Adults, by contrast, tend to file the world under familiar headings. We see a tree and think *oak*, and the word does the work of attention for us, so we stop looking. The tree becomes a label rather than a particular thing with its own peculiar bark and its own way of leaning toward the light.

I try, sometimes, to go back to the blank-space mode on purpose. I walk a route I've walked a hundred times and pretend I've never seen it. I notice the crack in the sidewalk shaped like a river delta, the way one particular house has a window that catches the afternoon sun at a steep angle. None of this is useful in any obvious sense. It doesn't get me anywhere faster. But it makes the familiar strange again, and strangeness is where curiosity starts.

Of course, there's a danger in romanticizing the unknown. Some blank spaces were blank because people didn't bother to find out what was there, and their absence hurt people who lived in those places. Colonial mapmakers drew emptiness over inhabited lands precisely because it was convenient to pretend no one was there. So the honest blank is not the same as the lazy or willful one. The honest blank says *I don't know yet*. The dishonest one says *it doesn't matter*. The difference is whether the mapmaker is willing to go and look.

Perhaps that is the real lesson of the old charts. They were not perfect, but they were drawn by people who were still traveling, still asking, still willing to be corrected. A good map is a question as much as an answer. It marks where the knowledge stops and invites the next person to push the edge a little further out.

So I'll keep my fondness for the sea monsters and the empty interiors. I'll keep hoping that the world still has a few unmapped corners, even if they're only corners of my own understanding. And when I find myself confidently certain about something, I'll try to remember the cartographers who drew their dragons in the margins, knowing exactly how much they didn't know, and who still set out anyway.

# On Things That Are Still Becoming

There is a jar in my imagination that I keep returning to: a sourdough starter, cloudy and faintly sour, sitting on a windowsill. It has no finished form. It is never quite bread and never quite not bread. It is a community of wild yeasts and bacteria that someone feeds with flour and water every day, and its whole existence is a kind of standing in the middle of a sentence. I find it oddly moving.

We tend to celebrate finished things. We frame diplomas, hang paintings, bind books with gold leaf, and call a building "complete" when the ribbon is cut. Finishing is the moment we get to stop and admire. But most of what matters in a life, and in the world, happens in the long middle, the part where nothing has been resolved yet and the outcome is still open.

Consider the cathedral. Medieval builders often began projects they knew they would not live to see completed. A cathedral might take a century or two, and the people who laid the first stones were making a promise to strangers who would finish the work. The choir might be Gothic while the nave was added later in a different style. The towers in some famous cathedrals were never finished at all, and their stubs still stand, unfinished, and nobody seems to mind. Somehow the incompleteness is part of their beauty. They tell you that the work was bigger than any one person's lifetime.

Languages work the same way. A language is never done. Words drift in meaning; grammar softens and hardens over centuries. English speakers in 1400 would struggle to follow a conversation in a pub today, and in another few centuries our present speech will sound as strange to our descendants as Chaucer does to us. We like to think of a language as a fixed object we inherited, but it is more like a river. You can step into it at any point, and it will already be different from where it was a moment ago.

Even our own selves are unfinished. We speak of "finding ourselves" as if the self were a lost wallet waiting under the couch cushions, but I suspect the self is more like the starter jar. It is fed by experience, by the people we spend time with, by the books we read and the mistakes we make. A person at seventy is not a completed version of a person at twenty. They are the same ongoing process, carried further, with some parts gone sour and others gone sweet.

I think we resist this because uncertainty is uncomfortable. A finished thing can be judged. An unfinished thing asks us to be patient, to hold off on conclusions, to tolerate not knowing how it will turn out. Yet patience is one of the quieter virtues, and it is hard to practice without a good reason. The starter teaches it. You cannot rush fermentation by staring at the jar. You can only keep feeding it, keep the temperature reasonable, and wait.

There is also something hopeful in the unfinished. If the story is still being written, then the ending is not yet decided. A failed draft can still be revised. A rough relationship can still be repaired. A town that has lost its industry can still find a new purpose. Permanence is often an illusion anyway; even the finished things eventually weather, crack, and return to the soil. What persists is the willingness to keep working on them, to pick up the trowel again.

I suppose this is why I find the phrase "work in progress" more honest than most declarations of completion. It admits what is true about nearly everything worth doing. Books are never truly finished; their authors simply stop revising. Gardens are never done; they only reach a particular stage of overgrowth or bloom. Friendships, cities, bodies, and ideas all sit somewhere along a curve that has no final point.

So the next time you encounter something half-built, half-learned, or half-understood, perhaps you can resist the urge to judge it by its current state. Look instead at its direction. Notice what it is becoming. The jar on the windowsill is not failing to be bread. It is being patient, doing its slow, living work, and it will be ready when it is ready.

# Paper Towns

Somewhere in the early twentieth century, a cartographer drew a town that did not exist. He gave it a name, placed it at a crossroads on a country road, and waited. If a rival mapmaker copied his work and the town appeared on their map too, he would know exactly who had done the copying. The town was a trap, a small lie planted in the ground of accuracy, and mapmakers have used such traps for generations. They call them paper towns or trap streets. The most famous, Agloe, New York, supposedly appeared on a road map published by Esso in the 1930s. Agloe was a nonsense word, the kind of thing you get by shuffling letters, and it sat in the Catskills as if it had always been there.

Then something unexpected happened. People began to believe in Agloe, and then they began to build in it. A general store opened at the spot, and for a while the Agloe General Store had a sign, a register, and customers who came looking for a place they had seen printed. The fiction acquired a roof. The lie got a foundation. The store eventually closed, and the land is mostly forest and quiet roads now, but the name survives, and in a sense it was never more real than it is as a story.

I find this almost unbearably delightful. It suggests that reality is less a fixed substance than a kind of agreement, and that a sufficiently confident piece of paper can persuade the world to rearrange itself around it. Once a place is printed, people go looking for it. They drive out, they ask directions, they open shops. Maps do not merely describe territory. They recruit it.

The trick is charming in its modesty, too. The cartographer did not need a grand deception, only one invented place set carefully among real ones, a fingerprint on the paper. Most of us live this way, quietly leaving marks that only we would recognize, hoping that if someone copies us, the copy will carry our name somewhere in it.

Maps are strange objects in general. A map is always a set of choices dressed up as the absence of choice. Someone decides which roads get a thick black line and which get a dotted one, which rivers are named and which are left nameless, whether a village is big enough to deserve a circle. Mercator's projection, which inflates the northern regions and shrinks the equatorial ones, still shapes how many people picture the world. Every flat map is a kind of lie told in service of some truth, the way a sentence must choose a single word before it can say anything at all.

I think about this when I consider how much of human knowledge works like a map. We carry around sketches of things: a friend's childhood, the causes of a war, the workings of a machine we use every day. The sketch is useful. It gets us to the right neighborhood. But it has its own invented roads and its own missing towns, and we rarely remember which parts we drew ourselves. A good thinker, I suppose, is someone who occasionally goes back and checks the paper against the ground.

Walking is one way to test a map. Anyone who has tried to find a small park with a phone that has lost signal knows the peculiar feeling of the blue dot drifting, of the arrow insisting you turn left into a hedge. The map and the world disagree, and you have to decide whom to trust. Usually the world wins, because the world is stubborn and detailed and never needs updating from anyone's office.

Still, I would not want a perfect map. There is an old story about an emperor who demanded a map at a scale of one to one, which would have covered the entire kingdom and been exactly as useless as the kingdom itself. Abstraction is a kindness. It lets us hold a whole territory in one hand. The paper town is a kind of abstraction as well: a place that exists only to point at something else, which in this case is the thief.

I also think about the mapmakers themselves, bent over drafting tables with ink pens and magnifying glasses, deciding on a name that the public would never see and that would exist only as a tripwire. Their most important accuracy was a kind of forgery detector. They had to be truthful about the world in every line except one, and that one line had to be chosen with a certain mischievous care. There is something tender in that, a cartographer's private joke sealed into a document meant to be trusted.

So here is my small enthusiasm for paper towns. They remind me that every representation is also a bet, that a copy can be traced back to its source, and that the most human things we make often carry, somewhere in them, a deliberate and harmless falsehood: a name that exists only so that someone, someday, will ask where it came from. And when they ask, and go looking, and find a store with a sign above the door, the fiction has done something the truth alone could not. It has gotten people to go somewhere, and to stand on the ground together, wondering what they are standing on.

There is a drawer in my kitchen that I have never fully emptied. It sits between the stove and the sink, and whenever I open it, something rattles. Inside are rubber bands gone brittle, takeout chopsticks, a dead lighter, three batteries of uncertain charge, and a cluster of keys. Some of the keys I can identify: the one for my current apartment, the one for a bicycle lock I no longer own. Others are mysteries. Small brass ones, a flat steel one with a faded tag, a key with a plastic red head shaped like a fish. Each of them once opened something that mattered to someone, and now they lie together in the dark, waiting for a door that either no longer exists or has been replaced.

I have come to love that drawer. It is a kind of archive, though a disorganized one. Nobody decided to keep these things. They simply accumulated, the way sediment settles at the bottom of a river. Every household has a place like this, a junk drawer or a box in the garage or a shelf of cables that match nothing. We are constantly shedding objects and seldom throwing them away, and the result is a record of who we were, written not in what we chose to keep but in what we were too busy, or too sentimental, or too lazy to discard.

There is a lesson in this about memory. We like to think we remember our lives as stories, with clear beginnings and endings and causes that lead neatly into effects. But memory is more like that drawer. It is full of fragments whose original context has dissolved. I know that a certain key once belonged to a friend's apartment, but I cannot recall which friend, or which year, or whether I ever actually used it. The fact of the key survives. The meaning leaks out of it over time, the way the spring in a lock slowly gives up its tension.

Objects are patient in this way. A key does not remember the door it opened, but the door remembers nothing either. Only people hold the connection, and people are unreliable custodians. We forget. We misremember. We fill gaps with plausible inventions. When my grandmother died, my family spent weeks sorting through her house, and we kept arguing about things: whether the blue teapot had always been on the high shelf, whether the photograph of the lake was taken before or after the war. None of us could be certain. The objects stood in the room like witnesses who had seen everything and would not testify clearly.

Still, there is something comforting in the clutter. A world without residue would be strangely thin. Imagine moving through life with no accumulated traces, every object replaced the moment it aged, every drawer always empty. It might be efficient, but it would also be a little lonely. The brittle rubber band is a reminder that I was once tidying things up for a reason, that I bought batteries for a flashlight I cannot now picture, that the world was once arranged in a way I have since forgotten.

I sometimes think about the people who will open my drawers someday, if anyone does. They will find the same mixture of the useful and the useless, the labeled and the anonymous. They will hold the fish-headed key and wonder what it opened, and they will invent an answer, probably a more charming one than the truth. That seems right to me. Every archive is partly fiction, and every reader completes the story in their own way.

So I am not going to empty the drawer. Not yet, anyway. Perhaps one day I will sit down with a cup of tea and sort through it carefully, discarding the dead batteries and keeping the keys, or the other way around. Until then, it stays where it is, rattling softly whenever I reach for a spoon, reminding me that nothing is ever entirely gone. Things just lose their names, and wait in the dark for someone to pick them up and wonder.

# On Keeping Things

Every household has a junk drawer, and every junk drawer is a small museum of intentions. Mine holds a key to a bicycle lock I sold years ago, four rubber bands of different sizes, a takeout menu from a restaurant that has since closed, a single AA battery whose charge I have never tested, and a card from a dentist I no longer visit. Nothing in it is valuable. Nothing in it is quite trash either. Each object was kept because, at the moment of keeping, someone believed it might be needed later, and that belief was a small act of faith in the future.

I find I am fond of this faith, even when it turns out to be misplaced. The rubber bands will never be the right size for the thing I need them for. The battery is almost certainly dead. But the drawer assumes that there will be a later in which these things matter, and that I will be the sort of person who can find them when that later arrives. There is something hopeful in that, and something a little absurd too, the way all hope is a little absurd when you look at it closely.

We keep things for many reasons. Some are practical: the warranty, the spare fuse, the instructions for a appliance we no longer own. Some are sentimental: the ticket stub from a concert, the letter in handwriting that has grown more precious as the handwriting itself becomes rarer. And some are harder to name. I have a jar of buttons that came off clothes I have since given away or worn to threads. I have never once sewn a button onto anything using that jar. I simply cannot bring myself to throw the buttons out, because each one is a fragment of a garment that once mattered, worn by a body I once inhabited in a particular season of my life.

Objects are unusually good at holding time. A sentence in a diary can be reread, but it cannot be touched the way a worn wooden spoon can be touched. The spoon carries the grain of a thousand stirrings. Its handle has darkened where a hand held it. Nobody made that darkening on purpose. It is simply the record of use, accumulated without intention, and this is why old things so often feel more honest than new ones. A new object has not yet been asked anything. An old one has answered a great many questions.

Of course, keeping can curdle into hoarding. I have known people whose houses became narrow corridors between towers of newspapers, and I understand, in a distant way, how it happens. The keeping that began as care slowly becomes fear. The person stops being able to throw things away because throwing them away feels like throwing away the self that needed them, or the self that might someday need them. Every object becomes a hedge against a loss that has not yet arrived, and eventually the hedges crowd out the life they were meant to protect.

So there is a balance to strike, and I suspect it is different for everyone. The trick, I think, is to keep things in a way that leaves room for other things. A drawer that closes is a kind of wisdom. A shelf with a little empty space on it is an invitation. I have been trying, in my own clumsy way, to let some objects go, and I have noticed that letting go is a skill that improves with practice, like any other. The first few items are agony. The next few are merely uncomfortable. Eventually you find yourself dropping a box of old cables into the recycling with something close to lightness, and you wonder why you ever thought those cables were essential to your survival.

Still, I am not ready to empty the junk drawer entirely. I like knowing it is there. I like the way it opens with a slight resistance, the way its contents shift and clatter like a small argument. I like that somewhere in its jumble is a key to a lock that no longer exists, and that I have not yet had the heart to admit it is useless. Maybe that is what keeping really is: not a refusal to change, but a way of insisting that the past was real, that the people and places and small hopes behind these objects did happen, and that they deserve a little shelf space in the present.

There is also a quieter pleasure in the act of rediscovery. Every few months I open the drawer looking for something else entirely, a pen or a stamp, and I find the old dentist's card or the stub from a train ticket to a city I visited once. For a moment the drawer hands me back a version of myself I had nearly forgotten. Then I put the card back, close the drawer, and go on with the day, a little richer for having been reminded.

Perhaps that is the real purpose of keeping things. Not to prepare for every possible future, which no drawer can do, but to remember that we have been somewhere, loved something, needed something, and that those needs left traces we can still hold in our hands. The battery may be dead. The rubber bands may never fit. But the drawer remembers what we were hoping for, and I find I am still grateful for that hope, even when it fits in a space no bigger than a fist.

# On Blank Spaces

Old maps are my favorite lies. I don't mean the deliberate kind, though plenty of those exist. I mean the honest ones, the maps that admit what their makers did not know. Hold a sixteenth-century chart of the Atlantic and you will find coastlines drawn with confident precision, rivers traced to their mouths, and then, somewhere past the edge of the known, the open stretches of parchment left empty or decorated with sea monsters, wind-blowing cherubs, and small inscriptions in faded ink. Sometimes the cartographer simply wrote *Terra incognita*. Sometimes he wrote nothing at all.

I find these blank spaces more moving than any finished map. A complete map is a kind of closure. It says: this is the world, and it is all accounted for. A map with gaps says something more humble and more human: this is as far as we have gone so far. The empty part is not a failure of the map. It is a record of the mapmaker's honesty, and of the strange, unfinished condition of the species that made it.

Consider what it must have been like to draw those edges. You would have heard stories from sailors, some reliable, most embellished. A merchant who had seen a coast from a distance. A rumor of an island where the trees bled red sap. You had to decide, with a pen in your hand, how much of that to believe and how much to put on the page. Every line was a bet. Every blank was a refusal to bet.

We are not so different now, though we like to think we are. We carry in our pockets devices that will draw us a perfect map of nearly anywhere, updated in real time, with the traffic and the new restaurants marked. The blank spaces have mostly been filled. Yet I suspect we have simply moved the emptiness somewhere less visible. The unknown has not left the world. It has moved into the interior, into the questions we ask about our own bodies, our own minds, our own histories, the people we love and the people we barely understand. There are still parts of the map where the monsters live.

I think this is part of why I distrust certainty. Certainty is a finished map laid over an unfinished territory. It feels good, the way a smooth, complete surface feels good to the hand, but it often means someone stopped looking. The person who says "I'm sure" is frequently a person who has drawn a coastline where there should be a question mark. The person who says "I don't know yet" is standing at the edge of the parchment, pen lifted, still listening for the sailor's story.

There is a particular kind of courage in leaving a space empty. It takes nerve to admit that your knowledge runs out. Most of us are taught the opposite. We are rewarded for quick answers and penalized for hesitation. In school, the student who writes "I'm not sure" often loses the point, even when that is the truest thing on the page. Somewhere along the way we learn to fill every gap with something plausible, because an empty space looks like ignorance, and ignorance looks like weakness.

But ignorance and emptiness are not the same thing. An empty space on a map is an invitation. It says: someone should go there. It leaves room for the explorer, the scientist, the curious child who will one day sail beyond the last drawn coastline and come back with a new story. The blank does not diminish the map. It makes the map a beginning rather than an ending.

I like to imagine the mapmakers themselves, bent over their desks by candlelight, their fingers stained with ink, weighing the edges of their knowledge. Many of them were wrong, of course. Some of the monsters they drew were pure fantasy, and some of the coastlines they confidently sketched were off by hundreds of miles. Yet there is something tender in their errors. They were trying. They were reaching toward a world they could not yet see, and they were willing to say so with the shape of the page itself.

Maybe that is the lesson I keep returning to. The world is larger than what any of us has charted. Our maps, whether they hang on walls or live inside our heads, will always have edges. The task is not to pretend those edges do not exist. The task is to draw them honestly, to leave the empty spaces empty, and to keep a little room in our lives for the things we have not yet learned.

So the next time you encounter someone who admits they do not know something, consider giving them a small gift of respect. They are standing at the coastline of their understanding, pen lifted, listening for the sailor's story. And somewhere beyond the edge of what either of you knows, there is a whole continent waiting, unnamed and unmapped, which is perhaps the most hopeful thing a map can contain.

# The Slow Leaving

Every year, the Moon moves a little farther away from us. It is only about 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the speed at which fingernails grow. We know this because, since the Apollo missions, reflectors left on the lunar surface have bounced laser pulses back to Earth, and the round-trip times keep stretching. The Moon is leaving, and it is doing so at a pace so gentle that no one alive will notice it happen.

I find this thought oddly comforting. Most things that change in my life change faster than I can track, and most of the slow changes go unseen. The Moon's drift is one of the few cases where the slowness is itself the information.

The cause is tides. The Moon's gravity raises bulges in the oceans, and because the Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, those bulges are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. The ocean's gravitational pull on the Moon therefore has a small forward component, which speeds the Moon up a little. A faster Moon swings out to a higher orbit. Meanwhile, the Earth loses a tiny amount of rotational energy to the friction of all that sloshing water, and its days lengthen by about two thousandths of a second per century. The Earth slows down, and the Moon gets pushed away, and the two effects are the same transaction seen from opposite ends.

What strikes me most is the historical record hidden in living things. Some corals grow daily layers, and some shells add ridges with each day and thicker bands with each month and year. Paleontologists who count these growth lines have found fossil corals from hundreds of millions of years ago that show around four hundred days in a year. Days were shorter then, perhaps closer to twenty-two hours. The rhythm of the planet was written into the bodies of animals, and we can read it now in the rock.

This means that the Moon has been a different object in the sky for most of Earth's history. It was closer, larger, and perhaps more dominant in the night. Its tides were more violent. Some researchers have speculated that the early tidal rhythms may have mattered for the origin of life, since tide pools repeatedly wetting and drying shoreline chemistry could have concentrated the molecules that eventually became cells. I don't know whether that story is true, and I notice how easily it feels true. A story that links the Moon to the first living things is almost too satisfying, and I want to hold it loosely. Still, the basic fact stands: the orbit we take for granted is a recent arrangement, and the sky has been rearranging itself the whole time.

There is something about this that unsettles my sense of scale. We tend to think of the sky as a fixed backdrop, the stars as permanent, the Moon as the Moon. But everything above us is in motion, and our small human lifetimes are a kind of photograph, a single frame in a long film that we only see one piece of. A person who lived in the Devonian would have seen a Moon that looked essentially like ours, except a bit bigger, and would have had a day that ended a couple of hours sooner. Neither of us would have thought the arrangement was strange. It would have been simply the world.

Perhaps that is why I like the image of the leaving Moon. It is a reminder that stability is a matter of timescale. Mountains rise and wear away. Continents drift a few centimeters a year, which is the same pace as the Moon's retreat, and the Atlantic widens by about the length of a fingernail annually. The planet is never finished. It just changes slowly enough that we mistake it for permanence.

I think about this when I look at the Moon on a clear night, which is nearly always bright enough to see the dark seas and the craters. A few thousand years from now it will be a little more distant, the eclipses will be a little rarer, and the total solar eclipses we currently experience because the Moon and Sun appear almost exactly the same size will eventually stop happening. The Moon's apparent size is shrinking, and in a few hundred million years total eclipses will be over. Our descendants, if there are any, will see only annular eclipses, rings of light where the Moon is too small to cover the Sun.

There is a kind of grief in that, though I suspect it is the wrong word. It is more like wonder mixed with the knowledge that the moment you are in is not the only one there could have been. The Moon was once closer and our days were shorter. Someday the days will be longer and the Moon will be a smaller disk in the sky. Every moment is a stage in a long process that no one planned and that no one is supervising.

So when the Moon rises tonight, fat and pale over the rooftops, I'll try to remember that it is leaving, and that it has always been leaving, and that it has also always been coming back in the way that matters, every month, reliable as a heartbeat. Both things are true. The slow leaving and the steady return are the same orbit, seen at different timescales, and the longer you look at it, the less it seems like a contradiction.
