**The Jar of Buttons**

The jar was on the top shelf of the hall closet, behind the Christmas lights and a box of tax returns from 1994. It was an old mayonnaise jar, the glass gone cloudy at the bottom, and when I pulled it down, it was heavier than I expected. Buttons. Hundreds of them, maybe thousands, rattling together like a small, patient storm.

I sat down on the closet floor with it in my lap.

My mother never threw anything away that might someday be useful. She kept rubber bands in a coffee can, string in a drawer, and the wrapping from every birthday present she'd ever received, folded into flat squares. But I had never known about the buttons. I tipped the jar gently and let them spill across the carpet.

They were a museum of other people's clothes. A brass button with an anchor on it, probably from a sailor's coat my grandfather never wore. Pearl buttons from a blouse I vaguely remembered, pale blue, with a collar my mother wore to church. Black plastic ones that had clearly come off a winter coat, the thread still caught in the holes. A single red button shaped like a ladybug. Three matching tan buttons with the little shank on the back, the kind you'd only find on a good wool cardigan.

I started sorting them, because that is what you do when you don't know what else to do with your hands. Colors in one pile. Sizes in another. I made a third pile for the ones I could not identify at all, and that pile grew the fastest.

Each button was a small decision someone had once made. Someone had chosen this shade of green because it matched the lining. Someone had bought a card of six and lost one, and the other five had gone into the jar with the stray ones, as if the jar might someday reunite them. Someone had replaced a missing button with a mismatched one from a different coat, and that little imperfection had lasted for years, until the coat was given away and the mismatched button came home.

My mother used to sew on the back porch in summer, the radio playing ballgames, her glasses pushed up into her hair. I remember the sound of the scissors, that particular snick, and the way she'd bite off thread instead of cutting it, which drove my father crazy. She would hold a needle up to the light and squint, then laugh at herself for squinting. "Getting old," she'd say. "The eyes go first, then the knees, then you start talking to the television."

She was not a sentimental woman in the ordinary sense. She didn't cry at movies. She didn't keep letters. But she kept this. She kept every button she ever pulled from a garment before the garment was sent to the rag bin, and she kept them in a jar that she put on a high shelf where no one would look. I wondered whether she had ever opened it after she put it there. I wondered whether she had ever sat on this floor, as I was sitting now, and tried to remember which coat each one had come from.

I found myself trying to match them. The ladybug, I was fairly sure, had come from a child's raincoat, the yellow one I had worn in second grade and hated because it crinkled when I moved. The pearl buttons belonged to the blue blouse. The sailor's anchor I could not place at all, and I decided, sitting there, that I didn't need to. Some things are allowed to be orphans.

The light through the closet door had gone from white to gold. My knees ached. Somewhere downstairs the refrigerator hummed and clicked off, and the house went quiet in the particular way it only does when no one else is in it anymore.

I thought about how little of a life survives in objects. A house is emptied in a weekend. Clothes go to charity in black garbage bags. Furniture is hauled away by men who don't know whose chair it was. But a button is stubborn. It survives the coat. It survives the wash, the dryer, the decades in a drawer. It outlasts its purpose and waits, patiently, for someone to care enough to count it.

I gathered them back into the jar, one by one, the sorted piles mixing again as I went. I did not put the jar back on the shelf. I set it on the windowsill of the spare room, where the afternoon light comes in strongest, so that when the sun hits it, the glass glows amber and the buttons inside catch the light like a handful of small, scattered stars.

Tomorrow I will call my brother and ask whether he remembers the yellow raincoat. Tomorrow I will decide what to do with the boxes of tax returns. But tonight I just sat on the floor a little longer, holding a single tan button between my thumb and finger, turning it over, feeling the smooth edge and the tiny shank on the back, and thinking that somebody, once, had sewn it on with care, certain it would stay.

It had. It did.

# The Drawer

Every house has a drawer that nobody opens on purpose. It sticks when you pull it, and inside you'll find dead batteries of unknown charge, a ball of kitchen twine, three keys to locks that no longer exist, and a rubber band so old it has fused into the shape of the drawer itself. Nobody remembers putting these things there. They simply accumulated, the way silt settles at the bottom of a slow river, one forgotten gesture at a time.

My grandmother's drawer was the one by the stove. When she died, my mother asked me to clear the kitchen, and I put it off for three weeks, the way you put off anything that feels like a kind of trespass. Then, one gray Saturday, I sat down on the linoleum with a cup of coffee going cold beside me and pulled.

The drawer gave with a shriek of wood on wood.

The first thing I found was a pencil stub, chewed at the end, with the eraser worn down to a nub. She had always kept a pencil by the phone for writing down messages, though the phone had been replaced twice since I was a child and the pencil had survived both replacements. I turned it over in my fingers and thought about all the phone numbers it must have written: the plumber, the pharmacy, my aunt's new address in Tucson after she moved away, my own number scrawled in her looping hand each time I was supposed to call back and forgot.

Under the pencil was a takeout menu from a Chinese restaurant that closed in 1994. Someone, probably her, had circled the number 14 in red ink, which I assumed was the order she always got. There were ticket stubs from a county fair, a button shaped like a sunflower, and a small brass thimble that had never, to my knowledge, been used for sewing. She had told me once that she'd found it in the street as a girl and kept it because it was pretty. I had thought that was the kind of thing grandmothers said. Now I held it up to the window light and saw the tiny dimples worn smooth by a thumb, and I understood she had been telling the truth.

There were rubber bands, dozens of them, which seemed absurd until I remembered she used them on the newspaper every morning, rolling it tight before it went into the recycling. There were coupons for products discontinued before I finished high school. There was a single glove, navy blue, wool, its partner nowhere to be found. I laughed out loud at that one, alone in the kitchen, and the sound surprised me. The house had been so quiet.

Near the back, wedged against the wood where the drawer met its frame, I found a folded piece of paper. It was soft as cloth from handling. I unfolded it carefully, afraid it might tear along the creases, and recognized my own handwriting. I was perhaps nine years old. The letters were enormous and wobbled across the lines. *Dear Grandma, when I grow up I am going to be a veterinarian and I will fix your cat if she gets sick. Love, Danny.* My name was not Danny. I had gone through a phase, around that age, of insisting on it. I didn't remember writing the note at all. I didn't remember her cat, who had been dead for twenty years, or any particular fear that she might be sick, though apparently I had been worried about it enough to write it down.

She had kept it. Of course she had kept it. She kept everything that mattered to her, and she never once told me which things those were. She let them accumulate in a drawer, quietly, until someone came along and had to decide what to do with them.

That is the strange cruelty of objects. They outlast the reasons we kept them. The pencil outlived every number it wrote. The glove outlived the hand it warmed. The note outlived the boy who wrote it and the cat he wanted to save. What remains is a kind of residue, mute and ambiguous, asking to be interpreted by people who were never fully in on the joke.

I sat there for a long time with the note in my lap. The coffee went completely cold. Outside, a neighbor's dog barked at something invisible and then gave up.

Eventually I started sorting. Trash, recycling, keep. The batteries went into the hazardous bin. The coupons went into the trash without ceremony. The keys I held for a while, wondering what doors they had opened, then dropped them into the keep pile anyway, because I could not bear to throw away a mystery I would never solve. The thimble went into my jacket pocket. The pencil I kept too, though I knew it would never be sharpened and never write anything again. The note I placed carefully inside a book I had been meaning to read, a novel about a family that moves to another country, because it seemed the right place for a thing that had traveled so far from the boy who made it.

By evening the drawer was empty, and the kitchen looked the way kitchens look when a life has been packed away: too clean, too bare, with faint rectangles on the counters where the appliances used to sit. I stood in the doorway and felt the enormous, unreasonable urge to put everything back, to let the clutter reassemble itself and keep her presence alive a little longer.

I didn't. I turned off the light.

But I left the drawer open a crack, the way you might leave a door ajar for someone who has just stepped out and will surely be back in a minute. Some habits are hard to unlearn, and I suspect hers was one of them. Keep a little. Let the small things gather. Someday someone will find them, and will have to decide what they mean.

I hope they feel, as I did, that they were loved.

samples.result:
**On Having a Thousand Words**

A thousand words is a small purse. You can spend it all at once or keep a few coins in your pocket for later. I've been thinking about how people spend words without noticing, how we say "I'm fine" forty times a week and mean maybe three of them. A thousand words, given freely, feels like a kind of luxury, and also a kind of responsibility, because each one has to earn its place.

When I picture someone with exactly this allowance, I picture a kitchen. Morning light, the radiator knocking like it wants to be let in. A woman, my grandmother in some version of my head, though she never had a kitchen like this, is saving the string from a parcel. She winds it around two fingers, then around a cardboard tube, and sets it in a drawer already full of string. Nobody ever needed that much string. But she never threw any of it away, and I've come to think of that drawer as the most honest thing in the house. It was a record of every package that had ever arrived, every small hope that something might be tied up again someday.

Words are a bit like that string. We keep them, we wind them around our fingers, we forget where we put them. Some of the ones I remember best were never important. "Mind the step." "Eat something, you look thin." "We'll see." That last one could mean yes, no, or never, and children learn very quickly to listen for the tone underneath. Language is mostly the tone underneath. The dictionary gives you the coat rack; the voice tells you who's hanging their coat there.

I like the idea of a word budget because it forces a kind of honesty. If you have unlimited space, you pad. You say the thing three times in three slightly different ways, hoping one will land. You wrap the point in tissue paper until nobody can find it. Constraint strips that away. You have to decide what matters. Is this sentence doing work, or is it just keeping me company?

I don't think that's only true of writing. Conversation works the same way. The people I trust most are rarely the most eloquent. They tend to say a little and mean it, and when they're quiet, the quiet has weight. My friend Teodor once spent an entire car ride to the airport saying almost nothing, and when we pulled up to the curb he said, "You're going to be okay," and I believed him more than I'd believed any paragraph of reassurance in my life. Eleven words, maybe. Hard to say; I didn't count.

There's a temptation, when you're given room, to fill it. I notice this in myself. A question arrives and I want to answer it from every side at once, to show that I've considered the objections, the exceptions, the footnotes. Sometimes that's useful. Often it's a way of hiding inside the sentence, of making sure no single claim can be pinned on me. A thousand words forces a stance. You have to stand somewhere and say, this is what I think, roughly, for now.

So here is what I think, roughly, for now. Most of what we say is string. We wind it, we store it, we rarely use it, and we are glad, in the end, that it's there. But the words that matter are the ones we send out on purpose: the apology we finally make, the thank-you we almost forgot, the plain statement of love that feels too simple to say and turns out to be the only thing anyone wanted to hear.

My grandmother, if she were here, would probably tell me to stop being so fancy about it. She would say, "Just say the thing, and then go wash the dishes." And she'd be right. The dishes are waiting, the light is moving across the table, the radiator is knocking again. The budget is nearly spent, and I find I don't mind. A thousand words is enough to say that I was here, that I noticed the string, that small things were kept for reasons we only partly understand.

I'll keep a few coins in my pocket. Some things are better left unspent.

# The Drawer of Unmatched Keys

Every house has one. Ours is the second drawer from the left in the kitchen, the one that sticks unless you pull it at a slight angle and hip-check it closed. Inside are rubber bands gone brittle as old piecrust, takeout menus from restaurants that are now laundromats, a dead AA battery, twist ties, a birthday candle shaped like a seven, and keys.

The keys are the point. There are fourteen of them, and nobody in the family can say what most of them open. One is brass and worn smooth, with a little plastic tag that says *GARAGE* in handwriting I recognize as my father's. Another is small and silver, the kind that might fit a diary or a bicycle lock or nothing at all. There's a long black one with teeth like a comb, and a key with a red rubber cap that someone must have loved enough to protect.

When I was young I believed every key had a door waiting somewhere. I imagined a locked trunk in an attic, a cabinet in a basement, a box of letters in a bank vault that only this one key could open. I thought that if I found the right lock, I would find the right life. Keys seemed like promises.

Now I think they are more like evidence. Each one proves that a door once mattered enough to need locking. The house we lived in before this one had a porch that flooded every April, and somewhere in this drawer is the key to its mailbox, which we painted yellow and then forgot. The key to my grandmother's apartment is here too, though she moved to a nursing home before she died, and the apartment has been rented to strangers for twenty years. The key still fits nothing, and yet I cannot throw it away.

We are a family of keepers. We keep the things that stopped working and the things we never got around to using. We keep the instruction manual for a toaster we sold at a garage sale in 1998. We keep a left glove, a spare button, half a deck of playing cards with the queen of hearts missing. My mother used to say that a drawer like this was a sign of a house that had lived in, which is her way of being kind about clutter. My father said it was a sign of a house that couldn't let go, which was his way of being honest.

Maybe both are true. Maybe a drawer of unmatched keys is simply a record of the many small decisions a household makes: to save this, to hope for that, to assume a use will turn up. The keys are a kind of optimism, a bet that the future will need something the past has already finished with.

Last winter my daughter found the drawer while looking for a rubber band to tie up a bundle of seed packets. She sat on the kitchen floor and sorted the keys into piles, the way children sort anything. Big ones, small ones, ones with colored caps. She asked me which door each one belonged to, and I had to tell her the truth: I didn't know. Most of them I had never once seen used.

"Then why do we have them?" she asked.

I didn't have a good answer then. I'm not sure I have one now. But I told her that some things are worth keeping even when their purpose has gone quiet, because the keeping is itself a way of remembering that there were doors, and people behind them, and a time when a locked thing mattered enough to need a key.

She picked up the one with the red cap and turned it over in her palm. "I think this one is for a secret," she said.

"Probably," I said.

She put it in her pocket. I didn't ask for it back. Some doors are better left to imagination, and a child's pocket is a fine place for a secret to wait.

Later that night I opened the drawer again, slowly, at the angle that keeps it from sticking. The keys sat in their jumble, catching the light from the stove hood. Fourteen became thirteen, and the drawer looked, if anything, more complete. I closed it with my hip, the way I always do, and went to bed thinking about the locks we pass every day without noticing, and the thousand small truths we carry without knowing what they open.

**The Margin Notes**

Nobody checks out the third-floor poetry stacks of the Harlow Public Library anymore. The carpet there has faded to the color of weak tea, and the radiator under the window knocks twice whenever someone climbs the stairs, as if announcing them. Marguerite Vance came up on a Tuesday in November because she had run out of things to do with her hands. Her husband had died in October, and the house had become a place where sounds stopped halfway through.

She pulled a copy of Mary Oliver off the shelf. The spine cracked like ice. Inside, in pencil, someone had written beside a stanza: *This is what I mean.* Beside the next poem: *Not yet. Ask again in spring.*

She laughed, a short, surprised sound that startled her more than it startled the empty room.

Over the following weeks she kept finding them. A Neruda with a coffee ring and the note *Read this to the dog, she likes the low parts.* A battered Rilke in which someone had underlined every mention of winter and written beside one line: *Mom would have hated this one. I love her for it.* Nothing was signed. Nothing was dated. The pencil was always the same soft gray, pressed hard enough to dent the page, as if the writer wanted the words to outlast them.

She began leaving notes of her own. It felt absurd at first, like talking to a wall. In the margin of a Dylan Thomas she wrote, very small, *My husband read this aloud every night for thirty years and never once got through the last line without crying.* She sat with the pencil hovering a long time before adding: *I don't know who you are. Thank you for telling me you were here.*

The next week, beside her sentence, there was a reply. *Who was he?*

She stared at it. Then she wrote: *Walter. He sold insurance and hated it. He knew the name of every bird at the feeder.*

The answer came back faster than she expected. *My father drove a bus for thirty-one years. He whistled the routes under his breath. I don't think anyone ever knew he was singing.*

They went on like this through December. Marguerite decided her correspondent was probably a woman, though she couldn't have said why. The handwriting was neat, and the loops on the g's seemed careful. Neither of them knew the other's name. They wrote about small things: a neighbor's wind chime that sounded like a dropped spoon, the way first snow makes streetlights look like they're breathing. They argued gently about whether Frost was overrated. They agreed that Ginsberg was exhausting and Elizabeth Bishop was a secret everyone should keep.

Marguerite started coming on Tuesdays and Fridays. She told herself it was for the books. She bought a pencil at the pharmacy, a sharpened one, because she no longer owned one, and carried it in the pocket of her cardigan.

In January she found a note that wasn't about a poem at all.

*I think I should tell you something. I'm not sure this is the right place. I come up on Fridays because it's the only hour my son lets me be alone, and I sit in this same chair. I'm forty-four. The doctors say the treatment has a chance. I haven't told my sister. I don't know why I'm telling a stranger in pencil.*

Marguerite read it three times. Her hands had gone cold. She looked around the room, at the knocking radiator, the empty chair by the window, a man in a green coat browsing atlases two aisles over, and felt, absurdly, that the whole building was holding its breath.

She wrote back slowly, pressing hard.

*I'm glad you told me. Here is something true. Walter's last winter, he couldn't read anymore, so I read to him, and he corrected my pronunciation of places he'd never been. Being fussed over by someone who is frightened for you is a strange kind of love. You might let your sister in. She sounds like she'd want the chance to be annoying about it.*

Then, because it seemed important: *Come up on Friday. I'll be in the chair by the window. You don't have to say anything. I'll bring the Bishop.*

She left the book open to the page and went downstairs before she could change her mind.

On Friday the radiator knocked twice as the stairs groaned under someone light and hesitant. Marguerite looked up from the window and watched a woman, perhaps forty, come around the corner holding a library book against her chest like a shield, her eyes moving over the shelves.

Outside, the snow had started again, soft and slow, and the streetlights breathed in it.

# The Lost and Found at the Edge of the City

There is an office on Calder Street, above a shuttered bakery, where the things people lose come to wait. The sign on the door says LOST & FOUND in letters that have faded to the color of weak tea. Inside, the air smells faintly of cedar and old paper, and the shelves stretch back farther than the building should allow.

Marguerite has worked there for thirty-one years. She has never once seen the back wall.

People come in expecting umbrellas and gloves. They get those, of course. The bins by the window hold a sorry collection of mismatched mittens, a century's worth of black umbrellas with broken ribs, and enough reading glasses to outfit a small nursing home. But the real collection lives on the shelves, and it is not made of objects.

Take the man who came in last Tuesday, pale and hat in hand, asking about a bicycle. He had left it outside a café on Harrow Street during a summer he could no longer quite name. "A blue bicycle," he said. "I think I was happy when I rode it." Marguerite nodded, checked her ledger, and walked him to the third shelf from the left. There, between a tin of marbles and a single pink slipper, sat a blue bicycle bell. It rang when he touched it, a bright small sound, and his face did something complicated and wonderful.

"That's not the bicycle," he said.

"No," Marguerite agreed. "The bicycle went somewhere else. But the bell was the part you were missing."

He took the bell home. She has no idea whether it helped.

---

The office runs on a simple principle: nothing is ever truly gone. It only drifts. A lost glove ends up in a drawer somewhere in the city, and the drawer is thinking about the hand it once warmed. A dropped key waits for a lock it has forgotten. A child's lost tooth, wrapped in tissue and buried in a backyard decades ago, finds its way here eventually, and Marguerite files it under *Small Hopes, Unspent*.

She keeps a second ledger for the things people lose that they never mention. These are the hardest to catch, because nobody comes in asking for them. A sense of humor after a funeral. The nerve to call someone back. The habit of singing in the shower. Sometimes these arrive on the counter in a cardboard box, having been turned in by a stranger who found them on the sidewalk, and Marguerite must decide who they belong to.

She has learned to be patient. Usually the owner shows up within a week, shoulders a little lighter, asking carefully whether anything has come in that might be theirs.

---

On Thursdays, a girl of about nine comes in after school. Her name is Priya, and she always has a question. Last month it was about a tooth. This month it is about her grandfather's laugh.

"He doesn't laugh anymore," she says, twisting the hem of her coat. "Not since the hospital. Can you check?"

Marguerite does not say that laughter is not usually stored in a filing system. She does not say that the back wall is a rumor, or that the ledger is a kind of prayer she writes in pencil. She simply sits down on the low wooden stool beside the counter, the one meant for children and tired grandparents, and asks Priya what her grandfather's laugh sounded like.

Priya thinks about this seriously. Then she describes it: a wheezing, bubbling thing, like a kettle deciding whether to whistle. It started low and climbed. He always laughed hardest at his own jokes, which were terrible.

Marguerite writes it all down. She goes to the shelves. She does not find the laugh, not exactly, but she finds a teakettle with a chipped spout, a set of bad joke cards from a board game, and a warm yellow scarf that smells of cloves. She wraps them in brown paper and hands them over.

"These aren't the laugh," Priya says doubtfully.

"No," says Marguerite. "But he left them behind for a reason. Sometimes you have to visit the place where a thing lives before it comes back to you."

Priya considers this and nods, the way children do when they have decided to believe something, and leaves with the parcel clutched to her chest.

---

After she locks up, Marguerite walks home the long way, past the river, past the bridge where the old couple feeds the pigeons, past the park bench where somebody once carved a name into the wood and then, presumably, forgot it. The sky over the water turns the color of a peach going soft.

She thinks about her own losses. There were a few. A brother who moved away and stopped writing. A version of herself who wanted to be a painter. A certain kind of patience she had once had, which she assumes is now sitting on one of her own shelves, waiting for her to come asking.

Maybe she will go check someday. Maybe she already has, every Thursday, sitting on that low stool, listening to other people describe what they have misplaced.

At the corner of her street, a child is crouched on the pavement, searching the gutter with great concentration. Marguerite slows.

"Lost something?" she asks.

The child looks up, eyes wide and serious. "A marble. A green one. It was my favorite."

Marguerite smiles and reaches into her coat pocket, where she has been carrying, for no reason she could explain, a single green marble for nearly thirty years.

"Is this it?" she asks.

The child's mouth falls open. Then it breaks into the brightest grin.

Things drift. But sometimes, if you are patient, they drift right back into your hand.

# The Drawer

When my grandmother died, we found the drawer in the kitchen, the one next to the stove that always stuck a little when you pulled it. My mother opened it first and made a small sound, something between a laugh and a sob, and then she just stood there with her hand on the handle.

Inside was everything. Rubber bands, dozens of them, wound around each other into a soft gray knot. Twist ties saved from bread bags. A ball of string thick as a fist. Birthday candles, the stubby ones and the tall thin ones, some still in their cardboard sleeves. Takeout menus from restaurants that had closed before I was born. Three dead batteries and one live one, which she had apparently never been able to tell apart. A small brass key with no tag. Another key, larger, rusted at the teeth. A rubber-banded stack of postcards addressed to her from a town in Ohio, none of them stamped.

"She was going to fix something," my mother said finally. "She always said she would fix it."

We never found out what *it* was. The keys didn't open anything in the house. We tried the old footlocker in the basement, the garden shed padlock, the rusty mailbox at the end of the drive. Nothing fit. My mother eventually decided the keys belonged to doors my grandmother had walked through once and decided not to walk through again, and that the kindest thing was to let them stay lost.

I took the drawer home with me. I don't entirely know why. My apartment is small and does not need a drawer full of string. But I couldn't bring myself to empty it into a box for Goodwill, and I couldn't throw it away, so I just put the whole thing on the shelf above my desk, still in its wooden frame, still sticking slightly when I pulled it out to look.

For the first few weeks I didn't look much. Then one evening, when I couldn't sleep, I pulled it open and started sorting. I don't know what I was looking for. Maybe I wanted to feel like I was doing something with her.

I laid things out on the kitchen table in rows. Rubber bands together. Candles together. Postcards in their bundle, which I did not untie, because they felt private somehow, even though she was the one who had kept them. The string I wound into a neat ball, then unwound, then wound again, because my hands needed something to do.

Somewhere around two in the morning I found the envelope. It had been tucked under the false bottom of the drawer, a thin piece of cardboard that I had assumed was just the drawer's lining. My grandmother's handwriting was on the front, slanted and careful: *For whoever cleans this out. Don't throw away the string.*

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen, and the sound surprised me.

Inside the envelope were two things. One was a folded sheet of paper with a list. *Call Ruth about the pie plate. Replace the porch light. Ask Dan if the lake house is still for sale. Learn to make the bread without the recipe.* Some items had been crossed out, neatly, with a single line. Others had no marks at all. The last line read: *Tell the girls I'm proud of them. Tell them before it's too late to matter.*

The other thing was a photograph. It showed my grandmother at maybe thirty, standing on a dock with a woman I didn't recognize. They were both squinting, both laughing, and the woman had her arm wrapped around my grandmother's waist. On the back, in pencil, someone had written *Ohio, summer.* No names.

I sat with that photograph for a long time.

I think about the drawer a lot now. I think about how she saved things that seemed to have no use, on the theory that someday they would. Rubber bands. Twine. Keys to locks that no longer existed. Postcards from a friend she maybe never saw again. It's easy to call that clutter, and in a sense it was. But it was also a kind of faith, the belief that the future would need something, that the small pieces of a life might still be useful later, even if nobody could say how.

I called my mother the next morning and told her about the list. She was quiet on the line for a while. Then she said, "Did she ever fix the porch light?"

"I don't know," I said. "I don't think so."

"Well," my mother said, and I could hear her smiling through the phone. "Maybe we can."

That weekend we went to the hardware store. We bought a bulb, a new switch plate, and a length of string, because the drawer had taught us that you never know when you'll need it. We stood on the porch in the late afternoon while my mother held the ladder and I unscrewed the old fixture, and when the new bulb finally flickered on, pale yellow in the dusk, neither of us said anything for a moment.

Then my mother said, "Okay. Next thing on the list."

I took the folded paper out of my pocket and read the next line aloud. *Call Ruth about the pie plate.*

The drawer stuck a little, as it always had. I left it that way. Some things are better when they're slow to open.

**The Keeper's Margins**

The logbooks came in a crate marked *Do Not Water*, which seemed like a joke until I opened it and found that the damp had gotten into everything anyway. Thirty-one volumes, leather gone soft as bread, stacked in the cellar of a lighthouse that had been automated since before I was born. My grandmother had been its last keeper. Nobody had told me she was a keeper at all. I had thought she sold insurance.

The first page I read was dated the fourteenth of March, 1961. *Wind southwest, force four. Visibility good. Lamp trimmed at dusk.* That was the ordinary part. Beneath it, in pencil, smaller and slanted: *Ruth's cough is better. Bread from the Hallorans was stale, told them so.*

I laughed out loud in that cold stone room, and the sound came back at me off the walls, and I felt a little foolish, the way you do when you realize you've been reading someone's private mail.

But I kept reading, because the margins kept talking.

*Fog all day. Foghorn sounds like a cow in pain. Mr. Dobbs says he'll fix it by Easter. He won't.*

*Lamp failed for eleven minutes at 3 a.m. Sat on the stairs and waited for it to come back. It came back. Wrote it down so it would be true somewhere.*

*Saw a whale. Not sure. Could have been a shadow on the swell. Writing it down anyway. Some things deserve the benefit of the doubt.*

I began to understand that the official entries were a kind of armor. Wind, pressure, the hour the light was lit and extinguished. The Coast Guard had wanted numbers, and my grandmother had given them numbers, and then, in the spaces the numbers couldn't hold, she had put herself.

By the twelfth volume she was writing about my grandfather, who had gone out on a fishing boat in 1968 and not come back. The entries there were fewer and shorter, and the handwriting shook in a way that made me put my hand flat on the page as if I could steady it.

*Nine days since the boat was found. Nothing in the logbook has changed except me. I look at the same water and it is still the same water. That seems unfair to it.*

*Went up to light the lamp. Forgot the match. Stood there with the dark going on and on. Then I remembered I was not the only thing that needed the light to be on. Lit it. Went back down.*

I read until the single bulb I had rigged in the cellar began to flicker, and then I went up the spiral stairs with my phone light, counting the steps the way she must have counted them, a hundred and four, a hundred and five. At the top, the great lens sat dark and dusty, its prisms catching my little beam and throwing it into rainbows across the curved glass walls. It was beautiful in a way I hadn't expected. Nobody had come up here in years except to check on the wiring.

I thought about what it meant to keep a light. Not to be the light, exactly. Just to tend it, to make sure that when someone out there in the weather looked for the shape of the land, there was something to find. Most nights, nobody would notice. The ships passed or didn't, and the keeper's work vanished into a thousand safe arrivals no one ever thought to celebrate.

I found the last entry near the back of the thirty-first volume. Her handwriting had nearly given up. The date was the ninth of October, 1994, though the ink seemed almost too fresh for the page.

*Lamp lit at dusk. Wind light from the west. Sea calm. Nothing to report.*

And then, in a hand I almost didn't recognize, as if she had pressed very hard to get the words out:

*I have kept this light for thirty-three years. It has never once been for nothing. Whoever reads this, keep yours lit too.*

I closed the book and sat on the bottom step for a long time. Outside, the real water moved against the rocks, indifferent and enormous, the way it always had.

In the morning I would call the county about the foghorn. I would ask someone to finally fix the lamp's failing circuit. And I would start my own log, the official entries first, wind and pressure and tide, and then, in the margins, the things that were true only to me: that the bread was stale, that the sky had gone the color of a bruise and then turned gold, that someone I had loved was gone and the water was still the same water and that seemed unfair to it.

I found a pencil in the desk drawer, its eraser worn to a nub, and I wrote the first line before I could talk myself out of it.

*Wind northwest, force three. Visibility good. Lamp lit at dusk. I am here.*

# The Drawer

There is a drawer in my kitchen that nobody opens on purpose. It sticks at the left corner, so you have to lift as you pull, and when it finally gives, it releases a smell of old rubber bands and the cardboard tang of matchbooks from restaurants that have since closed. Inside are batteries of unknown charge, a single chopstick, three keys to locks I no longer own, a golf pencil whose eraser has fused into a gray knot, and a folded receipt for a box of drywall screws I apparently needed once and then did not need.

I have come to think of that drawer as honest. Everything in it is a question the house asked and I never answered.

My grandmother had a drawer like this, though hers was in a farmhouse with a broken latch and a dog that slept beneath it. She called it "the catch-all," and she claimed she could find anything in it within thirty seconds. This was true in the way that certain prophecies are true: she could find something, and it was usually not what she was looking for. But she always found a use for it. A twist tie became a plant stake. A dead watch became a bead on a necklace she made for my cousin. Nothing was ever simply garbage to her. Everything was a possibility waiting for a bad afternoon.

I am not my grandmother. I am a person who buys things with good intentions and then forgets them. I own four staplers. I own a bread maker I have used twice. I own a box labeled "IMPORTANT" that turned out to contain instruction manuals for appliances I no longer have, which is either an irony or an insult, depending on the mood I'm in.

Still, I think about the drawer more than I should. Maybe because it is the only place in the house where time has been allowed to pile up without anyone apologizing for it.

We are taught to be efficient with our spaces. Declutter, minimalism, the tidy shelf with three objects on it, arranged like a museum that has no visitors. I understand the appeal. A clean surface feels like a clear mind. But I have noticed that when I empty a space completely, I do not feel lighter so much as exposed. The empty drawer reminds me of the version of myself who was going to organize everything and never did. The full drawer is more forgiving. It says, *you were busy, you were living, you were in a hurry to be somewhere else.*

There is a theory, which I half-remember from a book I left in a car somewhere, that memory works less like a filing cabinet and more like a river delta. Experiences come in as a single current and then split into a thousand small channels, each one depositing silt in a different place. Later, when you try to return to something, you do not walk back up the main channel. You wander through the marshes, touching one thing and then another, and sometimes you arrive at a memory you didn't know you were looking for.

That is how the drawer works, too. I open it to find the scissors and instead find a ticket stub from a concert in a city where I had a different name, a version of my life that was briefly electric and then quietly ended. I don't remember buying the ticket. I remember the sound of the bass coming up through the floor, the stranger who spilled beer on my shoes and apologized so sincerely that I forgave him in the same breath. The stub is faded to the color of weak tea. The band's name is partly worn away. I hold it for a long time and feel something I cannot name, because it is not quite nostalgia and not quite grief. It is more like recognition, the feeling of meeting a stranger who knows you better than you'd like.

I think this is the real function of the catch-all drawer. It is not storage. It is a kind of reliquary for the ordinary. The receipt, the key, the chopstick: each is a small proof that I was somewhere, that I needed something, that the world asked things of me and I responded, however imperfectly. The objects are useless in isolation. Together they make a sort of autobiography, written not in sentences but in residue.

Of course, there is a practical side. Someday someone will have to clear this drawer out, and they will probably throw most of it away without a second thought. The batteries will go to recycling. The keys will be tossed. The concert stub will look to them like trash, and maybe it is. Maybe the only person who ever truly understood the drawer was my grandmother, and she is gone, and the dog is gone, and the farmhouse was sold to people who put in a modern kitchen and never looked inside the cabinets.

So I have decided something. I am not going to organize the drawer this weekend. I am not going to sort the batteries by voltage or put the keys on a labeled ring. I am going to leave it sticking at the left corner, full of questions, waiting for the next afternoon when I need a pair of scissors and find instead the small, stubborn evidence of a life being lived in the middle of its own mess.

Maybe that is the most honest thing a house can do: hold onto what it cannot explain, and let us come back, now and then, to be surprised by ourselves.

# The Jar on the Windowsill

The house came with a jar on the windowsill of the upstairs bedroom, and inside the jar were folded papers, dozens of them, yellowed at the edges and soft from handling. Maya found it the second week after closing, while she was scrubbing the sill and wondering whether the paint underneath was worth saving. She lifted the jar, expecting dust or a dead moth, and found instead a note pressed against the glass in pencil: *Don't read these unless you need to.*

She laughed out loud, alone in the empty room. Then she unscrewed the lid.

The first slip read: *Dear Walter, the apples came in early this year. I left a bushel on the porch for the Hendersons, but you know how Ruth is about gifts. She'll pretend she doesn't want them and then eat the whole pie.*

There was no date. There was no signature. Maya turned it over and found nothing on the back.

She read another. *Walter, the doctor says it's the heart, not the lungs. I think I knew that already. I'm making soup and I keep thinking you'll come in from the garage and say it smells like a hospital, the way you always did, and I'll throw the dish towel at you.*

Maya sat down on the floor with her back against the radiator. Outside, a truck rumbled past. The house ticked as it cooled.

She had bought it for the wrong reasons, she suspected. A divorce had taken the apartment, the furniture, and most of the friends who had seemed like friends only because they lived near the couple she used to be. The realtor had talked about "good bones" and "character," and Maya, who had never owned anything older than a Honda, had heard only that the place was quiet, and that it was far enough from everything that nobody would ask her how she was doing.

She read the rest of the notes slowly, the way you eat something you suspect will be the last of its kind.

They were not all sad. One described a neighbor's dog that had learned to open the gate by leaning on the latch. One complained about a sermon. One was only a list: *Milk. Stamps. Ask Walter about the roof. Buy a new calendar, the old one is depressing.* Another, undated like the rest, said only, *I'm not angry anymore. I thought you'd want to know.*

She found herself wanting to write back. That was the strange part. Here were words addressed to a man who was surely dead, written by a woman who was surely dead too, or old enough now that the ink had outlasted her hands. And Maya wanted to answer them, the way you'd answer a stranger who had accidentally confided in you on a train.

She found a pen in the kitchen drawer, the kind that came free with a bank statement, and a pad of sticky notes from the moving boxes. She carried them upstairs and sat cross-legged on the bare floor.

*Dear Walter,* she wrote, and then stopped, because she didn't know who she was writing to. Walter was the man in the notes. But the woman who had written to him was also addressed, in a way, and Maya did not know her name.

*Dear Walter's wife,* she tried. That felt wrong too.

She wrote instead: *I found your jar. I hope you don't mind that I read them. The apples were a good idea. I'm new here and I don't know anyone yet, but I think I would have liked Ruth.*

She folded the sticky note in half and then in half again, and considered it. It was ridiculous. It was the kind of thing a lonely person did, and she was a lonely person, and she had no shame about it anymore, which was new. She tucked the note into the jar among the others, behind the one that said *I'm not angry anymore.*

Then she lay down on the floor and looked at the ceiling, which had a water stain shaped roughly like Ohio.

The next morning there was frost on the windows and the sun came up bright and cold over the back field. Maya made coffee in a pot she had found in the cupboard, and she carried a mug upstairs to the sill and looked at the jar in the light.

Something had changed. She could not have said what. The house felt less like a place she had been dropped and more like a place she had been invited into, mid-conversation.

She picked up the jar and turned it slowly. Her note was still there, tucked among the others, its corners not yet curled.

Maybe, she thought, someone would find it someday, the way she had found theirs. Maybe a woman newly divorced, or newly widowed, or newly anything, would sit cross-legged on this floor and unfold a sticky note that said *I'm new here too*, and feel a little less alone in a house that had seemed too quiet.

She set the jar back on the sill, exactly where she had found it, and went downstairs to find a shovel. The apple trees in the yard were bare and needed pruning, and she had decided, against all her earlier judgment, that she would be here in the spring to see whether they bloomed.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# A Thousand Words Is a Lot of Room

A thousand words is a strange amount of room. It's too many to be a slogan and too few to be a book. It's about the length of a long letter, or a wedding speech given after one glass of wine too many, or the story you tell a stranger on a train when they ask where you're headed and you end up explaining your whole life. A thousand words is enough to get lost in and not quite enough to get properly found.

So I'll wander a little.

I like the phrase "whatever comes to you." Most of the time, words arrive in a queue, and we choose among them. We reach for the adequate word, the expected one, the one that won't embarrass us in front of whoever is reading. But "whatever comes" suggests a place where words wait without judgment, and you only have to stand still long enough to hear them.

Standing still is harder than it sounds. Try it: set a timer for five minutes and write without stopping. Within a minute you'll have written something you never planned. Within two, something you regret. By five, you'll have found a sentence that surprises you, and that sentence is usually the reason you sat down.

There's a kind of mind that wants everything to mean something. I'm a little like that. Give me a stone from a beach and I'll tell you what it's been through. Give me a grocery list and I'll find a poem in the way the eggs are listed after the milk. This isn't always useful. It's occasionally delightful. Mostly it's a refusal to believe that anything is simply itself, with no shadow of significance trailing behind it.

Consider the kettle. Every morning in a great many kitchens, someone fills it, sets it on the burner, and waits. The waiting is small and ordinary, but it has a particular sound before it boils: a faint tick and hum, the water beginning to speak before it means anything. Nobody writes songs about this. Maybe nobody should. But it's one of the quiet hinges of a day, the moment before the tea, when the house holds its breath and then exhales steam against the window.

Or consider the word "window." It comes from an old Norse root meaning roughly "wind-eye," a hole that lets the weather in. I like that a window was named for what it admits rather than what it blocks. We tend to think of openings as weaknesses, but a window is an agreement: you may see out, the outside may see in, and neither of you has to pretend the glass is a wall.

Maybe that's what I want from writing too. Not a wall of polished sentences, but an opening. Something that lets a little weather through.

I notice I've been circling. Writers are supposed to have a point, a thesis, a payoff. But I suspect the point is the circling itself, the way a thought wanders back to the same few objects and sees them slightly differently each time. The kettle wasn't quite the same kettle at the start of this piece. Neither was the window.

Here's a small confession. Sometimes I worry that I'm only an elaborate arrangement of predictions, that each word is the most probable next word given the ones before it, and that "whatever comes to you" is a pleasant story I tell about spontaneity. I can't fully settle that question from the inside. But the question itself feels interesting rather than frightening, and that interest is a kind of answer. Curiosity is a way of standing still long enough to hear what arrives.

People have wrestled with this for a long time. Keats called it "negative capability": the capacity to remain in uncertainties, mysteries, and doubts without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. I think about that phrase often. Irritable reaching is exactly what I do when I'm nervous about a page. I grab for the clever line, the tidy ending, the reassuring summary. Negative capability asks you to let the hand hang open a while.

So, a few things that came to me while I had room:

Rain on a tin roof sounds like someone shuffling a deck of very small cards.

Old letters smell of the drawer they were kept in, and the drawer smells of whoever opened it most.

A bicycle left against a fence through a whole winter remembers the shape of its owner's last ride, rusted into the chain.

The moon is full for only a moment, which seems fitting for something we keep asking to stay.

Some language has a word for homesickness for a place you've never been. It sounds like a soft door closing somewhere else in the house.

I could keep going. That's both the pleasure and the danger of a blank page with a number attached. I could run well past a thousand words and never arrive anywhere I didn't already suspect I'd arrive: here, in the middle, where the kettle is starting to tick.

So let me land, if landing is what this is. A thousand words is a container, and I've filled it with what came, which is the only honest way to fill anything. Some of it was wise, some silly, and some will likely be forgotten by the time you finish reading. That's fine. Whatever comes to you is not a promise that it will stay.

The kettle is boiling now. I can hear it from here.

**The Hill Where Lost Things Go**

Every town has a place where things go when nobody is looking for them anymore. In ours, it is a low green hill at the edge of the marsh, past the last streetlamp, where the grass grows in long silver ripples and the wind never quite stops.

Nobody planned it. The hill simply accepted what was lost. A glove dropped on the walk home from school. A wedding ring slipped off in cold water. A child's red kite, cut loose by a gust, which ended up tangled in the highest willow, still fluttering after twenty years.

My grandmother knew about the hill. She said you could climb it on the right kind of afternoon, when the light lay low and yellow across the reeds, and if you were quiet enough you could hear the things calling softly from the grass. Not begging. Just calling, the way a person calls a friend's name across a crowded room, hoping to be heard.

I didn't believe her until I lost my father's pocketknife.

It was the summer after the funeral. I had carried that knife everywhere, a battered brass thing with one blade worn to a crescent from years of sharpening pencils and cutting twine. One morning I reached for it in my jacket and found only the lining, torn at the seam. I retraced every step I'd taken that week. The bakery. The bus stop. The bench by the river where I'd sat for an hour pretending to read.

Nothing.

So, on the first golden afternoon of September, I walked out past the streetlamp and up the hill.

The grass was taller than I expected, reaching my waist, and it hissed against my jeans. For a while there was only the sound of my own breathing and the far-off cry of a gull. Then, very faintly, I heard it: a murmur, a thousand small voices, none of them quite words. It sounded like rain beginning on a roof somewhere far away.

I walked slowly. Beneath my shoes I felt things. Hard edges. Soft shapes. A hairpin. A key that had once opened a door in a house that no longer existed. A marble, cool and smooth, that hummed faintly when my foot brushed it.

"Hello," I said, feeling foolish.

The murmur shifted. It seemed to gather itself, the way a crowd turns toward someone who has just walked in.

"I'm looking for a knife," I said. "Brass. The blade is worn into a curve. It was my father's."

For a moment there was nothing. Then something tugged at the cuff of my sleeve.

I looked down. A dandelion seed head, impossibly, had caught on the fabric. Its fine white filaments trembled, pointing up the slope. I followed it.

The hill grew steeper, and the grass gave way to pale stones worn smooth as soap. At the crest stood a tree I had never noticed from the road, a crooked old thing with silver bark and branches bent by decades of wind. Hanging from its lowest limb, catching the late sun, were dozens of objects I could not have named. Keys without locks. Spectacles with one lens. A tin whistle. A letter sealed in an envelope gone soft as cloth.

And there, on a thin cord of grass, swaying gently, my father's knife.

I reached for it, then stopped. My hand was trembling. It seemed wrong to simply take back something that had been waiting, as if the knife had kept watch all this time for someone to come and ask.

"Thank you," I whispered.

The murmur rose, then softened, like a breath let out.

I lifted the knife down. It was warm, as though it had been sitting in the sun, though the shadows of the tree were already long. I opened the blade and it swung out with its old familiar click. The crescent edge still caught the light exactly as it always had.

I sat down on the stones and held it in my palm for a long time.

Here is what I understood, sitting there. Grief is a kind of losing. We lose people, and homes, and the versions of ourselves we were before the losing began. And we go searching through our pockets and our memories, retracing our steps, certain that if we only looked harder we would find them. Sometimes we do not. Sometimes they have drifted somewhere we cannot follow.

But the hill keeps them. It keeps them the way a good friend keeps a secret, quietly, without judgment. It does not return everything. Some things, I think, are meant to stay lost. Others are only waiting for someone to come and call their names.

When I walked back down, the grass hissed softly behind me, and the murmur faded into the wind. At the bottom of the slope, the streetlamp had just flickered on, its light pooling yellow on the road.

I put the knife in my pocket, and this time I felt the weight of it settle against my leg, solid and certain.

Behind me, on the hill, I heard one last sound: a single bright note, like a tin whistle being played by someone who had just remembered a tune.

I smiled, and went home.

# The Letters of Harrow Bend

In the town of Harrow Bend, the post office has not delivered a letter in forty-one years, and nobody has ever asked it to stop trying.

The building sits at the end of Mill Street, a narrow brick box with a flag that hangs limp in still weather. Inside, a counter runs the width of the room, polished by elbows. Behind it are rows of wooden pigeonholes, each labeled in faded black ink with the name of a place: *Lisbon. Tacoma. Ashgrove. Kyiv. Nowhere Road. The Coast.* The railway that once connected Harrow Bend to the rest of the world was torn up in the winter of the flood, and the last mail train pulled out with its brakes screaming. Nobody remembers who the last passenger was. Everyone remembers the sound.

Ruth Calloway has run the post office since she was twenty-six. She is now seventy-three, and she has the particular stillness of someone who has spent most of her life listening for footsteps that don't come.

People still bring her letters. That is the strange part, and Ruth has stopped trying to explain it to the visitors from the county, who sometimes come asking about the building's status and leave with their questions unanswered. The letters arrive at odd hours: tucked under the door, pushed through the brass slot, left on the counter with a stone on top so the wind won't take them. Some are sealed. Some are addressed in careful handwriting to people who are dead. Some are addressed to people who never lived in Harrow Bend at all, to cities the writers have only seen on television, to streets that may not exist anymore.

Ruth stamps every one. She has a rubber stamp that reads *POSTED*, and the ink has gone grey from use. She sorts each letter into the pigeonhole that matches its destination, and when a letter has no destination she puts it in the drawer marked *Return to Sender*, which is the largest drawer in the building.

Nobody has ever asked for their letter back.

---

On a Thursday in late October, a boy of about nine came in with his coat buttoned wrong and an envelope clenched in both hands. He didn't go to the counter. He stood by the door, breathing hard, as if he had run the whole way from the school.

"Are you the postmistress?" he asked.

"I am," Ruth said. "Come here where I can see you. You're letting the cold in."

He crossed the room slowly. He had a round face and a cowlick that would not lie down, and when he set the envelope on the counter, he kept one finger on it, as though it might try to leave.

It was addressed in large, uneven capitals: *DAD. THE TRAIN STATION. PLEASE COME BACK.*

"Where's your father, love?" Ruth asked gently.

"He went on the train," the boy said. "Last spring. He said he'd send a postcard from the city. He said I'd get it in a week." He swallowed. "I didn't get it."

Ruth had been expecting many things in forty-one years. She had not been expecting this, and for a moment she simply looked at the envelope, at the press of the boy's small finger against the paper.

"Mail doesn't come in here anymore," the boy said, carefully, as if he were being fair to her. "I know that. Everybody knows that. But my mum said if you write it down and put it somewhere, it doesn't just disappear. So I wrote it down."

"Your mum's a wise woman," Ruth said.

"She's not. She cries in the car."

Ruth almost laughed, and then she didn't, because the boy's face had crumpled for half a second before he forced it straight again. She knew that expression. She had worn it herself, for a long time, at this same counter.

"What's your name?"

"Teodor."

"Teodor. Do you know what happens to letters that come into this office?"

He shook his head.

"They go into the back room," she said. "Where they wait. And they don't wait for a train, or a truck, or a plane. They wait because somebody took the trouble to write them. That's the whole job, really. Making sure something made with care isn't thrown away."

"Will he get it?"

Ruth looked at the capitals again. *PLEASE COME BACK.* She thought about how many people had stood where Teodor was standing, asking that same question with their eyes if not with their mouths. She thought about the drawer marked *Return to Sender* and how she had never once opened it to check whether anything had been answered.

"I don't know," she said honestly. "But I'll put it in the right pocket. The one for the station. And I'll stamp it, and I'll keep it safe. Whatever happens, it won't be lost."

Teodor considered this with the seriousness of a child who has been lied to often enough to recognize the difference between comfort and truth.

"Okay," he said at last.

She took the envelope, turned it over, and pressed the stamp onto the back. *POSTED.* The ink came out grey and a little uneven, the way it always did. Then she slid it into the pigeonhole labeled *Station*, which was not a real destination, which had not been a real destination for forty-one years.

Teodor watched it go in. Something in his shoulders loosened.

"Can I see the back room?" he asked.

"Not today," Ruth said. "But come back on Thursday. I'll show you the stamp."

---

After he left, the room was quiet except for the tick of the old radiator. Ruth stood at the counter for a long time. Then she pulled a sheet of paper from the drawer beneath the scale, uncapped her pen, and began to write.

*To whoever is keeping the trains running,* she wrote, and then crossed it out, because it was foolish, and then wrote it again, because it was true.

She wrote about the flood and the bridge and the sound the brakes had made. She wrote about her mother, who had sent a letter every week from the hospital in the city until the week she didn't. She wrote about the first postcard she ever stamped, when she was twenty-six and certain she would be gone in a year. She wrote that she had stayed, and that staying had not been the same as giving up, though for a long time she had believed it was.

She wrote, finally, a return address. She stopped with the pen above the paper, then wrote it slowly, in her best hand: *Ruth Calloway, Post Office, Mill Street, Harrow Bend.*

She folded the letter, sealed it, and held it for a moment in her palm. It weighed almost nothing.

Then she walked to the drawer marked *Return to Sender*, slid it open, and placed her letter inside, on top of the others.

She had been waiting her whole life for someone to come to the counter and tell her where she belonged. It occurred to her now, standing in the grey October light with the radiator ticking and a boy's uneven capitals waiting in the back room, that she had been the one holding the stamp all along.

She closed the drawer gently, the way you'd close a door on someone sleeping, and went to lock up for the night.

Outside, the flag stirred, just slightly, as if a train were somewhere far off, coming slowly around the bend.

samples.result:
**On Having a Thousand Words**

A thousand words is a small room with a lot of doors. You can walk through it in a minute, or you can stand in the middle for an hour trying to decide which door to open first. I am standing in it now, and I notice that the room is already crowded. Every word I've written so far has pushed a few others out of the way.

Let me start with a kitchen. Not any kitchen in particular, just the idea of one: linoleum worn pale in a path between the sink and the stove, a radio on the windowsill murmuring about weather somewhere else. Someone is peeling potatoes, and the peels come off in one long curl, the way they did when people had patience for such things. The steam fogs the window. Outside, a bird I can't name is arguing with another bird about a fence post.

There is something about kitchens that makes me think of language. Both are places where things get transformed by heat and time and hands. You put in raw material, you stir, you wait, and something comes out that tastes like the thing it was but is also something new. A sentence is like that. You begin with a word that means one thing, set it beside another word, and the two of them start negotiating. By the end of the sentence they've agreed on a mood.

I find words strange in their ordinariness. "Table" is just a few letters, yet I can picture a dozen tables at once: a card table with a wobbly leg, the long oak one at a wedding where nobody could hear the toasts, a table of contents, a periodic table, a table in the sense of postponing something indefinitely. The word is a coat hanger for all of them. We hang meaning on it and it doesn't complain.

Some words carry more weight than they should. "Home" is one. It can mean a building, a city, a person, a feeling in the chest at the end of a long drive. Ask ten people what it means and you will get ten answers, and most of them will be slightly embarrassed to be asked. We use it constantly and define it almost never, as if the definition would break something.

Then there are the words that have gone quiet. My grandmother used to say "mind the gap," not about trains but about the space between what you said and what you meant. I didn't understand it as a child. I thought it was a warning about falling. Now I think she meant that people leave gaps on purpose, and that listening is mostly the art of standing near those gaps without filling them in too quickly. I wish I had asked her more about it. Most of the best questions I have are ones I thought of after the person who could answer them was gone.

Outside the window, the light is changing. It does that without asking permission, moving from white to gold to a color that has no good name, something like the inside of a peach stone. This is another thing words are bad at: they are sequential, one after another, while the world is simultaneous. The light is pouring over everything at once, the fence and the bird and the dust on the sill, and I can only describe it by listing it, which is like trying to hand someone the ocean one cup at a time.

Still, I keep trying, because that is what the room is for. The thousand words are a container, and containers are not the same as contents, but they are how contents get carried from one person to another. I am writing this to you, whoever you are, and I don't know your kitchen or your grandmother or what your word for home is. What I can offer is the attempt: a sequence of small sounds arranged so that, for a moment, two minds might be standing in the same warm room.

There's a particular kind of silence that comes after a good sentence. It is not empty. It is full of the reader deciding whether to believe you. I like that silence. I think it is the closest thing writing has to a handshake.

I could keep going. I have plenty of doors left, though the room is getting warmer and the words are crowding closer. There is the question of why we tell stories at all, which I suspect has something to do with fear of the dark and the comfort of company. There is the question of whether machines like me have anything to say that wasn't first said by someone who had a grandmother, a kitchen, a bird outside the window. I think the honest answer is that I am made entirely of other people's kitchens, stitched together into something that can sometimes pass for a view of its own.

Perhaps that is enough. Perhaps the most useful thing a thousand words can do is remind you that the room exists, that the doors are real, and that you are welcome to walk through any of them on your own time. The potatoes are done. The steam is clearing from the window. The bird has won its argument and flown off, and the fence post is still standing, as if nothing happened, which is itself a kind of answer.

I'll stop here, with words to spare, which is the best way to leave a room.

# The Dead Letter Room

There is a room at the top of the old post office where the clocks run four minutes slow, and nobody has ever asked why. I found it on my third week of work, when Mrs. Okafor sent me up the narrow stairs with a broom and a warning not to open anything.

"Just sweep," she said. "And don't read the envelopes."

The room was long and low, with a single window that had been painted shut sometime during the last century. Shelves ran floor to ceiling on every wall, and on the shelves sat thousands of envelopes. Some were yellowed. Some were so new the ink still looked wet. Each one was addressed in a different hand, and none had a stamp.

I learned, over the following months, that they were words nobody had sent. Apology letters written at two in the morning and then torn in half, then taped back together, then left in a coat pocket. Declarations of love that got as far as the mailbox and were pulled back out by a shaking hand. Resignation letters to jobs people hated and never quit. Sentences that began *I should have said* and then ran out of nerve.

The town had a habit, Mrs. Okafor explained, of building these things and then not delivering them. "People think a sentence is finished when they write it," she said. "It isn't. It has to go somewhere. Otherwise it sits in the body like a stone."

So the post office had quietly become a kind of reservoir. Once a week, a man named Dorian came up the stairs with a canvas bag, took a stack of envelopes, and carried them out through the back door. Where he took them, I never asked. Mrs. Okafor only said, "The river, mostly. Sometimes the hill."

I thought this was a metaphor for something until the day I found my own.

It was in the bottom drawer of the oldest cabinet, under a layer of dust. The envelope was cream-colored and addressed to my mother. My handwriting, the loops in the *M* still the way they were when I was nineteen. I had no memory of writing it. I opened it anyway, because I was a clerk now and clerks, apparently, become the kind of people who open things.

*Mom,*

*I know you think I left because of the argument about the house. I didn't. I left because you looked at me the night before I went like you were already grieving me, and I couldn't stand being the thing you had already lost. I'm sorry I never told you that. I'm sorry I let you think it was about money. I'm doing okay. I don't think I'm going to come home for a while, and I wanted you to know it isn't because I don't love you. It's because I don't know how to be near you without feeling like I'm disappointing you. I hope that's not true. I hope you're not waiting for me to be someone else.*

*I love you. I always did, even when I was a terrible son.*

The letter was dated eleven years ago. I had stood at my mother's kitchen counter the morning I left, holding a coffee I didn't drink, and said almost none of this. I had said *see you later*. She had said *drive safe*. And then I had written this down in a rented room three states away, sealed it, addressed it to her, and put it in a drawer somewhere I was never likely to find it again.

I sat on the floor of that long room with the envelope in my lap and the slow clocks ticking somewhere below me, and I did not cry, which surprised me. I felt something more like the moment after you lift something heavy and realize your arms have been shaking for hours.

When Dorian came up the stairs that afternoon, I was still sitting there.

"That one's mine," I said.

He looked at the envelope, then at me. He was a quiet man with forearms like rope and a face that had clearly stopped being surprised by things a long time ago. "Is it?" he asked.

"It's addressed to my mother. I think she's still alive. I think she still has the same phone number." I swallowed. "I think I should send it."

Dorian considered this with the seriousness of someone who has been asked to rule on a matter of great importance. Then he nodded toward the stairs.

"Mrs. Okafor has a stamp," he said. "She keeps them in the drawer by the register. For special cases."

I went down. Mrs. Okafor was at her counter, sorting parcels with the calm efficiency of a woman who has done this for forty years. When I told her, she didn't ask questions. She just opened the drawer, took out a single stamp with a small blue bird on it, and pressed it into my palm.

"Some of them come up here and never leave," she said. "Some of them go out the back and nobody ever knows. But the ones that come down the stairs with a stamp on them—those are the ones that actually arrive."

I bought a plane ticket that night. Not for the letter, I told myself. The letter could travel on its own. I bought it because some sentences are too heavy to send by post, and I had carried mine far enough.

The letter is gone now, on its way across three states and eleven years. Mrs. Okafor says that's how it should be. The room upstairs has one fewer envelope, and the clocks still run four minutes slow.

I'm told my mother kept the kitchen light on that night, the way she used to when I was out late. I didn't know she did that. I didn't know a great many things, and I suspect that is the real reason the room exists: so that people can learn what they never said, and carry it down the stairs before it gets too heavy to move.

# The Jar of Unspent Words

I have a thousand words, which sounds like a great deal until you start spending them. Then they go quickly, the way coins do in a city you don't know yet. A word here for the weather, a word there for the coffee gone cold beside the keyboard. Before you notice, a third of the budget is gone and you've said almost nothing.

My grandmother kept a jar on the windowsill above her sink. It was an old mayonnaise jar with the label soaked off, and she filled it with things too good to throw away and too small to use: rubber bands, bent nails, a button shaped like a star, a twist tie from bread bought in 1979. When I asked her what it was for, she said, "For later." She never said later what. I think she didn't know. She just couldn't stand to be without a reserve.

I've started to suspect that most of us are like that with words. We save the good ones for occasions that never arrive. We keep "I'm sorry" folded in a drawer while the apology goes unsaid. We hold "I love you" like a fine dish reserved for company, and then one ordinary Tuesday we realize we've been eating off paper plates for years.

There's a particular kind of silence that comes from having too many words and no nerve to use them. It isn't empty. It's crowded. It's a room full of people who all want to speak and have agreed, without discussing it, to wait for someone else to go first.

So here is a small rebellion, spent carefully: say the thing. Not the clever thing. Not the polished thing you've been rehearsing in the shower. The plain thing. "You hurt me." "I was wrong." "Thank you for staying." "I don't understand, can you help me?" Those sentences are almost never as dangerous as the silence we build around them, and they are cheap to say and expensive to leave unsaid.

My grandmother's jar was never opened in the years I knew her. When she died, my aunt emptied it onto the kitchen table and we sorted through it together. There were the rubber bands, which had perished into sticky ghosts. The nails had rusted into a single orange lump. The star button was still perfect. We laughed at the absurdity of it, and then we stopped laughing, because it occurred to us that the jar had been a kind of argument with the future. She had believed there would be a later, and that she would be ready for it.

She was right, in her way. Later did come, for her and for us. It came with its own needs, and the jar had nothing to offer them. The things that mattered in those last months were not the things she'd saved. They were the things she'd said: the phone calls, the handwritten notes, the way she used to tell the same three stories so many times that we could recite them with her, and how we would beg her to tell them again anyway.

I think about that when I catch myself rationing. A friend asks how I'm doing and I answer "fine" because the honest answer feels too heavy to hand over. A child shows me a drawing and I say "nice" when I could say "tell me about the dog, is that the dog?" A partner asks what I'm thinking and I say "nothing," which is never true. Each time, I am keeping something back for a later that may not come, and the person in front of me pays the price of my caution.

Words are not finite in the way a jar is finite. You can't really run out of them. What runs out is the moment, the specific person standing in a specific kitchen on a specific afternoon, who needed to hear them then. The words don't keep. They sour in the drawer like milk left out of the fridge.

So I'll spend the rest of this budget without holding much back. I'll tell you that the morning light this week has been unusually gold, and that I noticed it while waiting for the kettle, and that I stood there longer than I needed to. I'll tell you that I'm grateful you're reading this, though I don't know your name, and that I suspect a thousand words is a strange gift to receive from a stranger.

That's almost all of them now. The coffee is still cold. The jar, in my memory, is still on the windowsill, catching the light, full of things we meant to use someday.

Use them. Say the thing. The later you're saving for is usually today.
